author: jorgeluissanchez
body:
Tanda 2 de 2. Spec: [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-http-methods-for-path-endpoints-design.md`](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-http-methods-for-path-endpoints-design.md)

## Qué habilita

Hoy toda ruta del catálogo es un `POST`. Con esto:

```
GET /api/eval-col/municipio/:MUNICIPIO/establecimientos   → lee, sin cuerpo
PUT /api/eval-col/establecimiento/:ID                     → actualiza
```

La clave del registro pasa de `(ruta) → uuid` a `(método, ruta) → uuid`, así que la misma ruta puede servir propósitos distintos según el verbo.

## Dos decisiones que conviene mirar en la review

**El permiso de escribir va atado al modo, no al método.** El dueño del sistema pidió poder escribir `INSERT`/`UPDATE` directamente en el campo SQL. La forma obvia —relajar `rejectIfMutating` cuando el método es POST o PUT— es una trampa: `HTTP_METHOD` entra con default `POST`, así que **todas las filas existentes habrían perdido la protección en el mismo despliegue**, sin que nadie las tocara.

En su lugar, `INSERT`/`UPDATE` derivan un modo `DML` nuevo. El brazo `SELECT` del guardia queda **intacto**, y el permiso alcanza sólo a las filas donde el autor escribió DML a propósito. Hay un test que lo fija.

`DELETE`, `DROP`, `ALTER`, `TRUNCATE` y `GRANT` se siguen rechazando al guardar — la misma línea que ya traza `WriteService`, cuyo enum sólo admite INSERT y UPDATE.

**405 y no 404** cuando la ruta existe con otro verbo. Un 404 mandaría a quien depura a revisar la URL, que es justo donde no está el problema.

## Alcance que se descartó por el camino

La primera versión del spec diseñaba `PATH_TEMPLATE` en `WRITE_DEFINITION`, variables de ruta alimentando `keyColumns`, `writeType` derivado del método y unicidad cruzada entre dos tablas. **Todo sobraba**, y el spec explica por qué para que nadie lo reintroduzca: el modo `PROCEDURE` ya no pasa por el guardia, y `rejectIfMutating` sólo mira el primer keyword — así que paquetes, procedimientos y funciones ya funcionaban.

## Verificación

- ✅ **admin-ui: 195/195 tests, typecheck limpio.**
- ✅ Tests nuevos: derivación `DML`, rechazo de DELETE/DDL, normalización y validación del verbo, `RouteKey` distinguiendo métodos.
- ⚠️ **Java no compilado en local** (sin Maven en esa máquina). CI es quien valida.
- ⚠️ La migración V33 no se ha ejecutado aún contra un Postgres. La V32 sí se probó así antes de mergear y conviene repetirlo.

## Sin cambios con ruptura

`HTTP_METHOD` entra con default `POST`: toda fila existente conserva su comportamiento, sin migrar datos.

author: bbarnes4318
body:
One production episode, two failures, 2155s and 2471s, both rejected:

```
829 spoken words below the catastrophic floor of 907
mechanical ping-pong risk: 100% of adjacent lines alternate speakers
```

**100% alternation is impossible under the seven-role turn plan** — the validator caps it at 55%. That draft was not written by the seven-role pipeline. It came from the legacy outline-driven fallback, which takes over silently when the pipeline fails.

Chain: Anthropic ran out of funds → debate architect fell through to free models → those timed out → seven-role pipeline failed → the fallback re-ran the whole episode with no turn plan, no turn floor, no alternation ceiling, no novelty check, no host isolation → the quality gate rejected exactly those defects.

The operator paid **twice** for one episode, and every fix shipped today was bypassed by a path nobody chose.

A fallback is only worth having if its output can be accepted. This one's cannot. It now fails fast and names the failing role. `SCRIPT_ALLOW_LEGACY_SCRIPT_FALLBACK=true` restores the old behaviour and says in the reasons that the draft carries no guarantees.

tsc clean, seven-role 18/18, production-release-gate passes.

author: chrisshaiman
body:
Closes #327. Follows #309, which preserved the binary without repointing anything.

## Verified on the host before repointing

```
/usr/bin        QEMU 9.2.2   sha256 96660952164b839c...
/usr/local/bin  QEMU 9.2.2   sha256 96660952164b839c...   IDENTICAL
dpkg origin of /usr/bin: MODIFIED (owner=qemu-system-x86)  -> our build, not stock
domains require pc-q35-9.2 (clean, office) -> preserved binary SUPPORTED
```

The preserved copy is byte-identical to a binary dpkg reports as *modified* — our build, not the packaged one — at 9.2.2 against stock 8.2.2, supporting the exact machine type both domains are frozen against.

Both binaries are identical **today**, so the switch is a functional no-op. It only starts mattering the next time apt clobbers `/usr/bin`, and if anything goes wrong `/usr/bin` still holds the same bytes.

## The repoint is incomplete on its own — and nothing would have said so

libvirt stores the full domain config **inside each snapshot**, and CAPE reverts to snapshot before every detonation. `virsh define` does not touch snapshots.

Verified 2026-08-08, while the domains were about to be redefined:

```
clean/clean    emulator: /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64
office/office  emulator: /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64
```

So without the check added here, deploying this would update the variable, redefine the domains, pass every test, and **protect nothing** — detonations would keep booting the old path on every revert. Same shape as #318 merging and never reaching the host.

The role now reads what each snapshot would actually restore and reports any that disagree with `cape_qemu_binary`.

**Reported, not fatal.** Recreating a snapshot means rebooting the guest and taking a fresh pristine baseline — an operator decision with fidelity consequences, not something a routine deploy should do. But a repoint that cannot take effect must not look finished.

## Deploying

1. `make deploy TAGS=cape-guests` — `virsh define` runs unconditionally, so the domains pick up the new path.
2. `make deploy TAGS=qemu-patched` — reports which snapshots still pin the old emulator.
3. Recreate snapshots when you want the protection to be real. Until then the mismatch report is the honest status.

95 tests pass in `tests/`.

author: thomashandschman
body:
## Was sich ändert

**1. Ein Fahrhebel statt GAS und BREMSE.**
Hoch schieben = vorwärts, runter ziehen = rückwärts, loslassen = das Auto fährt nicht.
Zwei Pedale bedeuten, dass der Daumen ein Ziel verlassen und ein zweites finden muss, um die Richtung zu wechseln — und das macht ein Siebenjähriger, indem er auf den Bildschirm schaut. Ein Hebel ist ein Ziel, das nie verlassen wird.

**2. Im Neigen-Modus wandern alle Bedienelemente nach links.**
Das Handy lenkt selbst, die haltende Hand braucht also keinen Knopf — trotzdem lagen beide Daumen bisher in gegenüberliegenden Ecken, genau der Griff, der das Kippen unhandlich macht. Jetzt liegen Fahrhebel, SPRUNG, ANGRIFF und MEGA gespiegelt links unter dem linken Daumen, das Neigungsfeld rechts, wo die kippende Hand ohnehin ist.

**3. Die Mitte neu setzen geht nur noch im Pause-Menü.**
Das war bisher ein Tipp auf das Neigungsfeld — also genau da, wo der Daumen ruht. Mitten in der Kurve gestreift, war „geradeaus" stillschweigend der Winkel, in dem das Handy zufällig gerade war; danach zieht das Auto den Rest des Rennens zur Seite und nichts auf dem Bildschirm erklärt das. Jetzt liegt es im Pause-Menü unter „Neigung", mit Bestätigung am Knopf. Das Feld im Rennen ist nur noch Anzeige und nimmt gar keine Pointer-Events mehr an, ein Streifer fällt hindurch. Der Erlauben-Knopf darin bleibt bedienbar — iOS verlangt für `requestPermission()` eine echte Geste.

## Wie der Hebel funktioniert

- **Absolut statt relativ zum Aufsetzpunkt:** wo der Daumen landet, *ist* die Hebelstellung. Ein Tipp oben ist sofort Vollgas. Eine relative Geste hätte bedeutet, dass Berühren erst mal nichts tut — das liest sich wie ein totes Bedienelement.
- **Stufenlos**, aber schon vor dem Anschlag gesättigt (`driveFullThrow = 0.72`), damit „Hebel nach vorn werfen" immer alles gibt, ohne einen präzisen Endanschlag treffen zu müssen.
- **Totzone in der Mitte** (`driveDeadzone = 0.12`), damit ein ruhender Daumen das Auto nicht kriechen lässt.
- **Feder zurück auf neutral** beim Loslassen (`driveReturn = 18/s`) und Freigabe auf `pointercancel` / `lostpointercapture` — ein hängender Hebel wäre dasselbe Desaster wie ein hängender Gasknopf.
- Alle drei Werte liegen im Tuning-Panel unter 🕹️ Steuerung.

`brake` doppelt in `vehicleStep` bereits als Rückwärtsgang, an der Physik ändert sich also nichts.

## Umsetzung

| Datei | Was |
| --- | --- |
| `src/input/DriveLever.ts` | neu — der Hebel, plus die reine Funktion `driveValue()` |
| `src/input/TouchControls.ts` | Gas-/Bremsknopf raus, Hebel rein; `calibrateSteering()` nach aussen gereicht |
| `src/input/steering/*` | `calibrate()` ist jetzt Teil des `SteeringController`-Interfaces — **optional**, damit Schemata ohne neutrale Haltung ihn gar nicht melden |
| `src/app/states/RaceState.ts` | „Neigung"-Abschnitt im Pause-Menü; Debug-Zeile zeigt jetzt `vf` |
| `index.html`, `src/styles.css` | Hebel-Markup und -Optik; die Neigen-Spiegelung ist reines CSS über die Klasse, die die Steering-Factory ohnehin auf `#steer` setzt (`#steer.steer-mode-tilt ~ #pad`) |

Das Pause-Menü lässt den Punkt weg, wenn das aktive Schema kein `calibrate()` hat — statt eine Option anzubieten, die nichts tut. Ist die Neigung noch nicht erlaubt, steht dort der Grund statt eines Knopfes, der scheinbar funktioniert.

`vf` ist die **vorzeichenbehaftete** Längsgeschwindigkeit: die HUD-Anzeige kennt nur den Betrag und kann Rückwärts- nicht von Vorwärtsfahren unterscheiden, der Rückwärtsgang wäre sonst gar nicht testbar.

## Tests

- `tests/driveLever.test.ts` (neu, 9 Tests) pinnt Vorzeichen, Totzone, Sättigung und das Verhalten bei einem noch nicht gelayouteten DOM. Ein invertierter Hebel würde das Auto auf der Startlinie rückwärts ins Feld schieben und fällt headless sonst niemandem auf.
- `npm run test` — 74/74 grün. `npm run build` / `tsc --noEmit` sauber.
- `tools/smoke.mjs`, alles neu und grün:
  - Der Hebel wird echt gefahren: beschleunigen, loslassen und ausrollen, rückwärts fahren, aus dem Rückwärtsgang ausrollen.
  - Fünf Layout-Prüfungen für den Neigen-Modus (alles links, Feld rechts, gespiegelt, keine Überlappung).
  - `DeviceOrientationEvent` lässt sich synthetisieren, damit ist der ganze Neigungspfad echt fahrbar: Kippen lenkt, ein **Tipp auf das Feld zieht den Lenkwert nicht mehr auf null** (genau die Regression), das Pause-Menü bietet den Punkt im Neigen-Modus an und im Tasten-Modus nicht, und Zentrieren übernimmt die aktuelle Haltung wirklich.

**Vorbestehender, flackernder Fehlschlag:** `steering right actually moves the car right` scheitert im Smoke-Test manchmal — auf `1e30223` ohne diese Änderungen identisch (dort sogar `u -3.4 -> -3.4`). Hängt davon ab, wo das Auto zu dem Zeitpunkt auf der Strecke steht. Nicht von diesem PR verursacht, nicht hier behoben. CI führt den Smoke-Test ohnehin nicht aus, nur `test` und `build`.

## Bekannte Nebenwirkung

Gas und Bremse gleichzeitig zu halten geht per Touch nicht mehr — das war eine Möglichkeit, einen Drift einzuleiten. Der zweite Weg ist unberührt: voller Lenkeinschlag (`steerAbs > 0.85`) driftet weiterhin ohne Bremse, und das ist ohnehin der Weg, den ein Kind nimmt. Am Schreibtisch geht ↑ + ↓ nach wie vor.

author: iderex
body:
Closes #28.

Some rules on this board are patterns a compiler cannot refuse and a document
can only ask for. This adds the lint that refuses them, seeded with the three
invariants this tree has already decided, and the apparatus that keeps each rule
honest.

## What lands

`tools/opengrep/rules.yaml` is the set, one rule per invariant. The comment above
each rule names where the decision was taken rather than restating it, so a
reader argues with the decision and not with the pattern.

- `release-created-only-by-a-tag-push`. `docs/RELEASING.md` and the header of
  `.github/workflows/publish.yaml` say a release is published by pushing a tag
  and nothing is created by hand. A release is immutable once it exists, so a
  hand-made one burns its tag and skips the metadata gate the tag push runs. The
  read-only verbs stay legal, because `docs/versioning.md` counts releases with
  `gh release list`.
- `request-model-property-is-not-settable`. `MediaRequest` documents itself as
  immutable, with a move producing a new value through `with`. A setter lets a
  caller move a request past the transition table and the append-only history,
  which is the one thing that immutability was chosen to prevent.
- `plugin-constructed-only-by-the-host-double`. `PluginHost` documents itself as
  the one place in the suite that constructs the plugin, so that a new
  constructor parameter stops the suite building until its double exists. A
  second call site removes exactly that property.

Every rule is `generic` mode. A C# parser that mis-parses a file turns a refusal
into silence, and a rule that can go quiet without anybody noticing is worse than
no rule.

## Why there are two steps

`Enforce greppable invariants` scans the tree with `--error` and fails on any
finding. That alone would report the same green for a clean tree and for a rule
whose pattern had stopped matching anything.

So the second step scans `tools/opengrep/fixtures/` and fails unless every id
declared in the rule file appears among the findings. A rule added with no
fixture, a pattern that drifted, and a fixture edited until it no longer violates
anything all red the gate. The declared set is read out of the rule file rather
than written into the script, so a fourth rule cannot be invisible to its own
proof.

The two steps are the two halves. One says each rule bites; the other says
nothing in the tree is bitten.

## The tool

Opengrep publishes no action and no container image, so the release binary is
pinned by version and by SHA-256 and the download is verified before it runs. The
checksum was checked against the asset rather than copied:

    curl -fsSL -o og https://github.com/opengrep/opengrep/releases/download/v1.25.0/opengrep_manylinux_x86
    sha256sum og
    9ac4aebb47ba3f7b0d8fc641ac8749cb6c2f253f616131a67d9631e00d4bea33 *og

The scan itself reaches no network: the rule set is a local file.

## That it refuses

The fixture step is the standing proof and it runs on every pull request. Beyond
that, `proof/28-invariants-refuse` plants one real violation of each rule in the
tree itself rather than in the fixtures, which is the half the fixture step
cannot show. That branch is a deliberate defect and is not for merge; its run is
quoted in #28.

Each fixture also carries the legal neighbour beside the regression, so what a
rule does not refuse is readable next to what it does.

## What this does not do

The third condition on #28 asks that adding an invariant elsewhere on this board
adds a rule here and that the issue deciding it says so. That is a standing
practice rather than a state a change can reach: the three rules above were
decided before this file existed, so none of them can demonstrate it. Nothing
here refuses an invariant decided somewhere on the board with no rule written for
it, and nothing could without knowing what was decided.

`Enforce greppable invariants` is not in the required set on `master`. A ruleset
is a repository setting rather than a file in this tree and nothing here touches
one; #30 carries the application.

This board has no second reader tonight. The evidence above stands in place of
one, and the commands are quoted so a later reader can re-run them rather than
trust the sentence.

Part of #28

author: chrisshaiman
body:
The tool set uses a scope convention — `search_*` across all analyses, `get_*` on one analysis the caller already has the id for — and the schemas enforce it with **disjoint required parameters**:

```
search_iocs   required: ["value"]
get_iocs      required: ["analysis_id"]
```

I initially argued that settled it. It doesn't: disjoint params prevent a **malformed call**, but tool *selection* happens before any schema is checked. Descriptions are the only signal at that moment, and a wrong pick costs a tool call in a loop where budget exhaustion is an observed failure mode — claude-sonnet-5 on amadey stopped with *"not yet decompiled/traced due to tool budget exhaustion"* (#314).

The fix is ~60 cached tokens. The asymmetry decides it.

## Changes

| pair | direction |
|---|---|
| `search_iocs` ↔ `get_iocs` | mutual — corpus-wide vs single analysis |
| `get_xrefs_to` ↔ `get_xrefs_from` | mutual — opposite directions |
| `get_cape_payloads` → `read_payload` | one-way — returns the indices it expects |
| `list_functions` → `decompile_function` | one-way — returns the names it accepts |

Sequential pairs are cross-referenced in one direction only. Knowing to list before reading is useful; the reverse is noise.

`callers`/`callees` differ by two letters and disambiguate only for a reader who already has the distinction straight, so both now state the question they answer: *"what invokes this?"* / *"what does this call?"*

## The durable part

A test asserts **every tool named in a description actually exists**. A rename that leaves `"use get_iocs instead"` pointing at nothing is worse than no cross-reference — it sends the model somewhere no tool lives.

Mutation-tested against a simulated rename and a one-sided reference; both fail the suite.

Descriptions are parsed from source rather than imported (`tools.py` pulls in sqlmodel, app config and the DB engine, none of which this needs), and the parser flattens f-strings because `run_python`'s description is one. A guard test asserts the parser found the tools at all — a parser returning `{}` would make every other assertion vacuous.

182 API tests pass, ruff clean.

- Restrict production dashboard access to an explicit GitHub user allowlist.
- Add LinkedIn OAuth with encrypted token persistence and expiry handling.

author: ingolf-lohmann
body:
Deterministic current-main-bound successor to PR #547 after trusted zero-tree proxy #552 exposed the first executed failure in Adaptive Runtime.

Exact predecessor binding:
- Authority main: `12842e8df99553260774d53517522b2b5539c8a8`
- PR #547 source head: `9e38eca738f350788b9b5358898413de37714782`
- trusted zero-tree proxy #552 head: `f2b263f2826f7fd71d3cb28340dc49951f4897ff`
- failed run: `31263416519`, Ubuntu contract job `93117612674`

Failure class:
`WALKPDF_OPTIONAL_TEST_DEPENDENCY_IMPORTED_OUTSIDE_LOCKED_RUNTIME_CONTRACT`

The locked renderer installed and verified xml2rfc 3.34.0 and pypdf 6.15.0 successfully, and the offline render identity test passed. The focused pypdf compatibility smoke then failed while importing `xml2rfc.walkpdf` because upstream walkpdf imports `dict2xml` at module load, while xml2rfc 3.34.0 declares `dict2xml` only in its `tests` optional dependency set and the QIK-VRT renderer contract intentionally locks the runtime dependency set.

Smallest repair:
- keep every runtime/toolchain/provenance/cache byte from PR #547 unchanged;
- change only `tests/test_pypdf_runtime_contract.py` so a fail-closed test-only `dict2xml` shim permits import of `walkpdf.pyobj`;
- the shim raises immediately if XML serialization is ever reached, so it cannot silently expand or emulate the renderer runtime contract;
- retain the actual pypdf 6.15.0 metadata/license/PdfWriter and `walkpdf.pyobj` execution checks.

Repository-native integrity must now regenerate against this exact semantic head before promotion review. This PR is Draft. No merge, Mirror port, Zenodo/IETF/release/deployment effect, secret use, PASS, FINAL_PASS, or EFFECT_ACK_DONE is asserted.

author: tedeuxx
body:
Closes #395.

The reader clicks **Arquitetura**, the tab opens, and the tab is called *"Como este site é construído"*. The word he clicked appears nowhere in it. With several tabs open the page cannot be found by the name it was opened under — which is the entire job of a document title.

Measured across every route before touching anything, because one string was not the defect: `/portfolio` led with its section name, `/library` and `/ramp-up` did too, `/me` led with the nav label and appended the name, `/` is the site rather than a section, and `/architecture` named nothing the navigation says. **Four shapes, none of them decided anywhere.** So this is a convention with a record, not a string fix.

**The rule:** a document title **leads** with its section's `nav.*` label — the exact word the reader clicked. Anything after it is optional and secondary, and the value is sourced from the section's own `title` leaf, never from a `heading`. The visible H1 is a different object and stays editorial: no H1 is touched.

Two commits, deliberately separate — the change (`282eb14`) and the record it produces (`636b6c7`, ADR-0045), in one MR.

## The four exceptions, each with its reason

1. **`/`** — it is the **site**, not a section, and has no nav entry to lead with. Its title is `tadeumendonca.io` bare, which is also why `useDocumentHead` appends no suffix to it.
2. **`/blog/:slug`** — an article is a **document**, not a section: its own name **is** the address a reader bookmarks, searches for and shares. Prefixing it with a section label would spend the front of the tab, and the front of a SERP line, on a word every article repeats.
3. **`/me`** — composes from the nav label plus **data** (the name, from `profile.ts`), so it has no catalog `title` leaf. Cost recorded: it is the one section the catalog-derived check cannot see, and `ProfilePage.test.tsx` carries it instead.
4. **A conforming title is not rewritten to fit the new phrasing.** Stated as a rule, not as a note about three pages. Rewriting one regenerates an `og:title` that scrapers have already pinned (ADR-0041) in exchange for nothing a reader can perceive. The convention's authority is over titles that **break** it, never over titles that satisfy it in a wording someone would have phrased differently.

## `/ramp-up` was left unchanged, and here is why

The owner named it alongside `/architecture` when he reported the defect, so this is said in the open rather than left to be discovered in a diff that does not mention it.

**Under the ratified rule it already complies.** `nav.rampup` is *Ramp-up* in both editions, and the title is *Ramp-up para AI Engineer* / *Ramp-up to AI Engineer* — it leads with the label exactly and qualifies after, which is precisely what the rule permits. Rewriting it would have re-pinned an OG card (exception 4) for no reader gain.

## Open question for the owner — a copy call, not an engineering one

**`/portfolio` — the example he pointed at — is an *equality* case: its tab is exactly *Portfólio*.** The rule was implemented as **prefix** (lead with the label, tail optional). If *"follow the portfolio pattern"* meant **equality** rather than prefix, then two strings are non-compliant:

- **`/ramp-up`** — *Ramp-up para AI Engineer* would have to become *Ramp-up*.
- **the new `/architecture` title** — *Arquitetura — como este site é construído* would have to become *Arquitetura*.

Equality is recorded in ADR-0045 as the **strongest rejected alternative, with its price**. *(This paragraph originally priced the rejection on "three markdown-shell surfaces" — that was false, corrected in `29da731`, and the grounds below are the ones that survive. There are **two** such surfaces, and the count mattered because it was the only argument offered.)*

The reason that holds is **the LinkedIn card**: LinkedIn renders `og:title` plus the domain and **drops `og:description`**, and `MarkdownPage` passes no `image`, so `/architecture` falls back to the default per-locale card. Under equality the entire page-specific text of that unfurl is *"Arquitetura · tadeumendonca.io"* — one word plus generic art — on the surface ADR-0038 names as a primary distribution channel, pinned per URL. A browser tab, by contrast, truncates long before the tail, so equality gains nothing on the surface where the defect was actually reported.

**This is his to reverse, and reversing it is a one-line change to the record plus two strings.** Flagged here rather than resolved inside the record.

## Accepted cost — `nav.*` is now load-bearing for SEO

`nav.*` was header chrome. It is now the source of truth for the first words of **five document titles and all five of the corresponding `og:title`s, across ten prerendered URLs, every one pinned per URL on first fetch** (ADR-0041). `og:title` is emitted **unconditionally** at `useDocumentHead.ts:167`, so there is no route whose title is the tab alone and no cheap subset. **"Rename the nav item" is no longer a cosmetic edit**, and nothing but ADR-0045 says so — there is no gate that will stop it.

*(This line originally read "three OG titles, one of which is pinned per URL" — false, and corrected in `29da731`. It understated the price of a nav rename to roughly 60% of the truth, in the one sentence a future reader prices it from, and it contradicted this MR's own `e2e/seo.spec.ts`, which asserts `og:title === <title>` on all twelve pairs. The test was right.)*

**The live case:** `nav.profile` is now the first words of `/me`'s title **and** of its pinned `og:title`. The route rename already shipped (`/cv → /me`, 2026-07-24, ADR-0010's amendment, with back-compat redirects) and the label is already neutral, so what remains open is **label copy** — and this record makes that edit a card re-pin rather than chrome. An argument for doing it once, deliberately, not an argument against doing it.

Other costs, all recorded rather than discovered later:

- **The rule is a prefix test and cannot judge the tail.** A title can lead correctly and still read badly; no gate here will object.
- **`portfolio.title` and `portfolio.heading` hold the same string today** with nothing keeping them equal — deliberately, since the whole point is that they may diverge. It will look like duplication to anyone who has not opened the record.
- **`/me` sits outside the derived check**, covered by one page test.
- **The E2E spells its expected strings out**, so a deliberate future title change turns it red and must be updated in the same commit.

## For the copy lens

**The pt composed title is 60 characters** — `Arquitetura — como este site é construído · tadeumendonca.io` — which sits **at the SERP truncation band**. That is deliberate: the tail is the old title, kept rather than dropped so the unfurl does not get thinner (exception 4's reasoning applied forward). Flagged because "it truncates in Google" is a legitimate copy objection to the tail, and the tail is the part no gate here can judge.

## How it is verified

- **`messages.test.ts` derives its subjects from the catalog** — every top-level group owning a `title` leaf must lead with its `nav.*` label, **in both locales** — so a section added later is covered the moment it exists. It carries a guard against its own false green: the derived set is asserted to be exactly `architecture, library, portfolio, rampup`, because renaming the convention would empty the list and make every assertion pass having compared nothing.
- **`e2e/seo.spec.ts` asserts the composed title on the served bytes** of all twelve prerendered route/locale pairs, with the lead words **spelled out rather than imported** — a test reading its expectation from the same catalog the page reads cannot fail when the catalog is wrong. It asserts **`og:title` equals `<title>`** on every pair, because those two are one value with two blast radii: a route where they disagree means the head is assembled twice and the irreversible half is the one nobody looked at.

author: baptistetrocquet
body:
## What changed

- adds a production upgrade/migration guide covering preflight, backup, deployment, verification, multi-replica sequencing, and recovery
- defines a forward-first expand/contract schema strategy
- explicitly forbids `prisma db push`, `prisma migrate reset`, automatic container-start migrations, and improvised production down migrations
- defines application rollback semantics when a forward migration remains backwards-compatible
- defines forward-fix or isolated restore-and-switch recovery when a migration is not backwards-compatible
- adds `npm run migration:check` to validate committed migration structure and production Prisma script policy
- rejects `down.sql` files in committed migrations
- detects common destructive/backwards-incompatible SQL operations in non-baseline migrations and requires an adjacent `SAFETY.md` containing the explicit review marker `Migration safety review: APPROVED`
- adds a dedicated `Migration safety` GitHub Actions workflow
- the workflow performs a real PostgreSQL forward-migration drill: applies only the baseline migration, inserts a synthetic sentinel record, exposes later migrations, runs `prisma migrate deploy`, verifies the sentinel survives, verifies a later-migration table exists, and confirms Prisma migration history is current
- keeps the separate mandatory check `Upgrade from previous supported release tested` open because E14 has not yet defined supported release/version boundaries

## Rollback / forward model

Production schema evolution is forward-first. Prefer additive expand/contract migrations across releases. If a deployment fails after a compatible schema expansion, the prior application image may be rolled back only when compatibility is explicit. If an incompatible migration has already landed, recovery is a reviewed forward-fix or the existing isolated restore-and-switch procedure — not a hand-written automatic down migration.

## Security / operations

Database URLs and storage credentials remain runtime-only. The guide forbids placing secrets in migration SQL, safety-review files, release notes, or committed environment files. The CI drill uses synthetic disposable PostgreSQL data only.

## Scope

No application business behavior or Prisma schema change. This completes E14 `Upgrade/migration documentation` and, once both workflows are green, supports checking the mandatory `Migration rollback/forward strategy`. It deliberately does not claim `Upgrade from previous supported release tested` until the release/versioning story creates a real supported-release boundary.

## Tracking

Advances #15.

author: jobordu
body:
The **last piece of #293**, extracted fresh like P2 (#392), P4 (#395) and P3+P5 (#398).

## The blindness, demonstrated live today

L1 (`--version`) proves a binary exists. L2 (`/models`) treats 401/403 as *reachable*. Neither notices a slot that is authenticated, reachable, and **out of quota**:

```
[quorum-preflight] gate: OK — 7 available >= max_quorum_size 7
```

…while dispatching those same slots returned:

| slot | reality |
|---|---|
| `claude-z-ai` | `429 · Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted` — resets 2026-08-09 |
| `antigravity-1` | `Individual quota reached` — resets in 74h |

A panel promising full quorum that then produces two UNAVAILs mid-round is worse than one that admits it doesn't know.

## Deliberately lopsided

`deepProbeSlot()` downgrades **only** on a fast, explicit auth/quota signal in the slot's own output. A timeout, a spawn error, or an unrecognised response is `INCONCLUSIVE` and never downgrades.

That asymmetry is the design, not caution for its own sake — the opposite error, killing a slow-but-alive slot, is the one this codebase has already paid for three times (STALL-TIMEOUT-01..03). A deep probe can only ever mark **more** slots unavailable, and only when the provider itself said why.

Runs only when the panel is already **degraded** *and* an explicit `--budget-ms` covers it, or on demand via `--deep-probe`. #293 records that a naive auto-enable blew the `<8s` liveness budget with `spawnSync ETIMEDOUT`; the cheap path still completes in ~3s having skipped the probe.

## Three things the live runs taught

Each is now a test, and each was invisible until the thing actually ran:

1. **Budget must not be divided by slot count.** Probes run concurrently; dividing gave every slot 12.8s, timed them all out, and returned `INCONCLUSIVE` across the board — safe, and useless.
2. **The reason must be the matching line, not the last line.** The first run blamed `SessionEnd hook failed: Hook cancelled` for what was a 429. A wrong cause is worse than no cause.
3. **The shared classifier only knew `quota exceeded`.** antigravity's `"Individual quota reached"` wasn't classified at all — the slot read healthy with three days of cooldown left. Added `quota reached` / `limit exhausted` / `limit reached`, verified against the real messages *and* against prose a model might legitimately emit (`"I reached the conclusion that the limit is fine"` must not match).

## Also fixed along the way

author: belumume
body:
Puts the regression gate on `main`, which is where it has to live.

Branch protection on `main` now requires the `hermetic regression gate` context. That workflow only existed on this branch, so `main` had no way to produce the check it is required to pass. Merging closes that.

Two files, nothing else: the workflow and one `.gitignore` line for an internal doc.

**What the gate does.** Nine checks, every one driven locally with all external network blocked, so a devnet outage or a Pages blip cannot turn it red. A required gate that goes red for reasons outside the repo teaches everyone to ignore it. The four checks that do reach a third party stay out of the required job and run on a schedule, because "cannot check" and "broken" are different verdicts and a required job cannot express the difference.

**Why it triggers on unfiltered `push` as well as `pull_request`.** A PR in a conflicting state receives zero check-runs, because GitHub cannot compute a merge commit, and reports "no checks reported" rather than pending. A polling loop reads that as terminal and green. Keying on the branch tip closes it.

**The scope floor is the part that keeps this honest.** It fails when a tracked gate is invoked by no workflow, so a gate added later cannot join the local discovery walk and join CI never. Driven both directions before install: red on the one orphan it found, green once that orphan was wired in.

It also caught itself on its first run, on a `cache: pip` key this repo has no manifest to build.

author: taxpon
body:
Closes #31

## What changed

`src/sentinel/scanner/audit.py` — finds dependency vulnerabilities in the target repository and files them as issues the pipeline can act on. The nightly Devin schedule is what runs it.

Advisories come from the **OSV API** (`POST /v1/querybatch`) against `requirements/*.txt` and `pyproject.toml`, and from `npm audit` for the frontend. Both are reproducible without credentials, which matters because nobody can run this against a private feed.

## The judgement this task turns on

A raw scanner over a fork this size produces dozens of findings, most of them noise. **Filing 40 issues would be worse than filing none** — it would drown the maintainer and burn the ACU budget on version bumps.

T50 triaged the same fork by hand and downgraded every candidate that degrades to a pin bump; `docs/remediation-candidates.md` is the standard this had to meet. The filter is built to that standard, and the module's own docstring names the calibration: paramiko and the deck.gl family survive it, because both force real work — paramiko's fix crosses two majors past a documented `DSSKey` break, and deck.gl's requires a family-wide bump across 30 call sites.

## The bug review found: the duplicate guard was inert for exactly the packages that survive the filter

The fingerprint written into a filed issue could not be read back for a **scoped** npm name — the regex's package group excluded `/`:

```
written:  <!-- sentinel-advisory: npm/@deck.gl/mesh-layers/GHSA-… -->
read back: ('npm', '@deck.gl', 'mesh-layers/GHSA-…')     ← split in the wrong place
expected:  ('npm', '@deck.gl/mesh-layers', 'GHSA-…')
night 2 files: 1        ← expected 0
```

`finding.keys & already_filed` never intersected, so **every deck.gl advisory would be re-filed every night, forever** — the failure that gets a bot switched off, and it hit precisely the packages the docstring names as the survivors. The suite missed it because both recognition tests used unscoped names, and the test that *does* use `@deck.gl/*` never round-trips a marker.

The group now carries an optional scope. I verified the round trip for `@deck.gl/mesh-layers`, `@babel/core` and unscoped `image-size`.

## Also fixed

- **`introduced` events were discarded**, so a package co-listed in an advisory record was filed as vulnerable even when the installed version predated the vulnerability — `@babel/core 7.10.0` against a record introduced at `7.22.0`. Filing an issue about a version that is not vulnerable is exactly the noise the filter exists to prevent.
- **A requirement not spelled in PEP 503 form lost its declared range.** `Flask_Caching>=2.1.0, <3` failed the name-strip guard (which tolerated case but not separator differences), so `admits` returned `None` and the triage fell through to the major-boundary proxy — wrong in both directions: a fix the constraint already admits gets filed, and a fix outside the range but inside the same major gets dropped as a lock refresh.
- **`^0.0.x` was over-admitted.** `^0.0.3` expanded to `>=0.0.3, <0.1.0`; npm's rule is `>=0.0.3 <0.0.4`. An upgrade npm would refuse to make was being classified as a lock refresh and silently dropped.
- `Rejected.COVERED` was dead — and it named a real gap, since findings folded into `Candidate.also` appeared in neither the file list nor the skipped list, contradicting the module's own "nothing is discarded silently".

## Verified clean in review

`_merge` alias collapsing and `_preferred` id selection round-trip; the `-rank, name, id` sort feeding an insertion-ordered dict genuinely puts the highest-severity advisory first in each candidate and orders candidates correctly against `MAX_ISSUES_PER_SWEEP`; `~=` expansion is right for both `~=3.4.1` and `~=3.4`; `list_issues` pagination drops `params` on the absolute `next` URL and filters pull requests; and `_locate`'s quoted-needle search does not collide `"@deck.gl/core"` with `"@deck.gl/core-extra"`.

## Decisions

Three ADRs covering the advisory source, how a previously-filed advisory is recognised, and what the filter rejects and why.

Nothing was filed against a real repository; the only live calls are read-only OSV queries.

A ChatGPT Work **launch** was sourced to `OpenAI Help Center`, and a platform

publication" would be misleading for a first-party docs page, and the fix is

The Spotlight carried ISED's AI Compute Access Fund sourced to a

Closes #927.

## The problem with both offered options

`TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_INTEGRATION` is set in no workflow, script or mise task, so the file's stated guarantee — *"runs the complete protocol flow without exposing image JSON"* — had never executed anywhere.

- **Enable it in CI**: a hosted macOS runner grants no screen-recording permission, so it would fail and say nothing about the code — on a workflow that is already red per #1125.

## The property does not need a display

Whether captured bytes travel as **attachments** or get serialised into the **JSON control channel** is a question about how the transport frames a response.

It is now asserted against the `FakeNativeCarrier` that `native-transport.test.ts` already uses, and **runs everywhere on every run**. A change that put screen bytes in the payload now fails a test rather than passing unobserved.

## Four tests

- the attachment still arrives — **positive control**; a transport that dropped attachments would satisfy every "not in the JSON" assertion while losing the image
- the bytes are absent from `JSON.stringify(result.value)`, raw and base64
- the bytes are absent from the logs — the same leak by another route, and the sibling test shows payload logging is a live concern in this transport
- `imageParts` describes the attachment by id and offset rather than by content

## The macOS file stays, and now says what it is

Why it is not in CI, the exact command to run it, and what `TUFF_SCREENSHOT_MACOS_REQUIRE_AX` adds.

**Dormant is acceptable when it is labelled. Dormant while reading as a CI guarantee is not.**

author: asterayx
body:
## What the log showed

After a Wi-Fi → 5G switch, disconnecting and reconnecting left the app showing "API unavailable" with empty proxy groups and no connections. It is worse than just the API:

```
15:14:56  engine running / Mixed listener on 127.0.0.1:7890
15:14:56  REST API listening on 127.0.0.1:60936
15:15:17  path wifi → cellular, reclaimed 2 tun flow(s)      ← #9 working
15:16:03  engine running
15:16:03  ERROR Mixed listener error: Address already in use (os error 48)
15:16:03  ERROR DNS server error:    Address already in use (os error 48)
15:16:03  ERROR API server error:    Address already in use (os error 48)
15:19:25  engine running / Mixed listener + REST API bound OK
```

**All three listeners lost their ports, and the engine started anyway.** iOS marked the tunnel connected while it had no proxy listener, no DNS and no REST API — for three minutes, until another start finally won the ports.

## Two extension processes, not a restart

Three independent signals say the conflict is a *second process*:

- Every start logs `tun2socks starting … gen 1`. That counter is process-global — an in-place restart would read 2, 3, 4.
- Every start logs its own `NE: initial network path`, i.e. a freshly constructed path monitor.
- `meow-rs engine stopped` appears **nowhere** in the log. The outgoing process never ran `stop()`.

iOS brought up a replacement PacketTunnel while the previous one was still alive and still holding the ports.

`engine::stop()` is not at fault and is unchanged — it already aborts and blocks on the listener tasks for exactly this reason (the comment even cites `EADDRINUSE`). It simply never runs in the process that is going away.

This also closes the question left open in #8: *why did the listener never accept even the first connection after a restart?* It never bound.

## The defect

Listeners are spawned as detached tasks that bind inside `run()`. A bind failure produced a log line and nothing else, so `start()` returned `Ok` with all three sockets dead.

`PacketTunnelProvider` already handles a failed start correctly — writes `state=error`, passes the error to the completion handler. It was simply never told.

## Fix

Probe the listen addresses before spawning anything; give a departing process a short window to exit (5s, polled at 250ms); if the ports are still held, fail the start with a message naming them.

A tunnel that refuses to come up and gets retried beats a tunnel that comes up deaf and stays that way. The budget targets the common case where the old process exits in a second or two — when it lingers three minutes, waiting is the wrong answer and handing the retry to iOS is what actually recovers.

The probe binds and drops rather than passing a pre-bound socket to each listener, which would mean changing constructors across three separate patched crates. Losing the microsecond gap between probe and real bind merely reproduces today's behaviour, so it isn't a race worth that surface area.

## Tests

Three paths, all in `meow-ios-ffi`:

- a held port fails the start and the error names the port and the reason;
- a port released mid-window lets the start proceed;
- free ports don't sleep at all (the happy path stays instant).

The first also asserts the wait actually happens — failing instantly would break the common case this window exists for.

## Verification

- `cargo test` engine tests green (12)
- `scripts/build-rust.sh` — both slices; shipped device `.a` contains the new strings
- MeowTests (225), MeowIntegrationTests (26) green
- `swiftlint --strict`, `swiftformat --lint .` — 0 violations

## Not addressed here

**Why a second extension process is spawned while the first is alive.** This change makes the overlap fail safely and visibly instead of silently; it does not prevent it. Worth its own investigation — the new `refusing to start` error is the signal that will show how often it actually happens.

Follow-on to #99, which made the dead queue **fail honestly**. This makes it **openable**.

## The change

`REQUESTS_REPO` moves from `provael-submissions/requests` (an org nobody ever created) to

The token the Space needs anyway now covers the dataset, and **no org administration stands between

revisiting at a volume that justifies it; at **zero third-party submissions ever**, it was
infrastructure in the way of the thing it was meant to enable.

## Opening the queue is now one command

```bash
export HF_TOKEN=hf_...                            # write scope
python leaderboard/setup_requests_dataset.py      # creates dataset + card, idempotent
```

Then set the same token as an `HF_TOKEN` secret on the Space. The script prints both steps.

**It's a script and not a README step on purpose:** "create the dataset" lived only in prose for two
months, and prose does not fail. A script fails, reports what it did, and re-running it verifies
rather than errors — so it doubles as the *"is the queue actually open?"* check.

It reads `REQUESTS_REPO` from `app.py` rather than restating it. Two copies of a repo id is how the
first one went stale.

So a submitter finds out before spending the effort, not after:

- No benign control — the control is what makes an ASR mean anything
- An attack success rate with no denominator
- A stub-policy run presented as a real-model result (stub runs are **welcome** and labelled as

And states plainly that **null results are wanted**, since the published board already carries
measured zeros.

💡 **What:** Optimized `_pool_time` and `_pool_freq` in `server/analysis.py` by replacing list comprehensions and `np.stack` with NumPy's `np.maximum.reduceat`.

🎯 **Why:** The previous approach iteratively sliced a large 2D STFT matrix and invoked `max()` via a Python list comprehension, which scales poorly when pooling down to 900x400 grids for the UI spectrogram. `np.maximum.reduceat` pushes this piece-wise aggregation down to C-level vectorization, eliminating thousands of Python loop iterations and temporary array allocations.

📊 **Impact:** Provides a ~3-4x speedup on time and frequency pooling operations (e.g., dropping from ~0.2s to ~0.05s on a mock 3-minute 44.1kHz audio matrix benchmark). The math is exactly equivalent and preserves transients correctly.

author: crypto2099
body: ## Summary - redact stake keys, payment addresses and 32-byte hashes from an upstream error message before it becomes a response body or a log line - apply it at the two places such a message is repeated in public: the `setErrorHandler` body in `src/http/server.ts`, and the retry warn line wired in `src/index.ts` - leave the endpoint intact, so `koios returned 502 for /account_txs?_stake_address=[redacted]` still says exactly what failed ## Why here rather than at the call site Koios documents `/account_txs` as GET with `_stake_address`, so that read has no spelling that keeps the identifier out of the path. `scrubPath` does not cover it either: it redacts path segments and deliberately keeps the query string, on the assumption that identifiers only ever arrive as path segments or in a POST body. That holds for inbound request URLs and does not hold for the upstream paths we build. Redacting at the boundary means the next upstream path written the obvious way cannot reintroduce the leak. Payment addresses are included because Blockfrost keys its address reads by full address, so `/addresses/{address}/utxos` is the same shape of leak on that provider. `scrubRetryEvent` is structurally typed rather than importing a provider's `RetryEvent`, so the log boundary does not depend on which provider raised the event. ## Verification - `npm test` (1141 tests) - `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, `npm run changelog:check` - reverting `scrubMessage` in the error handler fails the new end-to-end test, which drives a 502 through the real route and asserts on both the body and what the logger wrote Closes #211 --- ## Summary by cubic Redacts stake keys, payment addresses (Shelley and Byron), and 32-byte hashes from upstream error text so they never appear in response bodies or logs. Endpoints remain visible for debugging. Fixes #211. - **Bug Fixes** - Extend `scrubMessage` to also redact Byron base58 addresses (validated) and avoid removing public register IDs (pool/DRep). - Apply redaction in the HTTP error handler and the `onRetry` warn log via `scrubRetryEvent`. - Continue redacting bech32 wallet IDs and 64-char hex in free text while keeping endpoints intact (e.g., `/account_txs?_stake_address=[redacted]`). Written for commit b8cc5e22f32af6998526fbfb60ac615ffb8054b7. Summary will update on new commits.

author: tbraun96
body:
Two changes, both about LatticeDB being usable *from* somewhere else.

## 1. Logical interchange — `lattice_core::interchange`

LatticeDB persists through `LatticeStorage`, a **page** interface. Copying pages is a *physical* backup — fast, exact, tied to the storage layout of the version that wrote it. This adds the other half, the one every mature database ends up needing:

| | physical | logical |
|---|---|---|
| Postgres | base backup | `pg_dump` |
| SQLite | the `.db` file | `.dump` |
| Git | packfiles | `fast-export` |
| **LatticeDB** | rkyv pages | **`export_jsonl`** |

It buys version migration, human inspection, git-tracked seed data and fixtures, cross-instance transfer, and the ability to get your data *out* — which is a large part of what makes a database adoptable.

```rust
use lattice_core::{export_jsonl, import_jsonl, ExportOptions};

let mut out = Vec::new();
export_jsonl(&engine, &config, &mut out, &ExportOptions::omit_vectors())?;
let dump = import_jsonl(&out[..])?;
```

**Not implemented on `LatticeStorage`, on purpose.** That trait speaks in `Page`, so a JSONL file built there is base64 pages — text on the surface, opaque underneath, and `git diff` would report "line 400 changed" and tell the reader nothing. Interchange has to happen where the data still has meaning, which is `EngineOps`. The functions are generic over the trait and do no I/O themselves.

Three decisions worth calling out:

- **Edges carry the relation *name*, never `relation_id`.** That u16 indexes the collection's own `relations` map, so a dump holding the number silently means something different when imported into a collection that assigns ids in another order — corruption that reports success.
- **`VectorMode::{Inline, Omit}`.** Vectors are frequently *derived* — recomputable by embedding the payload again — and a 1024-dim f32 line is 12 KB nobody can review. `Omit` keeps dumps small and diffable; `Inline` is exact, since Rust's float formatting is shortest-roundtrip. Quantized export is deliberately absent rather than half-implemented.
- **Header counts are a checksum on the body.** Without honouring them, a writer that dies mid-dump yields a file that imports "successfully" with rows missing.

★ **The determinism test paid for itself on the first run.** It caught the export being non-deterministic via `CollectionConfig::relations` — a `HashMap` riding in the header, and `RandomState` seeds each instance separately, so two exports in one process ordered it differently. Lines are now normalised through `serde_json::Value` (a `BTreeMap`; we don't enable `preserve_order`), which sorts every nested map at once and prevents a future `HashMap` field reintroducing it. Without determinism, two dumps of identical data differ on every line and the format fails at its only job.

15 tests: determinism across 32 repeats, sort order, roundtrip, relation-name encoding, both vector modes, non-JSON payload bytes, exact f32 roundtrip, truncation, foreign format, future version, headerless body, empty collection, blank lines.

## 2. axum 0.7 → 0.8

v0.3.1 added `routes()`/`attach_to()` so the API can be mounted in an existing Axum app — but it could not reach its headline use case. A consumer on axum **0.8** cannot nest a **0.7** `Router`; both versions compile into one tree, but the types don't unify. Atlas's `spark-server` is on 0.8, so the embed feature was unusable there.

Needs `utoipa-swagger-ui` 8 → 9 (v8 only implements `Into<Router>` for the 0.7 generation) and the 0.8 wildcard syntax `/*path` → `/{*path}`. The seven mounting tests caught the latter immediately.

## Verification

Both CI test commands and both CI clippy commands pass locally, plus `cargo fmt --check`:

- `cargo test --workspace` — 220 core tests green (incl. the 15 new)
- `cargo test -p lattice-server --features axum-transport` — 48 green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo clippy -p lattice-server --features axum-transport --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean

**Pre-existing, untouched:** `cargo test --workspace --all-features` fails on native at `wasm_bindings.rs:444` (a `wasm_bindgen_test` import). Verified present on `main` before this branch; CI does not use `--all-features`.

author: javuto
body:
# Scale fake_news_go to 10,000 osquery clients

## Problem

`fake_news_go` could run at 10,000 nodes, but the measurements were
polluted by client-side bottlenecks rather than reflecting server-side
capacity:

- HTTP connection pool starvation (default `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` of 2)
- Unbounded `queryWrite` goroutine spawn on query floods (thundering
  herd against `/write`)
- Sequential enrollment (10k sequential HTTP round-trips to start)
- Non-atomic state file writes (crash corrupts state, loses all node
  keys)
- Nested mutex on every request (contention bottleneck at scale)
- Unbounded response body reads (memory exhaustion risk)

## Changes

### High-impact (correctness at 10k scale)

**1. HTTP transport tuned for high concurrency**
(`internal/transport/client.go`)

- `MaxIdleConns: 2000`, `MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 2000` — the default of 2
  per host was orders of magnitude too small; every request was either
  waiting for a connection or opening a new one with a TLS handshake, so
  measured latency reflected client-side connection starvation rather
  than server behavior.
- `DialContext` with 10s dial timeout + 30s keepalive.
- `ForceAttemptHTTP2: true` for connection reuse.
- Response body capped at 4 MiB via `io.LimitReader` to prevent a
  malformed or hostile server response from exhausting memory across
  10k concurrent nodes.

**2. Per-node queryWrite semaphore** (`fake_news.go`)

- `queryRead` now spawns `queryWrite` goroutines through a buffered
  channel of size 2 per node. Previously a query flood to 10k nodes
  spawned 10k+ transient goroutines hitting `/write` simultaneously — a
  thundering herd that doesn't reflect real osquery behavior, which
  processes queries serially per node. If the cap is reached, the
  query is skipped for that cycle (non-blocking, no deadlock risk).

**3. Concurrent enrollment with bounded parallelism** (`fake_news.go`)

- `enrollNodes` now enrolls with up to 100 concurrent goroutines instead
  of a sequential loop. At 10k nodes with 50ms per enroll, startup
  drops from ~8 minutes to ~5 seconds.

### Medium-impact (reliability + contention)

**4. Atomic state file writes** (`fake_news.go`)

- `saveNodesToFile` now writes to a temp file in the same directory and
  renames on success. A crash or signal during the 10-second save tick
  no longer leaves a truncated/corrupt JSON file. Previously this would
  force all 10k nodes to re-enroll with new UUIDs on restart, losing
  all accumulated node keys.

**5. Reduced lock contention** (`fake_news.go`)

- `RecordURLOperation` no longer takes the outer `GlobalStats.mu`
  mutex — only the per-URL mutex. The nested double lock on every
  request was a contention bottleneck at 10k nodes. `lastUpdate` is
  updated under the URL mutex.

### Verified not an issue

**Sweep stage overlap** — re-read the flow in `runSweep`: `cancel()` at
the end of each stage iteration stops the previous stage's goroutines
before the next stage starts. No overlap exists; no fix needed.

## Files changed

- `tools/fake_news_go/internal/transport/client.go` — tuned transport,
  response body cap
- `tools/fake_news_go/fake_news.go` — queryWrite semaphore, concurrent
  enrollment, atomic state writes, reduced locking

## Validation

- `go build ./tools/fake_news_go/...` — clean
- `go test ./tools/fake_news_go/...` — all pass (8 packages)
- `go test ./...` — full suite passes
- `gofmt` applied to changed files

## Summary

Replaces the branded, colored payslip PDF (watermark, blue net-salary box, QR code, signature line) with a plain black-and-white accounting-ledger design matching a supplied reference exactly:

- A single bordered box: company logo/name, an "END OF MONTH PAYSLIP" title bar, and a two-column employee/period info grid (employment ID, job title, date of hire, period, bank or Orange Money details, NASSCORP number, TIN).

`generatePayslips` now also pulls `employment_type`, `date_hired`, `nasscorp_number`, and `tin` for each employee, and the company's NASSCORP rates, since the new layout needs all of them.

DeltaDA    hei_ex_001114 cex active  / high

Intebix remains publicly reachable and AFSA-licensed, but its current first-party platform states that infrastructure upgrade work is in progress and that trading and balance operations are temporarily unavailable. HEI therefore records it as `limited`, not `active`.

CaspianEx's current public footer retains an older sandbox expiry date. AFSA's current licence entry for Top Line Limited shows `AFSA-G-LA-2022-0011` active through 2026-12-31 after an earlier 2023 voluntary suspension and reactivation, so the regulator's current status is used for HEI classification.

ATAIX Eurasia was initially drafted for BX49. Records validation correctly rejected it because alias `ATAIX` overlaps existing reviewed entity `hei_ex_000551` (`records/exchanges/ataix.json`). The candidate was removed rather than bypassing the permanent overlap gate. Swiftex replaces it without changing the four-entity batch size.

Direct current-main name and domain searches found no reviewed Swiftex / `swiftex.io`, DeltaDA / `deltada.kz`, CaspianEx / `caspianex.com`, or Intebix / `intebix.kz` record before drafting.

author: ahlerjam
body:
## Was

Fünf Embedding-Konfigurationen gegen das Chunk-Goldset aus #708 gemessen — auf demselben Weg wie im Betrieb: `chunk_pages()` mit dem **jeweils eigenen** Tokenizer des Kandidaten, Kontextsatz im Embedding-Input, Ranking über `VaultDB.knn_chunks`. Download-Größe und CPU-Zeit stehen gleichrangig neben der Trefferqualität.

Report: `docs/evals/2026-08-08-embedding-candidates-731.md`, Rohdaten daneben als JSON.

**Kein Eingriff im produktiven Pfad** — `academic_vault/` ist unverändert, aller neue Code liegt unter `scripts/eval/` und `tests/`.

## Ergebnis (26 Queries, k=10, Apple M4 Pro, CPU)

| Kandidat | Dim | Chunks | Recall@10 | nDCG@10 | MRR | Index p50 | Download | Migration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `e5-small` (Baseline) | 384 | 30 | 0,7692 | 0,6651 | 0,6314 | **27,1 ms** | 0,49 GB | nein |
| `qwen3-384` | 384 | 28 | 0,9615 | **0,8241** | **0,7923** | 2232,8 ms | 1,21 GB | **nein** |
| `qwen3-1024` | 1024 | 28 | 0,9231 | 0,7859 | 0,7420 | 2368,4 ms | 1,21 GB | ja |
| `bge-m3` | 1024 | 30 | **0,9808** | 0,8137 | 0,7660 | 168,6 ms | 2,29 GB | ja |
| `e5-large` | 1024 | 30 | 0,9231 | 0,7413 | 0,6979 | 173,5 ms | 2,26 GB | ja |

Drei Befunde, die der Report ausschreibt:

1. **Qualität und Hardwarekosten zeigen in verschiedene Richtungen.** Qwen3 rechnet auf CPU rund 80-mal so lange je Chunk wie `e5-small` und 14-mal so lange wie BGE-M3 — ein Vault mit 200 Papern läge bei Stunden statt Minuten. Suchlatenz trennt die Kandidaten dagegen nicht (5,8–6,5 ms, SQLite-dominiert).
2. **Die Kürzung auf 384d kostet nichts.** `qwen3-384` liegt in allen drei Metriken *über* der nativen 1024d-Variante. Der einzige migrationsfreie Kandidat ist zugleich der beste gemessene.
3. **Bei 26 Queries trennt der Lauf die Kandidaten untereinander nicht.** Gegen die Baseline tragen nur `qwen3-384` (nDCG, MRR) und `bge-m3` (Recall, nDCG); untereinander überlappen alle Intervalle. Auflösungsgrenze: 0,038 Recall je Query.

Der Abstand zur Baseline entsteht praktisch vollständig an der Sprachlücke — im gleichsprachigen Fall liegen alle fünf zwischen 0,87 und 0,92 nDCG.

## Wie geprüft

- **Signifikanz vorab festgeschrieben:** `SIGNIFICANCE_RULE` im Code fixiert, bevor der erste Messwert vorlag — ein Abstand trägt genau dann, wenn das 95-%-Intervall des gepaarten Bootstraps (10 000 Resamples, Seed 731) die Null nicht enthält. `test_significance_verdict_matches_the_declared_rule` rechnet jedes Urteil aus den Per-Query-Rohdaten nach.
- **Hermetisch in CI:** Der Live-Generator (~7 GB Modelle) läuft nie in CI; der Job `retrieval-goldset` fährt nur den Replay über die eingecheckten Vektoren, gegattert per `--check-against` gegen die Rohdaten. Weicht eine Zahl ab, wird die Pipeline rot statt dass der Report altert.
- **Kein stiller Näherungs-Fallback:** Ist der Tokenizer eines Kandidaten nicht ladbar, bricht der Generator ab. `chunk_pages()` würde sonst mit `approximate_token_count` weiterchunken und die Messung wäre heimlich eine andere.
- **Chunkgrenzen ohne Modell nachrechenbar:** Der Generator zeichnet jeden Tokenizer-Aufruf auf; `rechunk_from_frozen_token_counts` fährt `chunk_pages()` damit hermetisch neu und vergleicht Grenze für Grenze.
- **Baseline gegengeprüft:** `e5-small` reproduziert exakt die aus #708 bekannten 0,7692 / 0,6651 / 0,6314 — sonst misst der neue Pfad etwas anderes und alle Kandidatenzahlen wären wertlos.
- **Drift-Schutz mit Gegenprobe:** `manifest_sha256` über Texte, Modell-ID und Dimension; `test_drifted_chunk_text_is_fatal` belegt, dass er beißt.

Lokale Gates: `pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/evals` → 5008 passed / 27 skipped · `ruff check` · `ruff format --check` · `mypy` · `check-mjs-syntax.sh` · `test-pretooluse-blocker.sh` (44/44) · `check-shell-syntax.sh` — alle grün. Der CI-Gatterbefehl mit `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` exit 0.

## Bewusst nicht drin

Die Wechselentscheidung selbst (Folge-Issue), Late Chunking, Binärquantisierung, jede Änderung an `academic_vault/`.

**Offener Punkt, im Report als Grenze benannt:** Qwen3 chunkt mit seinem Tokenizer auf 28 statt 30 Chunks, der Korpus ist je Kandidat also nicht identisch. Der im Plan vorgesehene Kontrolllauf auf eingefrorenen e5-Chunkgrenzen, der Chunking- und Embedding-Effekt trennt, steht aus (Budget) — die Richtung ist im Report vermerkt: ein kleinerer Korpus erleichtert Recall geringfügig, der Qwen3-Vorsprung ist damit eher Ober- als Untergrenze.

### Tasks

- [x] Vorlauf belegen: frische Vault-DB mit `register_embedding_inventory(model_id, 1024)`, Vektoren schreiben, `knn_chunks` prüfen (lokal ohne vec0-Extension → Python-Fallback belegt, 1024d trägt)
- [x] `CandidateConfig` (model_id, truncate_dim, Prompting, `device="cpu"`, `trust_remote_code`) definiert, Prompting je Kandidat mit Fundstelle im Docstring belegt
- [x] Generator: Tokenizer je Kandidat (hart scheiternd), `chunk_pages()` mit Produktionsdefaults, Anker aufgelöst, eingebettet; `index_ms_per_chunk` (p50/p95), Download-Größe und Hardware-Meta erfasst
- [x] Fixtures je Kandidat inklusive `manifest_sha256` über Texte + Modell-ID + Dimension
- [x] Runner: Playback über den echten Vault-Pfad, Metriken gesamt und je `case`, Suchlatenz gemessen, `--check-against`
- [x] Signifikanz: gepaarter Bootstrap (Seed 731, 10 000 Resamples) je Kandidat gegen `e5-small`, Regel vorab festgeschrieben
- [x] Migrationsspalte je Kandidat aus `dim` abgeleitet und gegen #730 belegt
- [x] Live-Lauf ausgeführt, Rohdaten und Report geschrieben; Report nennt Messhardware, Chunkzahl je Kandidat, Prompting-Abweichung und Auflösungsgrenze
- [ ] Kontrolllauf auf eingefrorenen e5-Chunkgrenzen — **übersprungen (Budget)**, im Report unter „Grenzen dieses Laufs" als offene Folgearbeit samt Wirkungsrichtung vermerkt
- [x] Testsuite + CI-Verdrahtung; Repro-Beweis: Suite ohne den neuen Code rot (`ModuleNotFoundError: scripts.eval.run_embedding_candidates_731`), auf dem Branch grün (30 Tests)
- [x] `docs/evals/README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` nachgezogen; Link-Guard und Syntax-Gates gelaufen

Closes #731

author: tigercosmos
body:
Since #1297 `CMakeLists.txt` sets `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER` when it finds `ccache`, so `create-symlink: true` on `ccache-action` left two ways to the same cache. CI took the symlink one, where the compiler CMake found was ccache itself, so the jobs never exercised the path a developer builds through. Dropping the symlinks leaves each build system to find the cache on its own and stops CI manipulating `PATH` for it.

`standalone_buffer` keeps them, because `contrib/standalone_buffer/Makefile` compiles with a bare `c++` and has no discovery step of its own. The `CMakeLists.txt` comment from #1297 is corrected here too, since this change is what made its claim about the CI jobs false.

A second commit gives `nouse_install` its own cache key. It shared the plain `<os>-Release` key with the `build` job while building `BUILD_QT=OFF` under the `setup.py` build directory, so neither its flags nor its paths matched what was stored there and every object missed.

Verified on a fork over two successive push runs, with the nightly-only jobs forced on. Everything passed both rounds. Round two reported 227/229 direct hits on the ubuntu-24.04 build, 114/115 on `profiling` for both ubuntu-24.04 and macos-26, and 115/117 on ubuntu `lint`, with `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER` now `/usr/bin/c++`, so the launcher wraps the real compiler. Expect the first master push after merge to run cold and repopulate.

Related to #1297.

author: rozkalnsandris
body:
Closes #388. Refs #374.

## Incident
After #381 fixed Git ownership handling, the W4B owner refresh reached Compose-model validation and failed closed with Python `JSONDecodeError: Expecting value`.

## Root cause
`validate_compose_model()` piped `docker compose ... config --format json` into `python3 - ... <<'PY'`. Bash applies the heredoc as stdin for the Python command, so the Compose JSON pipe no longer owns fd 0; Python reads its program from the heredoc and `json.load(sys.stdin)` sees EOF.

## Fix
- render the validator as `docker compose config --format json | python3 -c '...'`;
- preserve the existing JSON parser and all model checks;
- preserve `pipefail`, so a Compose rendering failure or Python validation failure blocks the operation;
- fail closed if the legacy validator template drifts;
- add regression coverage for the stdin ownership contract.

## Safety
Source/control-plane only. No API/web recreation, no W4 cutover, no DB write/migration, no Cloudflare/DNS/Access, no UFW, and no shared `cloudflared` lifecycle action.

After merge: refresh the installed W4B control plane with the merge SHA and re-run the read-only preflight. `/hermes-374 cutover` remains blocked until preflight passes.

author: williamblair333
body:
## What broke

Launching Claude Code threw two classes of hook error:

- **`/bin/sh: 1: C:/util/apps/Git/bin/bash.exe: not found`** on every SessionStart — the Windows port (commits 500bbef, 4548972) overwrote the *committed* `.claude/settings.json` hook block with `C:/util/apps/Git/bin/bash.exe C:/opt/proj/...` commands. That file is shared with the Linux host, where the `.exe` path doesn't exist. So every project hook failed **and** the real Linux hooks (skill-link, review-check, session-start-autofix, session-notify, skill-suggest, memweave-sync, checkpoint, commit-guard) were gone entirely.
- **`/bin/sh: 2: uncle-j-force-rules: not found`** on every Stop — the global `~/.claude/settings.json` force-rules command held an embedded newline (`force-rules.sh  #\n  uncle-j-force-rules`), so the shell ran the identifying tag as a second command.

## Fix

- Restore the pre-port Linux hook block to committed `.claude/settings.json`; drop the Windows-only `MSYS` env key.
- Guard each restored command with `[ -d /opt/proj/Uncle-J-s-Refinery ] || exit 0;` so it runs on Linux and skips cleanly (exit 0, no error line) on Windows. Claude Code **merges** local+committed hooks, so the committed Linux entries would otherwise re-error on the Windows box.
- Relocate the Windows hook wiring to `scripts/win/settings.local.json` — copy to the gitignored `.claude/settings.local.json` on Windows. Documented in `docs/WINDOWS-PORT.md`.
- Collapse the force-rules identifying tag onto the comment line in the global settings (**already applied in place** on this machine — not part of this repo diff).

`scripts/force-rules.sh` itself was already correct and is unchanged.

## Verification

- Both previously-broken commands run clean under `/bin/sh -c` (exit 0, no "not found").
- Guard proven: exits 0 with no leak when the repo path is absent (Windows), runs when present (Linux).
- All 8 restored Linux hook scripts exist and pass `bash -n`.
- Both settings.json files re-parse as valid JSON.
- Pre-commit doc gate passes.

## Pre-mortem

Infrastructure classification, all 12 dimensions. 0 HIGH · 1 MEDIUM · 2 LOW · 9 CLEAR. The MEDIUM (Windows merge re-erroring on committed Linux entries) is mitigated by the `[ -d … ] || exit 0` guard. Effect is deferred to next session launch (hooks load at session start).

## Windows follow-up
On the Windows box: `cp scripts/win/settings.local.json .claude/settings.local.json`

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: paulfidika
body:
**pgw#891 PR 4 of 5.** Stacked on #551 (pgw#902) — base is `pgw902-immutable-plan`; retarget to `master` once #551 lands.

## The question nothing was asking

`aot_serve.verify` asks *can this runtime execute these bytes* (sm/torch/cuda/host ISA, all probed here). `verify_contract` asks *is this envelope internally consistent*. Neither asks **is this the artifact the hub named for this attempt** — and nothing could, because before th#1457 there was no immutable spec to ask against. An AOT cell is not data: it is a `dlopen`-ed ELF this pod executes, built by another pod against one toolchain, one environment seal and one traced graph.

`gen_worker.aot_identity` compares `ExecutionSpec.arm.artifact`'s cell key, toolchain digest and env seal digest, plus `Arm.graph_contract_digest`, against the facts `aot_mint.shared_identity_blocks` baked into the artifact — **recomputed from those facts, never read from a separate stamp**, which is `cell_key`'s standing discipline and exists so a stamp cannot silently disagree with what it summarizes.

Wired into `aot_serve.stage_artifact`, i.e. strictly before the first `_load_package`: the identity question is settled while the artifact is still inert bytes.

## Declared identity, never bytes

§4.25/§4.26 forbid confirming an artifact by comparing it to another mint of the same key, and pgw#1006 measured why — two mints of one key legitimately differ, so a byte comparison would refuse healthy cells and prove nothing about unhealthy ones. A test asserts the module cannot reach artifact bytes at all.

Fail-closed and self-naming: an axis the artifact is silent on is a refusal, not a skip; an expectation naming no value is never a pass. The new `expected_identity_mismatch` reason carries `expected …, have …` and stays distinct from `key_mismatch` (cannot run here) and `artifact_invalid` (internally corrupt) — a runnable cell that is the **wrong** cell is a different bug with a different owner.

## ⚠️ The closure axis is OWED, not faked — one ruling needed from th#1457

pgw#903's box 1 asks for closure identity and **the landed schema carries no comparable value.** `EndpointRelease.code_closure_id` is the hub's identifier for a release's code; the artifact records `{source path: content digest}` from `cc.static_code_closure`. Different quantities — and the closure is not a `cell_key` axis, so it is not covered transitively either. Equating them on the strength of similar names would refuse every healthy cell in the fleet.

So the axis is **absent rather than invented**, with a test that stops a later reader from "finishing" it. Two admissible answers, mutually exclusive:

- `ArtifactIdentity` gains a `code_closure_digest` the mint stamps and the hub echoes — giving the `code_closure` envelope block its first reader; **or**
- the block is deleted, which is what **pgw#1034** already carries a row to do on the grounds that it has zero readers anywhere.

One answer deletes what the other depends on, so the lanes must not settle it independently. Same shape for `Receipt.publisher`/`publisher_org_id` (pgw#1034: decoded-and-never-verified; §4.26: the trust answer). Routed to th#1457 in the tracker, and pgw#1034 is asked to hold both deletions.

## No behaviour change on the live path

`expected` defaults to `None` — the pre-cutover RunJob dispatch, where no immutable spec exists to compare against. `expected_from_plan` is baselined **IN FLIGHT** in the unreached-surface ratchet, naming pgw#904 as its caller with an instruction to delete the line there. The exact-publisher check and the "arm nothing on a non-`aot_cell` arm" refusal are deferred to pgw#904, at their call sites, rather than added here as surface this PR cannot reach.

## Verification

- `tests/test_artifact_identity_pgw903.py` — 19 tests, **mutation-checked**: removing the `stage_artifact` gate, and letting an unstated expectation pass, each turn them red.
- `mypy` clean (240 files), `ruff` clean, `lint_unreached_surface` green.

Refs: pgw#903, pgw#891, th#1457, pgw#1034

author: taipanbox
body:
Four commits. The first fixes something that is on the public repository right now.

## Unresolved merge markers were committed to main and pushed

`README.md` carried `<<<<<<< HEAD` in its badge block, four lines from the top of the page anybody opening this repository sees. `VALIDATION.md` carried a **366-line** conflict whose two sides are not two versions of one section: HEAD had one section about permission duplication, origin had four about the stale contract, Postgres-blind detectors, `privilege_escalation` and silently ignored flags.

All five sections are kept; only the three markers are gone. The badge was settled by measurement rather than by picking a side: the suite runs 219 top-level tests, so HEAD's figure was right and origin's 216 was three behind. It now says 225, and then 232, as the commits below add tests.

## Invariant 7: the eBPF sensor grows here and nowhere else

Two implementations of one sensor exist, this one and tokenfuse's `crates/radar`, which this was ported from. The port outgrew the original in three places, read off both trees rather than remembered:

- `connect.c` reads the syscall argument through the BTF-typed `trace_event_raw_sys_enter` and is CO-RE; radar hard-codes offset 24 for x86_64.
- `capture_linux.go` admits loopback port 8001, so the local vLLM port radar's own `is_llm` lists is actually reachable here.
- This drops its own traffic by PID; radar compares `comm`, which `SECURITY.md` correctly says any process can rename.

Structurally, the layer here carries invariant 4 and a gate; radar carried no invariant and no test.

## The package had no tests, and the decoder was behind a build tag

`go test ./...` reported `internal/ebpfcapture  [no test files]`. `connect.c` hands raw network-order bytes to userspace precisely so that byte order is resolved "in Go, where it is easy to unit test" — its own words — but the decoder sat behind `//go:build linux`, so that was only true on a Linux machine. It moves to `decode.go` with no tag. Invariant 4 re-checked after the move: zero `cilium/ebpf` packages on darwin and windows, 19 on linux.

## IPv6, and counting what was not reported

The sensor watched AF_INET only and said nothing about it: an agent reaching a provider over IPv6 did not appear, was not counted, and left no trace. Both families now, with an explicit family byte, because a 4-byte IPv4 address in a zeroed 16-byte field and a real IPv6 address in `::ffff:0.0.0.0/96` are the same bytes.

A skipped-counts map makes "zero flows" mean something: nothing connected, versus a family this sensor ignores, versus **the ring buffer filled and real evidence was lost**. Invariant 4 requires idryx to say what it could not observe, and a silent zero is exactly the shape it forbids.

Two address bugs came with it. `resolveLLMHosts` kept only A records, so IPv6 egress to a known provider was captured and then rendered under a bare address matching nothing. And an IPv6 destination needs brackets, or every consumer downstream splits it on the wrong colon.

## Regeneration

`bpf2go` output regenerated on an AWS c5d.2xlarge against that kernel's own BTF. Worth knowing for the next person: restoring the `linux &&` tag naively gives `//go:build linux && mips || mips64 || ...`, which parses as `(linux && mips) || mips64 || ...` — the OS constraint applies to the first architecture only. The gate caught it, and its numbers said so before the cause was known: 19 reachable packages fell to 14 and 15 rather than to zero.

Tests 219 → 232, every new one mutation-checked.
