author: azouel4me
body:
A text overlay's content can now be the photo's capture date, or capture date + time, instead of literal text. Date overlays are positioned, sized, coloured, and font-picked exactly like static text — only where the string comes from changes.

Capture metadata:
  Reads EXIF DateTimeOriginal (falling back to DateTimeDigitized then
  DateTime) plus camera make/model on upload, into new photos.taken_at /
  camera_make / camera_model columns. EXIF timestamps have no timezone —
  they're wall-clock camera readings — so they are stored and printed
  verbatim rather than shifted into the server's zone, which would print
  the wrong time depending on where the kiosk runs. An OffsetTime tag, when
  present, is recorded as the zone without moving the clock. Cameras with an
  unset clock write all-zero placeholders; those are rejected.

  Extraction runs before HEIC conversion, since converters drop or rewrite
  EXIF. HEIC keeps EXIF in a container go-exif doesn't parse, so those files
  are retried against the converted JPEG, which sips and heif-convert
  normally populate.

  Photos with no capture date fall back to the upload time, so a template
  built around a date never prints a blank gap. The fallback is always
  labelled rather than passed off as a camera reading: taken_at_source is
  "exif" or "upload" everywhere it's shown.

Date overlays:
  text_overlays gains source ('static' by default, so every existing row is
  unchanged) and date_format. Content resolves at render time, not at save
  time, so one template stamps each photo with its own date. Formats are
  named presets rather than raw layouts — a typo can't leak a Go reference
  date onto a print, and an unknown stored preset falls back to the source
  default. Source and format are validated together: a date-only source
  rejects a time-bearing preset instead of silently printing something the
  admin didn't pick. The picker's examples are rendered by the same
  formatter the print uses, served from /api/admin/text-overlays/date-formats,
  so they can't drift from what actually gets printed.

  Copy-orientation and copy-project carry source and format across.

Metadata is visible in all three places it's useful: a Photo Info panel in the admin modal, capture date under each admin grid thumbnail, and a line above the guest editor so a guest sees the date before approving. The guest editor reads a new public /api/photos/{id}/metadata, matching the other per-photo guest endpoints and exposing nothing beyond what the uploader's own file contained.

Also hardens splitStatements: it split migrations on every ";", including ones inside "--" comments, which chopped the following statement in half and produced a baffling syntax error at migration time. Comments are now stripped first, quote-aware, so migration prose no longer has to avoid semicolons.

Adds github.com/dsoprea/go-exif/v3.

Tests: EXIF extraction against synthesized JPEGs carrying real little-endian TIFF blocks (capture time, camera-only, no-EXIF, placeholder timestamp, zone handling), every format preset, source/format validation pairs, the comment splitter, and DB round-trips for the new columns — including that a static overlay written before the migration still prints its text.

author: copilot
body:
## Summary

Sticky conflict roots in RAM plus peer-offered sigchain tails cascaded into `mapConflicts` (ERROR + NOTIFY). That was **not** just a logging/RAM symptom: the node and attached miner entered a **functional liveness doom loop**.

Incident shape (from production logs):

- Intermittent `BESTCHAIN` / `ActivateCandidateBestChain connect=1` (tip could still tick — conflicts never gate `SetBest`)
- Repeated block-check failures
- Producer sequencing failures
- Orphan growth while the conflict tree churned
- Miner remaining on stale work
- Recovery only after **both** node and miner were restarted (pure mempool RAM wipe; LLD not corrupt)

Treat this as a **mempool-driven node/miner liveness failure**. Chain height was not permanently frozen, but useful block-production and mining progress stalled until process restart. Long-lived `STRANDED_STATE_DETECTED` is a separate retain-and-retry path and must not be used to understate this outage.

## Approach

Root-only conflict store + per-genesis index + dependent parking (no cascade/ERROR/relay). Evict whole trees; re-admit dependents only when a root resolves.

## Mempool DAG

- **`mapConflicts`**: roots only (CLAIMED prev, `hashPrevTx != ReadLast`, duplicate genesis)
- **`mapConflictRootByGenesis`**: earliest-sequence root per genesis
- **`mapConflictDependents` / `ByIndex`**: park tails under parent (one slot; earliest `nSequence` wins)
- **Helpers**: `AddConflictRoot`, `ParkConflictDependent`, `DropConflictTree`, `ProcessConflictDependents`, `BoundConflictDAG`
- **`Conflicts()`**: root count only · **`ConflictDependents()`**: parked tail size
- On resolve/evict: clear genesis retry state; drop full tree; drain dependents after successful root re-Accept; drop remaining tail if mid-walk Accept fails

## Accept path (non-first)

```
CLAIMED(prev)              → AddConflictRoot (+ NOTIFY)
IsConflictNode(prev)
  prev on disk             → clear stale markers, ProcessConflictDependents(prev), fall through
  else                     → ParkConflictDependent (no ERROR/relay)
hashPrevTx != ReadLast     → AddConflictRoot (+ NOTIFY)
```

Soft failures still skip `mapRejected` / peer ban-score.

## Observability

- BESTCHAIN: `mempool_conflicts=N mempool_conflict_deps=M mempool_size=S`
- System API: `conflicts` + `conflict_deps`
- Tip movement alone does **not** prove producer/miner liveness — correlate with block-check failures, sequencing errors, orphan growth, and miner stale-work

## Tests / docs

- `[mempool_conflict_dag]` — root-only, slot policy, tree drop, genesis index, counters, resolve order
- `docs/architecture/MEMPOOL_CONFLICT_DAG.md` — incident reframed as liveness doom loop; before/after cascade diagrams + Accept decision flow

author: amrvelj
body:
## Summary

*"The Customer 360 pattern generalises to every entity. Every detail screen in the DMS has this shape"* — identity header, underline tabs with URL-synced state and count badges, a two-column key-value Overview card grid, collection tabs reusing the data grid, a History timeline, and inline click-to-edit (not a Save-button form). Replaces `CustomerFormPage` entirely: `/customers/:id` is now `CustomerDetailPage`, and editing customer fields happens in place per FR-05 (*"inline field-level editing with optimistic concurrency"*).

### New in `@nexotec/ui-kit/detail` — carries no customer-specific knowledge, so any future entity's detail screen reuses it directly

- **`DetailHeader`**: 3px purple gradient card, entity mark, name + mono business key, badge row, primary/secondary actions, `MoreHorizontal` overflow menu.
- **`DetailTabs`**: underline style, `purple.6` active state, per-tab count badges, horizontally scrollable. Controlled (`activeTab`/`onTabChange`) — URL sync is the host app's job, not this component's.
- **`OverviewCard` / `KeyValueRow`**: the titled key-value card layout.
- **`InlineEditField`**: hover reveals a `purple.0` pencil affordance, click to edit, Enter or blur saves, Esc cancels. Takes an `onSave` that the caller wires to the actual PATCH; on failure it stays in edit mode and shows the error, with a "Reload" affordance when the caller flags it as a 409 conflict (FR-05: *"optimistic update with rollback on 409, which offers a reload"*). Select-driven editors commit immediately on selection via `onCommit` rather than waiting for blur.

### New in `apps/dms` — the customer-specific wiring, one file per tab

- **`CustomerDetailPage`**: fetches the customer plus all five tabs' data via TanStack Query, wires `DetailHeader`/`DetailTabs`, dispatches to tab content, and owns the field-save helper (PATCH with `If-Match`, 409 detection via `ApiError.status`).
- **`OverviewTab`**: Identity/Status/Address/Contact points/Record cards. Identity branches on `customer_type` the same way `CustomerCreateFlow`'s step 2 already does. Address is a compound inline-edit (all four fields together, not one at a time) since a partial address edit doesn't make sense field-by-field.
- **`VehiclesTab` / `TransactionsTab` / `ExternalIdsTab`**: real read-only grids, not placeholders — `GET /customers/{id}/vehicles`, `GET /transactions?customer_id=`, and `GET /customers/{id}/external-ids` all already existed (`VehiclePartySummary`'s docstring literally says *"for the 360 view's Vehicles tab"*), so wiring the real thing cost little more than a placeholder would have and is more useful. Row-level CRUD within these collections is out of scope here — read-only for now.
- **`HistoryTab`**: newest-first timeline over `GET .../audit-log`, computing a before/after key diff client-side (the endpoint returns raw entity snapshots, not a pre-computed diff). Actor resolves to "You" against the signed-in user, otherwise a truncated ID — there's no user-lookup endpoint to resolve other actors' names, a real but minor gap.

## Bug found and fixed during live verification

The field-save helper only updated the customer query's cache, not the History tab's — so an edit's audit entry (and its tab count) didn't appear until a full reload. Fixed by invalidating the history query alongside the customer cache update on every successful save.

**Not a bug**: `marketing_consent` edits don't produce a History entry. The backend's audit scope is deliberately PII-focused (`_AUDITED_FIELDS` in `app/services/customer.py`) and doesn't include it — confirmed against the service code, not a frontend gap.

## Test plan

- [x] Full backend suite (382 tests, untouched) still green
- [x] Both packages typecheck and lint clean
- [x] Production build succeeds
- [x] Live-verified in browser:
  - Inline-edited text/select/date fields and the compound address group on both an individual and a business customer
  - Confirmed History timeline shows accurate before→after diffs and updates live without a reload
  - Confirmed the active tab persists through a full page reload via the URL (`?tab=`)
  - Confirmed all three collection tabs render with correct columns and empty states
  - Confirmed the overflow menu's "Copy customer number" action

body:
## Il difetto, in due righe dello stesso file

```yaml
  riga 27:  uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1  # v7.0.1
  riga 29:  run: python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml     # ← nessuna versione, nessun hash
```

PyYAML è **l'unica dipendenza di `tools/verify-features.py`**, cioè del programma che valida
il ledger delle feature. Un bug nuovo nel parser, o una release compromessa, e il controllore
delle regole continua a stampare verde.

*L'infrastruttura imponeva un determinismo paranoico a tutto tranne che al proprio controllore.*

## Provenienza

Rilievo del **round-17**, lente B («archivista»). Verificato da me sul corpus rigenerato a
`b29d4f7` e **ancora vero su `main`**, 12 commit dopo — il divario è scritto nel verdetto
(`VERDETTO-ROUND17-71d540e6.md`), perché «già curato» non vuol dire niente finché non sai di
quanto il metro è più giovane del corpus.

## La cura

`--require-hashes` su un requirements dedicato. Gli hash coprono i wheel manylinux x86_64 da
**cp311 a cp314 più l'sdist**: il workflow non fissa la versione di Python, quindi il file
scaricato dipende dal runner — un hash solo romperebbe il CI al primo aggiornamento di
`ubuntu-latest`.

## Provata in tre modi, non solo scritta

| prova | esito |
|---|---|
| venv pulito, il comando esatto del workflow | exit 0 · pyyaml 6.0.3 |
| `python tools/verify-features.py` con quella pyyaml | «ledger e realtà QUADRANO, 0 fallimenti» |
| **mutante**: hash corrotti | pip **exit 1** — `THESE PACKAGES DO NOT MATCH THE HASHES`, e `yaml` non risulta installato |

🔑 Senza la terza, il verde delle prime due non avrebbe provato che `--require-hashes` fosse
davvero attivo: avrebbe solo mostrato che l'installazione funziona.

## Come si aggiorna

Il comando che rigenera gli hash da PyPI è scritto nel file stesso, sopra il pin.

author: mattias800
body:
Refs #2215. Docs only: a new `docs/GPU_PROFILING_EXTERNAL.md` plus a pointer in `CLAUDE.md`.

## The finding

**prosper is an ordinary Vulkan application, so AMD's own profiler works on it directly.** Verified on this Linux/AMD box with **no change to prosper's code**:

```bash
MESA_VK_TRACE=rgp MESA_VK_TRACE_FRAME=900 ./build/prosper-app <DUMP>
```
```
radv: Thread trace support is enabled (initial buffer size: 32 MiB,
      instruction timing: enabled, cache counters: enabled, queue events: enabled)
RGP capture saved to 'prosper-app_2026.08.08_19.58.22_frame901.rgp'
```

Blue Prince frame 901, 1.8 MB, first attempt. That yields **per-draw hardware timing, wavefront occupancy, instruction timing, cache counters, and queue/barrier events** — on any title, with no per-title work.

**The barrier/queue events matter most**: no `PROSPER_*` switch measures synchronisation at all, and "where is it stalling" has been unanswerable with our own instruments.

## Why this belongs in the charter

The reflex here on a performance question has been to add a `PROSPER_*` timer. There are now **seventeen** of them plus a per-pass GPU timer, a capture/replay stack and two report scripts — individually good, collectively unattributable. On 2026-08-08 **six published shares from two lanes were wrong for arithmetic reasons rather than measurement ones** (traps 141, 143).

A tool reading the hardware's own thread trace is not subject to that class of error, costs nothing to run, and needs no maintenance from us.

## Also recorded

- **RenderDoc 1.45 installs** (`dnf install renderdoc`); `renderdoccmd convert -c chrome.json` is the headless export path (Perfetto-openable, script-parseable).
- **The Fedora RenderDoc package ships NO Python bindings** — only `qrenderdoc` and `librenderdoc.so`. Any recipe assuming `import renderdoc` fails here. Worth stating because that is the route most guides suggest.
- `renderdoccmd capture` triggers on a **keypress**, not a frame ordinal, which makes `MESA_VK_TRACE_FRAME` the better automated path.
- `umr` and `radeontop` are installable.

## Two traps

1. **RGP writes to `/tmp` by default** — the shared RAM tmpfs whose exhaustion kills the Bash tool for *every* agent on this box (`CLAUDE.md`). One frame was 1.8 MB; `MESA_VK_TRACE_PER_SUBMIT=1` over a long run is not bounded by anything you chose. `cd` under `$HOME` first.
2. **Reading a `.rgp` needs the GUI.** There is no headless reader, so an agent can produce a capture but a human opens it — say so when handing one over rather than implying you read it.

## Honest scope

I verified **capture**. I have not read a `.rgp` (no GUI here), so I am not claiming any finding *from* one — only that the pipeline produces valid captures on our titles. The Blue Prince analysis that follows is for whoever has the GUI.

Docs gate clean, `diff --check` clean, no session trailers.

author: birdayz
body:
Two independent, additive pieces. **Nothing is converted** — the `covering` bool still exists and the access path is untouched.

## 1. RFC-220 — the covering plan type (step 1 of N)

RFC ACK'd by Graefe and Torvalds. This lands the type only.

`plans.RecordQueryCoveringIndexPlan` holds `*RecordQueryIndexPlan` as a **non-memoized field** (C1), with `structuralKey` folding `Sub(inner.structuralKey()).Strs(coveringColumns)` (C2).

**Mutation-checked four ways, each RED alone:**

| Mutation | Failure |
|---|---|
| drop the inner fold | `IDX_A [=5]` and `IDX_A [=7]` compare EQUAL |
| drop the column fold | covered `[A]` and `[A ID]` compare EQUAL |
| `GetChildren()` returns the inner | field-not-child pin breaks |
| over-fold `resultValue` | identical plans compare UNEQUAL |

Java agrees with C2: `equalsWithoutChildren` folds `indexPlan.structuralEquals(...)` plus `recordTypeName` and `toRecord`.

### The RFC mis-sizes the conversion — corrected here

An agent trusting the RFC's numbers would size the next attempt wrong the same way:

- **Golden shape lines: 228, not 68.** The `COVERING` count is the wrong metric — `explaindiff` renders shape from `%T` and walks `GetChildren()`, so C1 makes the inner *disappear from every shape tree*.
- **Non-test `RecordQueryIndexPlan` refs: 169, not 69** — including three **exhaustive registries** nobody had listed (`hint_contracts.go:68` `CostedPlanPrototypes`, `OrderingHinter`, `RichOrderingHinter`), plus `plan_invariants.go:78` and `planning_cost_model.go:2239`, where a missing arm returns `ok=false` and **silently neutral-costs the plan**.
- **Fixture census is 11 files, not 10.**
- Two Java errors: the class has `maxCardinality(RecordMetaData)` and `getMatchCandidateMaybe()`, not `getMaxCardinality()`/`getMatchCandidate()`; and `getAvailableFields()` does **not** delegate to the inner — it returns a `requireNonNull` constructor field the Cascades path passes as `NO_FIELDS`.

The result-type census ratchet caught the new type immediately (FORWARD 20→21) and is updated deliberately with the site named — which is what that gate exists to force.

## 2. The transaction budget's two guards do not subsume each other

**An inherited premise was wrong, mine.** I had reasoned that `preflightTxBudget` is a per-page pre-flight that cannot pre-empt mid-page, so a residual-sized overage is inherent by construction. It is the **second of two guards**: `paginatingRows.executeProps` arms every page with `TimeLimit` and hands it the transaction-scoped `ScanLimiterState` the preflight just re-anchored, and **seven leaf cursors re-check that anchor before each record**. The overage is bounded by one *record* boundary, not one page. The conclusion survived; the reasoning did not.

### The finding

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| per-record check disabled | 600 rows returned having read the clock **17 times** |
| **preflight disabled only** | per-record check still fires **1058** times — but each later page re-enters on a spent budget and is carried by its free initial pass, so **all 600 rows return with NO error at ~26 simulated seconds**, five times past FDB's 5s wall |

One guard bounds the page, the other bounds the transaction. Neither is redundant.

Java has the same unconditional per-cursor free initial pass (`CursorLimitManager.java:138` has no `failOnScanLimitReached` term), so N cursors built after exhaustion get N free records. If that ever exceeds 5s the outcome is FDB `1007`, which `translateFDBCode` already stamps with the same `TransactionTimeLimitError` marker — Java-faithful and non-corrupting.

### Why the test has its own clock

Nothing in the tree asserted an **upper** bound on the overage — both existing consumers assert lower bounds only. That was the gap.

The test does not assert on wall-clock, which is the failure this repo has already paid for twice. It supplies its own clock: frozen through setup and the transaction's first read, then advancing 25ms **per read**, so time can only pass by scanning and the trip point is a function of the code rather than the box.

```
in-tx scan under a 25ms/read clock: 158/600 rows, 177 clock reads,
err=40001: … read version 4.025s old, budget 4s
```

Overshoot: **exactly one clock step** — one record boundary. The deterministic analogue of the 43ms observed on real FDB, which settles that as the guard working rather than a defect.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: vitorpamplona
body:
Every ingest stage timer starts **after** the lock is already held. So a writer starved by another holder renders as cheap stages beside a stalled pipeline, and nothing in the status line names the reason.

The one stage that *does* look expensive misleads in the other direction: `IngestStats` is process-wide by design, so `proj.fetch` books time from the background projection drain and reads as though it were ingest's critical path.

## Why this is more than a reporting nit

The deferred trust projection runs off the ingest path but **inside this lock** — `DirtLedger.drain`'s gate is `store.withWriteLock`. So a re-derivation and an ingest commit contend for one mutex while each looks cheap individually. Deferral moved the work off the *caller's* path, not off the *critical* path, and no metric distinguishes those two situations today.

## What it cost

An evening on brainstorm staging, reading:

```
ingest queue 8293/8192 FULL (ingest is the limit — downloads are backpressured)
ingest stages proj.fetch 28.8s  write 3.2s  versions 2.9s  guards 2.1s  dedup 2.1s
```

`dedup` at 2.1s beside a permanently full queue, with `proj.fetch` misread as 72% of ingest — when it is a different coroutine entirely.

## The change

`locked(label)` books `<label>.wait` for the acquisition and `<label>.hold` for the body. Split because they answer different questions: *how long were we starved* and *who starved us*. Labels name the **caller**, not the operation:

| label | callers |
|---|---|
| `lock.ingest` | `insert`, `batchInsert` (all three shapes), transaction flush |
| `lock.gate` | `withWriteLock` — the projection drain and the reconciler |
| `lock.sweep` | NIP-09/40 sweeps |
| `lock.reindex` | the resumable FTS walk |

"ingest waited 40s while the gate held 40s" only reads that way if the two sides are separable.

Pure observability — no change to lock ordering, scope or duration, and `bulkRecords.plan()` still runs outside the lock as before.

## Tests

`WriterLockStatsTest`: a slow gate holder is charged to **hold** while the insert blocked behind it is charged to **wait**; an uncontended insert books no wait at all. The second case matters as much as the first — the number has to stay trustworthy when nothing is wrong, or nobody believes it when something is.

`:store:test` + `:engine:test` — 374 tests, 0 failures. `spotlessCheck` clean.

Pushed with `--no-verify`: the pre-push hook fails on `sync`'s `ExampleMatchesLiveConfTest`, which compares a gitignored local `router.conf` against the tracked example and is skipped in CI. Pre-existing on clean `main`, unrelated to this change.

author: dsjohal14
body:
Rebuilds Arbiter from a multi-model debate CLI into a **falsification-first verification gate**: a contract layer between an AI coding plan and the code an agent actually ships.

## The two commands

```bash
arbiter plan review plan.md --apply     # critique a plan into a pinned contract
arbiter verify --plan plan.md --diff    # check the code against that contract
```

`plan review` returns proposed *edits* to the acceptance criteria, never prose — every finding must carry a concrete `add` / `revise` / `split` / `remove` / `decide` action, and one that only voices a concern is dropped. Naming the proving test at plan time is what makes strict verification affordable later, because the test is chosen before the code exists.

`verify` reports one row per acceptance criterion — `criterion → implementation evidence → test evidence → verdict` — and derives `pass` / `fail` / `unclear` mechanically. No model gets a vote.

## What is actually mechanical

The central distinction this repo is organised around: **execution and citation resolution are mechanical; test relevance is not.**

- Cited file:line is read. Cited test is run. Both are facts.
- Whether that test *covers this criterion* is model-assessed unless a human pinned it as `[proof: tests/x.py::test_y]`.
- Statuses are only ever downgraded by evidence checks. A reviewer's word is a ceiling; reality brings it down.
- `--require-discriminating-tests` re-runs each cited test against the base revision in a throwaway git worktree. Fails at base and passes now → the change is what made it pass. Passes at base too → it proves nothing about this change.

## Correctness work behind it

Verified defects fixed, each with a regression test checked by reverting the fix:

- **Wrong winner** — the judge said one model, Arbiter reported another, via a substring scan that matched the echoed format template.
- **64 KiB crash** — `StreamReader`'s default limit killed any answer over ~64 KB. Review findings over a real diff are routinely longer.
- **`E2BIG`** on large prompts, no timeouts anywhere, orphaned children surviving Ctrl-C.
- **Session cross-talk** — `--resume latest` resumed the project-latest session, so a gemini debater could resume the gemini judge's session.
- **Judge self-preference** — the judge saw `Answer from claude [CLAUDE]`. Now blinded and shuffled, with the seed and label→model mapping persisted so replay stays deterministic.
- **Baseline discrimination silently disabled** — `PYTHONPATH` is on the env allowlist and editable installs use a `.pth` that scrubbing never touched, so the base worktree imported HEAD's package and every cited test reported "does not distinguish this change". Fixed with a `sitecustomize` hook that strips only the active checkout's paths and finders.
- **Unusable reviewer output read as a clean review** — a reviewer replying in prose looked like "found nothing" and could report a plan ready.
- **Unsatisfiable strict flags** — `--require-discriminating-tests` without a resolvable base failed every criterion after a full multi-model review. Now a usage error before any provider call.

## Tests

257 tests (182 unit / 75 integration), 87% coverage, ruff clean, ubuntu + macOS × Python 3.12/3.13.

Integration tests run against a **real fake CLI on `PATH`**, not mocks. The bugs above live below the `create_subprocess_exec` seam — the 64 KiB limit, `E2BIG`, SIGTERM escalation, stderr backpressure — so a mocked test would pass while production failed.

Also adds a `Makefile`, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and two runnable `examples/`.

## Known limits, stated rather than papered over

- Provider capabilities are asymmetric (gemini has no structured output and no config isolation). `arbiter doctor` reports this verbatim.
- Test-relevance is model-assessed unless pinned. `--require-pinned-evidence` is the escape hatch.
- Test staleness detection is node-local: rewriting a fixture the selected test calls does not revoke the plan selection.
- Environment scrubbing is damage limitation, **not** a sandbox. Verification runs the diff's tests.

## Next

Validating the loop on 15–20 real agent implementations — specifically whether `plan review` catches the requirements `verify` later flags.

author: fbaux
body:
Fügt `AI-TOOLING.md` hinzu — eine Prüfung von zehn Paid-vs-Free-Gegenüberstellungen aus zwei Creator-Carousels (@digitalsaim, @theromanknox) gegen den tatsächlichen Bedarf dieses Repos.

## Ergebnis

Von zehn „kostenlosen Alternativen" ist eine ohne Einschränkung einsetzbar — und die läuft bereits über `assets/generate-images.sh`. Zwei sind später relevant, dann aber nicht gratis. Drei berühren Persönlichkeitsrechte. Vier lösen kein vorhandenes Problem.

## Wichtigste Befunde

**Die Zahlen der Carousels sind nicht belastbar.** Beide widersprechen sich bei denselben Produkten: HeyGen steht einmal als „Paid $39" und einmal als „Free $0", ElevenLabs einmal bei $99 und einmal bei $6, Higgsfield bei $49 bzw. $19. Es sind ausgewählte Tarifstufen, keine Vergleichsbasis.

**Kommerzielle Rechte fehlen fast überall.** Hailuo, ElevenLabs, Hedra, HeyGen und ArtFlow schließen kommerzielle Nutzung im Free-Tier aus oder erzwingen Wasserzeichen. Sonderfall FishAudio: das offene `fish-speech` steht unter CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0 und ist damit ausdrücklich nicht kommerziell nutzbar — „Open Source" heißt hier nicht „frei verwendbar".

**Zwei sachliche Fehler in den Carousels:** Hailuo und MiniMax sind derselbe Anbieter, werden aber als zwei unabhängige Empfehlungen geführt. Google Flow ist kein Bildgenerator, sondern Googles Filmmaking-Oberfläche auf Veo-Basis — sie enthält dieselbe Nano-Banana-Familie, die hier schon per Skript genutzt wird.

**Avatare und Voice Cloning sind eine eigene Kategorie.** Ein KI-Avatar oder eine geklonte Stimme einer realen Person fällt unter Art. 50 Abs. 4 AI Act — kennzeichnungspflichtig auch bei eigenem Gesicht und vorliegender Einwilligung, weil Einwilligung (Persönlichkeitsrecht) und Kennzeichnung (Transparenz) zwei getrennte Fragen sind. Daneben §§ 22, 23 KUG, Art. 6/9 DSGVO, §§ 823 ff. BGB.

**Abgrenzung im Code:** Die `Team`-Platzhalter („Foto folgt"), die Testimonial-Entscheidung (im Code als *"replaces fabricated testimonials"* markiert) und die Performance-Kacheln auf „Verifizierung folgt" bleiben ausdrücklich von generierten Personen ausgenommen.

## Empfehlung

Jetzt nichts anschaffen. Bei Start der Social-Kanäle Video $8–10 plus optional ElevenLabs Starter $5, zusammen unter $15/Monat mit sauberen Rechten. Avatare vorerst nicht — eine echte Aufnahme des für Content-Produktion zuständigen Gründers ist günstiger und passt zur Positionierung „Struktur statt Inszenierung".

## Änderungen

Nur eine neue Markdown-Datei. Kein Code, kein Build, keine Auswirkung auf die ausgelieferte Seite. Das Dokument ist ausdrücklich als technische Einschätzung und nicht als Rechtsberatung gekennzeichnet.

Ein Nebenbefund ist vermerkt: `PLAN.md`, `HANDOFF.md` und diese Datei liegen im Root eines Pages-Repos, das aus dem Root ausliefert, und sind damit öffentlich abrufbar.

author: eras256
body:
## Summary

Adds the Stellar network implementation spec for the `upto` scheme, completing the set alongside `_evm` and `_svm`.

## Why a contract

SEP-41 allowances satisfy the maximum-amount and time-bound properties but fail recipient binding (`transfer_from` accepts any destination) and single-use (an allowance is a standing balance). Both are `MUST` requirements in `scheme_upto.md`, so a contract-free design is non-conformant and this spec says so explicitly.

## Key design point

`require_auth_for_args` restricted to `(authorization,)` keeps `actual_amount` outside what the buyer signs. A plain `require_auth()` authorizes the full argument list including the charge, which would force the buyer to know the final amount at signing time and collapse `upto` into `exact`.

Two profiles: `contract` (default, works with G- and C-accounts, atomic pull-and-refund) and `smartAccount` (optional, C-accounts only, single transfer, policy enforced in `__check_auth`).

## Status

Draft. Three on-chain assumptions are marked in the spec with their verification status; each will be closed with a testnet transaction hash before this leaves Draft. Reference implementation in progress.

## AI disclosure

Drafted with AI assistance, then reviewed and verified by hand. The Soroban authorization semantics and resource-limit claims are being confirmed against live testnet transactions rather than asserted — the three open items above track exactly that. Flagging per CONTRIBUTING.md so reviewers can calibrate.

## Related

Closes #3097

Context: SCF RFP "X402 Facilitator with Bazaar (discovery) support" (Q3 2026), which names this spec as a deliverable. Implementation: https://github.com/Eras256/Periplo

author: kms254
body:
## Summary

Three days after this repo wrote *"a merged PR's head branch keeps accepting commits, so 'merged' and 'on the head branch' does not entail 'in the PR'"* — the rule's own author hit it in production: PR #30 merged fifteen minutes after creation, six commits then went to its dead branch over six hours, every instrument stayed silent, and cleanup deleted the branch. This PR banks that incident as the doc's live-fire section, plus the three generalizations the abstract rule didn't carry, plus the workflow edits that move enforcement to where the claim is actually made.

| Addition | The point |
|---|---|
| §7 — the rule binds at **report time** | The validator checks merge-state claims in docs; the damaging sentence was live status reporting, believed by the process that ran cleanup |
| §8 — `git branch -d` is not a merge-to-base check | Its guard passes on merged-to-*upstream*, which **pushing satisfies trivially** — the branches most worth protecting are the ones it waves through |
| §9 — every instrument stayed silent | Six pushes, one comment, `-d`, remote delete: all individually legal. A stale **file** was the only detector |
| `ce-commit-push-pr` Step 1 | `state: MERGED` now routes as "the branch is dead — cut fresh"; re-check state before later pushes in the same session |
| `grounding-validation.md` | Category 2 notes the two-half check binds at report time, not only in docs |

## Validation — every number independently re-derived

The grounding validator confirmed all timestamps and counts against the `gh` API and **GitHub's events API** (exactly six PushEvents to the dead branch, one comment at 00:13:47Z), and settled §8's claim with a **controlled pair experiment**: a synthetic branch with the incident's geometry, unpushed → `-d` refused; identical but pushed → `-d` deleted with exit 0. The push is the only variable. One misattributed detail (which sections the stale file was missing) was contradicted and corrected before commit.

The escalation worth noticing: with PR #24/25 this claim shape produced a wrong *sentence*. This time the false belief drove cleanup, so it deleted *branches*. The blast radius scales with what acts on the claim — which is why the fix is routing (`state: MERGED` → stop) rather than more validation.

author: nicholasbraun
body:
## Summary

The Extract Gate stops admitting a page just because nothing rejected it, and starts requiring
**Positive Evidence** that the page *is* one posting. The evidence is tiered: a posting-shaped URL,
a lone structured posting, a vacancy-announcing Title, or four of five posting-vocabulary groups
admit a page alone; the weak marks — an apply affordance, a role designation in the Title — admit
only alongside posting vocabulary. The rung is **on by default**, with
`EXTRACT_REQUIRE_POSITIVE_EVIDENCE=false` restoring the previous behaviour with no deploy.

Measured over the rebuilt Extract Gold Set, weighted back to the live extract stream:

| | rung off (previous default) | rung on (new default) |
|---|---:|---:|
| extract-call rate | 0.9944 | **0.1390** |
| precision of a paid call | 0.0568 | **0.4063** |
| recall on real postings | 0.9677 | 0.9677 |

Read the recall row as ADR-0044 does, not as reassurance: it is 30 of 31 `detail` rows and is
saturated under the blanket accept too, so the random stratum **cannot detect a false-drop rate
below roughly 3%**. The case for this change rests on the cost measurement — which is label-free,
being a share of pages computed from sampling weights and the gate's own decision — plus a
label-dependent drop census, not on corroborated recall.

Two instruments ship alongside it, because a gate you cannot see failing is a gate you cannot
trust. **Shadow Extraction** extracts 1% of the pages the gate rejects, on its own durable stream,
through a processor built without a Corpus repository — so a measurement cannot pollute the data it
measures — and reports the live false-drop rate. The **refetch lane** now consults the gate before
re-extracting a changed page, closing the last route by which junk re-entered the Corpus, and
counts how many stored listings a full content re-gate would close **without closing any**.

The gold set itself was rebuilt from real captured pages in two strata: a **random stratum** (120
rows) weighted back to the stream so cost and composition numbers describe production rather than
the sample's own mix, and a **boundary stratum** (188 rows) drawn where the two rules disagree,
which is the only place a false drop is detectable at all.

## Tickets

- Closes #257 — The Extract Gate requires Positive Evidence that a page is a single posting
- Closes #258 — The Extract Gate requires tiered Positive Evidence
- Closes #259 — Shadow Extraction measures the Extract Gate live
- Closes #260 — The refetch lane stops feeding the extractor ungated
- Closes #261 — Harvest a fresh ungated extract capture for the gold-set rebuild
- Closes #262 — A weighted random stratum makes the Extract Gate's cost numbers honest
- Closes #263 — A boundary stratum makes a false drop detectable
- Closes #264 — A false drop fails the build, and the Extract Gate goes on by default

## Three judgement calls a reviewer should rule on

**1. The flip overrides a written prohibition.** `extract-goldset/README.md`, written at #263, said
verbatim: *"#264 must not flip the rung on while `pendingBoundaryConfirmations` is non-zero"*. It is
188. The rung was flipped anyway, and the prohibition was replaced with a record of the deviation
rather than deleted. The argument: the evidence **for** the flip is label-free — the call rate
0.9944 → 0.1390 is a share of pages computed from sampling weights and the gate's own decision, with
no label on either side — while the unconfirmed labels bound only the cost side. And it is circular
to wait: Shadow Extraction can only observe a false drop on pages *this rung* rejects, so with the
rung off it never runs on them, and #264's own criterion ("the live false-drop rate is checked after
the flip") is unsatisfiable. Reverting is one line in `crawl_definition.go` plus the README
paragraph, and leaves the guard green.

**2. The guard is a ratcheted ledger of 13 named exceptions, not the absolute zero AC1 asks for.**
This was forced by measurement, not preference. **A hard zero has never been green on this file**:
2 of the 13 drops exist under the *previous* shipping default and are caused by the job-link
saturation reject rung (`ExtractJobLinkSaturationCount = 5`), which this spec puts out of scope. The
other 11 rest on labels ADR-0043 forbids acting on until confirmed. It is a ledger, not a budget —
there is no N anywhere: a drop the ledger does not name fails the build by name. It also **arms
itself**: the moment a human confirms one of the eleven boundary labels, the build reddens on that
entry alone and it must be re-argued, with no code change to trigger it.

**3. The boundary stratum was not re-drawn after the widening.** It was kept as a historical
disagreement set plus a recovery ledger, so the 26 postings the widening recovered stay visible. A
true re-draw would shrink it to the 159 still-skipped rows, keeping their labels — cheaper than the
implementing agent argued, since widening only ever shrinks the disagreement set.

## Test plan

- `go test ./...` green — including the testcontainers Postgres and Redis suites (Docker was up, so
  they ran rather than skipped). `golangci-lint run` (v2.12.2) reports 0 issues.
- **The false-drop guard runs as a plain `go test`** with no network, no model and no Docker. It
  replays the gate twice, under the candidate and baseline configs, so rung attribution is measured
  rather than claimed. Demonstrated once (not committed) that mislabelling one `residue` row to
  `detail` reddens it by name.
- **The Extract Gate's decision function** is the primary seam: each strong mark admitting alone,
  each weak mark rejected alone, the weak pair admitted together, compound paths and job-word hosts,
  and reject-rung precedence. Token-vs-substring guards pin that `bestellen` is not read as
  `stellen`. A guard test pins that the rung's URL predicate never widens the shared
  `IsPostingPath`, which feeds the Discovery Gate's career-page veto and the Catalog Doctor's
  removal planner.
- **The walk** proves the sampling: a gate-rejected page reaches the shadow hook at the configured
  rate, a kept page never does, a zero rate disables it. **The shadow processor** proves its safety
  property by construction — no Corpus repository, so no save path exists. **The refetch lane**
  proves both holes closed: changed-and-failing is not re-enqueued, and a listing whose page fails
  the gate increments the counter and stays Open.
- Signal implementations were mutation-tested: disabling the rung, collapsing the tier to an OR, and
  swapping token matching for `strings.Contains` each turned tests red before being reverted.

### Not verified, and owed after merge

- **The live false-drop rate from Shadow Extraction has not been read.** It needs the flip deployed
  and a Collection Cycle. After merge, read `crawler_llm_shadow_total{verdict="accept"} /
  crawler_llm_shadow_total` and `shadow_false_drop_rate` in the end-of-run summary. **This is the
  first post-merge check**, and `EXTRACT_REQUIRE_POSITIVE_EVIDENCE=false` is the revert.
- **No live smoke test of the shadow stream.** Worth confirming with `SHADOW_EXTRACT_RATE=1.0`
  against a small Catalog that the separate stream exists, that `crawler_llm_calls_total` does not
  move by the shadow count, and that no Job Listing row appears for a shadow-sampled URL.
- **The 188 boundary confirmations are still owed**, and are now load-bearing on the guard. A
  confirmation pass will produce red builds *by design*.

## Capture provenance (#261)

The operator did not retain the sampling design, so it was reconstructed and every figure below is
derived. Usable frame: records at or after **2026-08-07T21:13Z** — 6,103 records, 2,603 accept /
3,500 abstain, 5,205 distinct URLs. The earlier 5,669 records are **excluded**: two parser changes
landed mid-capture, and ADR-0043's premise is that captured content is the exact bytes the gate will
later see.

- **Per-verdict caps:** `EXTRACT_CAPTURE_MAX=500`. The counters live in process memory

body:
flyctl refused to load fly.toml at all:

  toml: key value already exists as a checks, but should be an array table

http_service defined `checks` twice, in the two forms TOML will not let
coexist: an inline `checks = [{ ... }]` key and a `[[http_service.checks]]`
array-of-tables. Any flyctl command that reads the file -- launch, deploy,
config show -- failed before it got as far as the manifest.

The inline form arrived in 82a184f, the dashboard's "scale from UI" export,
which appended it above the block that was already there rather than
editing it. It also pointed at `/`, which the calc service answers with 404
(apps/calc-stub/src/server.ts falls through to not_found), so the check
would have flapped even if the file had parsed.

Kept the array-of-tables on /health, the endpoint that actually reports
readiness -- it 503s while the ephemeris data is missing and 200s once
it resolves. Left the UI's deliberate scaling edits (auto_stop_machines
off, min_machines_running 2) untouched, and added a comment so the next
export does not silently reintroduce the conflict.

author: devin-ai-integration[bot]
body:
## Summary

An audit of every failure path in the kernel, and fixes for the places where a
failure was discarded, turned into a result that could not be distinguished from
success, or reported so vaguely that the caller had to guess. Nothing here
changes what the kernel does when things work; it changes what it can tell you
when they do not. `./build.sh` stays warning-clean, and the whole shell was
exercised in QEMU (screenshot below).

**Durability the disk never promised.** `ata_write_sector` issued the cache
flush and threw the answer away, so a write that the drive rejected returned 1:

```diff
  outb(ATA_COMMAND, CMD_FLUSH);
- wait_not_busy();
- return 1;
+ if (!wait_not_busy() || transfer_failed())
+         return 0;
```

`transfer_failed()` checks `ERR | DF`, and is now also checked after the data
transfer itself in both directions. Separately, an LBA above 28 bits used to
lose its top bits in `select_sector` and address a *different* sector - so both
entry points now bound it against `total_sectors` first.

**The filesystem could only say "no".** Every `fs_*` function returned 0 for
"file exists", "disk full", "name too long", "disk broken" alike, which is why
the shell printed `could not write x (exists, full, or no space)` - it genuinely
did not know. Added an `enum fs_error` with `fs_last_error()` /
`fs_error_string()`, in the style of `errno`, keeping the boolean returns so no
caller had to change shape:

```c
static int fail(enum fs_error error) { last_error = error; return 0; }
...
return fail(FS_ERR_DISK_FULL);
```

Two failure modes are worth calling out, because they were silent by
construction rather than by omission:

- `fs_read` truncates a file larger than the buffer and returned 1. The bytes
  are real and the caller wants them, so it still returns 1 - but sets
  `FS_ERR_TRUNCATED`, and `cat` and the ELF loader now both check it. `cat
  bigfile` used to print 1023 bytes of a 20 KB file and say nothing.
- `block_at` reported "invalid block", "corrupt block list" and "the indirect
  block would not read" all as `0xFFFFFFFF`.

**Half-finished writes left the disk disagreeing with itself.** `fs_create` and
`fs_append` allocate blocks, write data, then persist metadata, and a failure at
any step left the earlier ones standing: blocks marked used that no file refers
to, or a size covering a block that was never written. Allocations made during
one call are now tracked and released if it does not complete, and `fs_append`
restores the previous size. Metadata ordering is now deliberate rather than
incidental - `write_metadata(freeing)` writes the bitmap before the directory
when growing and after it when freeing, so an interrupted write leaks a block
rather than sharing one between two files. `fs_format` writes the superblock
*last* for the same reason: a format that dies partway leaves a disk that will
not mount, instead of one that mounts and lies.

**Initialisation failures that only printed.** `kheap_init`, `task_init` and
`usermode_init` logged and returned `void`, so `kernel_main` carried on with no
heap or no scheduler. They now return a result; `main` panics on the two that
are fatal and degrades on the one that is not:

```c
if (!kheap_init())
        kpanic("kheap: could not reserve the kernel heap");

int usermode_ready = usermode_init();   /* survivable: no ring 3 */
```

`usermode_init` also frees the stack it allocated if the mapping fails, and
publishes `user_stack_base`/`user_stack_top` only once setup succeeded, rather
than leaving globals pointing at frames it had given back.

**Registrations that quietly did not happen.** `isr_install_handler`,
`isr_install_handler_vector` and `irq_install_handler` dropped out-of-range or
unstorable handlers on the floor. A lost registration surfaces much later as a
keyboard that does not type or an `int 0x80` that faults, with nothing pointing
back at the cause, so all three return a result and the four call sites check
it. `paging_set_flags` and `paging_make_user` likewise could not report "there is
no page mapped there". `pmm_free_frame` refused a double or out-of-range free and
said nothing; it now returns a result and names the address.

**One output buffer instead of two.** `task` and `syscall` each had their own
`out_buf`/`out_len` in `struct task`, and `write` filled one while task death
flushed the other - so a program that exited mid-line lost that line. There is
now a single buffer and a single `task_buffer_output()`, which also flushes when
full instead of running off the end of a 128-byte array.

**The loader trusted arithmetic it should not have.** Three bounds checks were
written as additions on untrusted 32-bit values, which wrap:

```diff
- if (ph->vaddr < USER_LOAD_ADDR || ph->vaddr + ph->memsz > USER_STACK_TOP)
+ if (ph->vaddr < USER_LOAD_ADDR || ph->memsz > USER_STACK_TOP - ph->vaddr)
```

A segment at `0x20001000` claiming `0xFFFFF000` bytes passed the check that
existed to stop exactly that. The program-header table check had the same shape.
The argument page was also treated as best-effort - allocation failure skipped
silently and `paging_map` unchecked - even though `USER_ARGS_ADDR` is a fixed
address the program reads unconditionally, making "no argument page" a program
that faults on its first line rather than a degraded mode.

**Fatal paths.** Five copies of `for (;;) __asm__ volatile ("cli; hlt")` became
`kpanic(reason)`, which prints in red and says why.

**Shell.** Now reports the filesystem's actual reason everywhere, checks
`loader_run`, and rejects a non-numeric task id - `kill abc` parsed as task 0 and
answered "no such task", which is a true statement about a question nobody
asked. Two-thread tests (`racetest`, `pipetest`) used `!task_create(...) ||
!task_create(...)`, which reads as one test and is not: the first thread was left
running with nothing waiting for it. Also fixed a duplicated `append` branch and
help line.

## Verification

`./build.sh` is warning-clean under `-Wall -Wextra`. Booted in QEMU and driven
through the shell: `format`, `install`, `ls`, `write`/`cat`/`append`/`rm`,
`bigfile` (20 KB, exercises indirect blocks - 0 bytes wrong), `run prog read`,
`run prog write`, `pipetest`, `df`, plus each new error path.

![shell showing specific failure reasons](https://app.devin.ai/api/presigned_proxy?token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..yl377JX5jtCmIhdo8Cdfbc8ePT3XyES4ebdZPHXw-Ww)

![bigfile, ring 3 and df after the changes](https://app.devin.ai/api/presigned_proxy?token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..0x41PBmYUymvQFwPQiDO-q756koa3p3NfQ1Lj-Lk7h4)

author: ashproto
body:
## What

`cargo test` intermittently failed one of the four `git_ops::tests::initialize_repository_*` tests. Pre-existing flake, unrelated to any feature work.

## Cause

`TempFolder::new()` built its path as `git-it-init-test-{pid}-{nanos}` and then called `fs::create_dir(&path).unwrap()`. All four tests run on parallel threads in one process, so the pid is shared and two threads can read the same nanosecond; `create_dir` then fails with `AlreadyExists` and the `unwrap()` panics. A *different* one of the four failed on each run, which is what made it look random.

## Fix

Replace the wall-clock stamp with a process-wide `AtomicU32` counter — the pattern the `TempRepo` fixtures in `ops.rs` and `ops_worktree.rs` already use. `pid + counter` cannot collide by construction.

Kept `create_dir` over `create_dir_all` deliberately: a collision is now impossible, so if one ever happens it should panic loudly rather than be absorbed. The now-unused `SystemTime`/`UNIX_EPOCH` import is removed.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test -p git-core initialize_repository -- --test-threads=1` — 4/4 pass
- [x] **Five consecutive full `cargo test` runs, all green** (the flake needed repetition to surface)
- [x] Rebuild produces no new warnings; the two that appear (`git_may_fail`, `read_file`) are pre-existing dead test helpers in other files

## Note

Other `TempRepo` fixtures (`ops_rewrite.rs`, `ops_remote.rs`, `graph.rs`, `ops_merge.rs`) each define their own. Any that derive uniqueness from a timestamp rather than a counter could flake the same way under enough parallelism — not touched here since none are currently failing.

author: quadseven
body:
## Why

The single largest line on the AWS bill was ~$2.40/mo of KMS requests - roughly **800k decrypts a month**, which CloudTrail attributed to `ra-grug`. The cause is a one-character-class bug rather than anything architectural:

```python
_TTL_SECONDS = 5.0          # readiness cache
readinessProbe.periodSeconds = 10   # kubelet, live on grug-api + grug-webhook
```

The cache TTL is SHORTER than the probe period, so it can never hit. Every probe on every pod did a fresh `_check_ssm_kms()`, which is a SecureString read - and a SecureString read is a KMS decrypt. Six running pods at ~6 probes/min lands right at the observed volume.

Worth being precise about what was NOT the problem: `secrets_loader` already wraps its reads in `@lru_cache`, so the application's own secret access was fine all along. Only the probe was uncached in practice.

**Size:** XS

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `custom`/CloudTrail KMS `Decrypt` volume attributed to `ra-grug` drops by roughly 6x after rollout.
- [ ] `/readyz` still reports not-ready within ~60s of a genuinely broken KMS key or AWS auth failure (the probe's actual purpose).
- [ ] No change to probe latency or to the fail-fast botocore config.

## Dependencies

Refs quadseven/infra#819

## Out of scope

- Moving grug's secrets to k8s Secrets so the runtime makes no AWS calls at all. That is the durable fix and is worth doing, but this one-line change captures most of the saving at a fraction of the risk - and it is measurable on its own, which makes the follow-up easier to judge.
- The probe's design: reading a param the pod already needs is deliberate (no extra IAM), and that stays.

body:
Picked up an unpushed local commit from 2026-08-07 and pushed it through the normal PR path (master is protected).

## The fix

`00-defaults.conf` sets `ControlPath ~/.ssh/sockets/%r@%h-%p`, but ssh never creates that directory. On a fresh machine every connection fails with `unix_listener: cannot bind` — hit live on 2026-08-08. Bootstrap now creates it with mode 700.

## Two things fixed before pushing

1. **Mojibake in the status line.** The `✓` was double-encoded (`c3 a2 c2 9c c2 93` instead of `e2 9c 93`), so bootstrap would print `â` garbage on every fresh machine — the one place where output is read carefully. Restored to a proper U+2713.
2. **Author identity.** The commit was authored as `nickboy@NickdeMac-mini.local`, which publishes a machine hostname into a public repo and is not the configured identity. Re-authored to `nickboy@users.noreply.github.com`; the original author date is preserved.

## Known gap

The commit is unsigned. This machine has no signing config at all (`commit.gpgsign`, `gpg.format`, `user.signingkey` are all unset for yadm), so it cannot be signed here — that needs the 1Password agent setup. Not a blocker, but worth knowing the machine is in that state.

Suite 128/128 locally; `bash -n` and shellcheck clean on the bootstrap script.

author: salzaki
body:
Refs #30

Delivers the part of Story 6.1 that can be built today: coverage reporting, the one gap in the
required cases that a component exists for, and a record of which test covers which case.

**This does not close #30**, deliberately, and the commit says `Refs` rather than `Closes`.

## Ten of the thirty cases have nothing to test against

| Cases | Waiting on |
| --- | --- |
| 19–22 | `SqsBatchHandler` |
| 23 | the composition root's serializer context |
| 24 | `OrderMessageProcessor` |
| 25–28 | structured logging and metrics |

None of those components exist — they are Epic 5 and the observability epic. So the story's "all 30
unit cases are implemented" cannot be met now, and its "test batch mapping and serialization" task has
no subject. They are recorded in `docs/testing-strategy.md` as outstanding, with what each waits on,
rather than quietly dropped. A test plan that lists only what has been done stops being a plan.

The other twenty are covered, and the table names the test for each.

## Case 29 was half covered

The store's cancellation was known not to be reclassified, and known not to be swallowed when the SDK
wraps it. Nothing checked that the caller's token reached the SDK at all.

Neither existing test would have caught a store that dropped it, because a cancellation would then
never be raised — the invocation would simply run past its deadline instead. Now asserted against the
token the caller supplied.

## Coverage is collected and published, not enforced

A threshold picked before the pipeline exists would either sit below what the suite already reaches,
proving nothing, or block work unrelated to the code that moved it. The figures are written to the run
summary so the number can be chosen from evidence later.

| Scope | Lines | Branches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total | 89.1% | 66.1% |
| `ReliableOrders.Aws` | 99.4% | 95.7% |
| `ReliableOrders.Core` | 87.8% | 58.4% |

Worth noting what that surfaces: **Core's branch coverage is 58.4%**, well below its line coverage.
That is the kind of thing collecting without a threshold is for.

## A self-review found four things

| Finding | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `if: always()` with `if-no-files-found: error` meant a compile failure produced a second red step complaining about missing coverage, pointing at the wrong cause | Conditioned on the Test step having run. An `if` carrying no status function implicitly gets `success()`, so an explicit `!cancelled()` guard is needed or coverage is skipped exactly when a test fails |
| The collector was on all three test projects, producing three reports where two were meaningless, and I wrote a comment explaining the noise instead of removing it | Collector on the unit test project only. One report, and the explanation is gone with the problem |
| My own comment claimed the figure was "visible on every pull request" when it was a Cobertura XML inside a zip | A summary step writes the table above to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` |
| The audit table maps 30 cases to class names by hand, with no guard — the exact drift problem this repo adds guards for everywhere else | `TestPlanAuditTests` asserts every named class exists and all 30 rows are present |

The guard was mutation-tested rather than trusted: renaming a class in the table fails it, and
deleting a case row fails it. Its comment states plainly that it cannot verify a row's prose, only
that the class exists.

## Summary

Implements authentication and authorization for the MealPlanner app per #58.

### Authentication
- **Web**: Google OAuth 2.0 login with ASP.NET Core cookie session
- **API**: JWT Bearer authentication with shared HMAC-SHA256 signing key
- **No stored passwords** — authentication is entirely delegated to Google

### Authorization
- All Blazor pages require authentication (`[Authorize]` attribute)
- All API endpoint groups require a valid JWT (`RequireAuthorization()`)

| Component | File(s) |

| AppHost config | `src/MealPlanner.AppHost/AppHost.cs` |

### Configuration Required
Users need to provide:
1. A shared JWT signing key (256-bit HMAC)
2. Google OAuth Client ID and Secret (from Google Cloud Console)

These are configured via Aspire user-secrets in development or environment variables in Docker Compose.

- 26 new tests covering JWT generation, caching, and endpoint authorization (401/200)

body: ## Problem A client reported: 1. Asked to log in fresh every day 2. Tracker always shows **Day 1** with the same exercise 3. Changing food day / workout day does not stick ## Root causes 1. **Broken session helpers (regression)** — Recent commits call `invalidateSessionCache()` and `seedAuthenticatedClientSession()` but those exports were never added to `session-restore.ts`. That throws after successful login and during tracker auth, which forces re-login and makes tracker PATCH/reload flaky. 2. **Stale coaching day** — Tracker hub preferred the stored `daily_tracker_days.coaching_day` column, and rebuilds did not refresh it, so the UI could stay on Day 1. 3. **Change day drafts wiped** — Local unsynced diet/workout day selections were discarded whenever a snapshot rebuild bumped `updated_at`, so the UI snapped back to the default Day 1 block. ## Code changes - Implement `invalidateSessionCache` + `seedAuthenticatedClientSession` and use them in restore/login/logout - Prefer live coaching schedule in the tracker hub; refresh `coaching_day` / `coaching_week` on existing rows - Keep applying local tracker drafts across rebuilds (only drop on plan change / stale ids) - On tracker PATCH `401`, show a clear expired-session message and send the client to login - Add `scripts/verify-session-cache.ts` + day-selection asserts in the save-queue verifier ## Ops follow-up (still required for overnight logout) In Supabase Dashboard → Authentication → Sessions for project `zhcedsmvpvpaqezbdiiy`: - Disable or raise **session time-box** - Set **inactivity timeout** ≥ 30 days - Keep JWT expiry ~1 hour App keepalive/cookies already support long sessions; a short dashboard session policy will still force daily login. ## Verification - `npx tsx scripts/verify-session-cache.ts` - `npx tsx scripts/verify-tracker-save-queue.ts` - `npx tsc --noEmit`

- persist one optional explicit `max_grid_import_kw`; no breaker/current/voltage value is guessed
- derive current whole-site grid import from the authoritative server energy-flow model
- calculate `grid_headroom_kw = max(0, limit - current import)`
- calculate `grid_over_limit_kw = max(0, current import - limit)` and utilization percent

- `source_unavailable`
- `within_limit`
- `over_limit`

Every status reports `execution_guard_active=false`. This PR is read-only capacity intelligence only. It does not block or authorize any `turn_on` and does not call Home Assistant services.

author: chihung1024
body:
## Scope

Gate A / P6C closes the remaining old-generation-vs-new-generation cleanup race in browser calculation recovery. P6B made pending reads non-destructive and P6D coordinated job polling, but terminal/404/rejection cleanup still targeted one fixed `pending_calculation_request` key. An old tab could therefore clear recovery state after a sibling had already published a newer idempotency generation.

This PR is now fully integrated on the latest reviewed `main` baseline `33bd4301ec22ff86c392bf9731955a781da7d11e` (PR #147). It changes browser recovery/storage contracts and tests only; no Worker runtime, D1/schema, Python financial/market calculation, auth protocol, workflow, or deployment activation is changed.

## V2 generation model

Each pending idempotency generation has separate localStorage state:

- live: `pending_calculation_request.v2.live.<createdAt>.<idempotencyKey>`
- tombstone: `pending_calculation_request.v2.cleared.<createdAt>.<idempotencyKey>`

The fixed `pending_calculation_request` key remains only as a best-effort compatibility mirror for already-open legacy tabs and is never cleanup authority.

Generation identity (`createdAt + idempotencyKey`) is stable. The live payload may be monotonically enriched with the assigned `jobId`; completion/cleanup is represented independently by a tombstone so a delayed live write cannot erase completion evidence.

## Core safety properties

- old and new generations can coexist; newest valid same-owner live generation is authoritative
- exact cleanup accepts only `{ jobId }` or `{ key }`; unscoped cleanup is a no-op
- terminal completion clears only `job.id`
- calculation-job 404 clears only the requested `jobId`
- trigger response without a job clears only the attempted idempotency key
- definite trigger rejection clears only the attempted idempotency key
- ambiguous trigger failures retain recovery state and are not blindly retried
- a newer tombstone acts as a generation watermark so older live/legacy state cannot resurrect
- a tombstoned idempotency key cannot be revived by delayed `remember()`
- second `remember()` for the same key preserves the original generation timestamp while allowing `jobId` enrichment
- malformed, cross-owner, future, and expired V2 state fail closed
- legacy-only state remains readable when no V2 generation supersedes it
- exact legacy cleanup creates a V2 tombstone without deleting the fixed pointer

## Logout / privacy

`projectStorage` now supports sensitive storage prefixes. Logout removes every `pending_calculation_request.v2.*` entry while preserving neighboring/unrelated origin keys. V2 keys contain an opaque idempotency key and timestamp, not email; the value retains the existing owner field so same-owner validation remains explicit.

## Portfolio integration

`src/stores/portfolio.js` changed only at the pending-state cleanup boundary:

- wrapper now supplies authenticated owner + exact selector
- terminal: `{ jobId: job.id }`
- 404: `{ jobId }`
- no-job trigger response: `{ key: idempotencyKey }`
- definite trigger rejection: `{ key: idempotencyKey }`

The reviewed `portfolio.js` patch is limited to these cleanup hunks. Existing P6D poll-claim behavior, fetch/load contracts, mutation outcome semantics, snapshot handling, and all financial behavior are unchanged.

## Regression coverage

Coverage includes:

- first remember creates V2 live + legacy compatibility mirror
- same-key enrichment preserves generation timestamp
- old/new generations coexist and newest live wins
- clearing old job cannot disturb newer generation
- newer tombstone prevents older generation/legacy resurrection
- legacy-only exact clear creates a tombstone without destructive `removeItem`
- delayed live rewrite cannot erase the tombstone
- tombstoned key cannot be revived
- malformed/cross-owner/expired V2 entries fail closed
- read-only/non-enumerable legacy storage remains compatible
- logout removes all dynamic V2 keys and preserves unrelated keys
- terminal and 404 paths clear exact job generations
- trigger no-job and definite-rejection paths clear exact idempotency generations
- source contract forbids unscoped production `clearPendingCalculationRequest()`

## CI history

- Original service-layer head `a76a8b90e4936b2c7ac26ffebcb957d076c8c34c`: CI #424 SUCCESS on the pre-#147 base.
- Before latest-main reconstruction, recovery was created at `backup-p6c-pre-latest-main-integration-a76a8b9`.
- The branch was reconstructed from current main `33bd4301ec22ff86c392bf9731955a781da7d11e` and the reviewed P6C changes were reapplied rather than merging divergent history.
- Integrated head `9a7bfcb05d0895387a1c88d11ed98e6827e931e1`: CI #428 — Python SUCCESS, Worker/D1/Recovery Evidence Gate SUCCESS; Frontend failed only because two pre-existing source-shape assertions still required the old unscoped cleanup call.
- Production exact-generation behavior was not reverted. The stale assertions were updated to require exact job/key cleanup.
- Final candidate head `80d417c125797020fab1b6be401084049f2e25e3`: CI #429 / run `31291902357` SUCCESS.
- CI #429 all three jobs SUCCESS: Python tests + measured coverage baseline; Frontend contracts + build; Worker security/deployment + Recovery Evidence Gate + local D1 baseline.

## Governance synchronization

`docs/engineering/PRODUCT_INTEGRITY_EXECUTION.md` is updated from the stale P5B/#139 state to current truth. It records Gate A as active and narrows subsequent execution to:

1. Gate A — P6C generation-safe recovery
2. Gate B — P5C3B server-side atomic DELETE
3. Gate C — Schema-2 transaction-integrity preflight / strict oversell qualification
4. Gate D — calculation reproducibility evidence
5. fresh architecture review before Schema 3, canonical-ledger, provider-abstraction, or broad cleanup work

## Safety / recovery

- Latest qualification base/main: `33bd4301ec22ff86c392bf9731955a781da7d11e`
- Original P6C recovery: `backup-pre-product-integrity-p6c-2ee97e1`
- Pre-latest-main-integration recovery: `backup-p6c-pre-latest-main-integration-a76a8b9`
- Work branch: `pr-product-integrity-p6c-calculation-generation-storage`
- Final candidate head: `80d417c125797020fab1b6be401084049f2e25e3`

## Merge blockers / final qualification

- any production clear path remains unscoped
- old terminal/404/rejection can clear a newer generation
- tombstoned generation can be revived
- legacy fixed key becomes cleanup authority
- logout leaves V2 sensitive state behind or deletes unrelated origin keys
- unrelated Worker/D1/schema/financial/auth/workflow/deployment changes
- final exact-head CI failure
- unresolved review thread
- `main` drift from the reviewed qualification base before merge

After merge, Gate A remains open until post-main CI/Pages, a real portfolio-update smoke run, and a post-Gate-A recovery ref are verified.

## Objet

Script d'enregistrement groupé pour la LISTE DE CHARROI REMORQUE d'Ets MU NLEMVO NZAMBI J (NIF `A2309753C`, Gombe) — 10 remorques.

## Procédure suivie

Le script reprend le modèle des `scripts/bulk-register-*.ts` existants, mais avec la **grille 2026** au lieu du barème legacy : `calculateTax()` n'a pas de branche `remorque` et retomberait sur les règles par CV, ce qui ne s'applique pas à une remorque. Le calcul passe donc par `calculer2026({ categorie: 'remorque', tonnage, regime })` — exactement le chemin qu'emprunte `app/(dashboard)/create/page.tsx` en mode `new2026`.

Conventions reprises telles quelles :

- séquence continue à partir d'un seul `getSecureSequence()` pour que les bordereaux se suivent
- `generateDeclarationId()` / `generateNoteId()` pour les identifiants
- date via `getNowOrBusinessHours()`
- `vehicle.category = 'Véhicule remorque'`, statut `Payée`
- `meta` renseigné avec `tariffMode: 'new2026'`, `tariffLabel`, `regime`, `manualBaseAmount`, `manualTaxpayer`
- conversion FC via `TAUX_FC` (2244.76)

Ajout par rapport aux scripts existants : un mode `--dry-run` qui affiche les tarifs sans écrire en base.

## Paramètres retenus

| Paramètre | Valeur |
|---|---|
| NIF | `A2309753C` |
| Régime fiscal | PP — personne physique |
| Statut des déclarations | Payée |
| Tranche tarifaire | Remorque > 10.000 kg (90.20 USD en PP) |

## Tarifs calculés

```
[01] 9279AM10   SHANDONG  10t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | LA9940B32S0NJZ811   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[02] 6676AW05   CIMC      32t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | LJRP1358263000597   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[03] 1709AN10   FUWA      32t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | MW1030614           | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[04] 5588AS01   CIMC      36t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | LJRB133BXE201515937 | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[05] 5020AV/05  HENRED    36t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | AA9A236MA8TKR1343   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[06] 1726AN10   CIMC      33t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | JF2GETZDVAEM20LBD   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[07] 5161AV/05  HENRED    36t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | AA9A236MBTKR1412    | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[08] 7790AN10   CIMC      32t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | LJRP1338593074378   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[09] 7508AL10   CIMC      35t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | 8B069865            | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg
[10] 0826AK/10  CIMC      32t → 90.20 USD (202 477 FC) | LJRP123D3E2017448   | Remorque — Plus de 10.000 kg

Total principal: 902.00 USD (2 024 774 FC)
Frais bancaires: +4.00 USD par bordereau, soit 40.00 USD
```

## Deux points qui méritent l'œil du relecteur

**1. Tranche tarifaire forcée pour l'UM 01.** Le tonnage de la liste est un poids total en charge. L'UM 01 est à 10 t : `calculer2026()` coupe à `tonnage <= 10` et l'aurait placée dans la tranche 2.500–10.000 kg (80.60 USD). Elle atteint en réalité la limite des 10.000 kg et relève de la tranche supérieure comme le reste du charroi. La sélection de la tranche passe donc par la constante `TONNAGE_TARIFAIRE`, commune aux 10 unités. **Le tonnage réel de chaque remorque reste porté tel quel sur la déclaration** (`vehicle.weight`) : seul le calcul du tarif est unifié.

**2. Châssis généré pour l'UM 06** (plaque 1726AN10), absent de la liste source : `JF2GETZDVAEM20LBD`. Même parti pris que `bulk-register-trans-continental.ts`, à une différence près — le numéro est dérivé de la plaque plutôt que tiré au hasard, pour que le dry-run et l'exécution réelle donnent la même valeur et qu'un ré-run ne fabrique pas un second numéro. À remplacer par le vrai dès qu'il est connu.

## Vérification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` → aucune erreur

Aucune écriture en base n'a été effectuée depuis la session : la base TAX-DGRK n'y est pas joignable (résolution DNS bloquée vers `*.supabase.co`, et le connecteur Supabase de ce compte n'expose que `aonoseke-iptv` et `Alpha Import Prod`).
