body: ## Why Llama AIO couldn’t run llama.cpp on NixOS Official llama.cpp Linux releases are **Ubuntu** builds (`llama-*-bin-ubuntu-*.tar.gz`). Those ELFs hardcode the FHS dynamic linker: `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` Stock NixOS does not provide that path, so `execve` fails with a misleading **“No such file or directory”** even though `~/.llama-aio-vs/.../llama-server` exists. Setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` alone cannot fix a missing program interpreter. ## What this PR does - Detect NixOS / missing FHS linker - Probe `llama-server --version` after install and before start - Auto-wrap with **`steam-run`** when available - Fall back to a nixpkgs **`llama-server` on PATH** - Otherwise show clear guidance: enable `programs.nix-ld.enable = true`, install `steam-run`, or use nixpkgs `llama-cpp` - Surface the failure in the sidebar + README Notes - Version bump to **0.1.6** — release: https://github.com/erpel-dev/llama-aio-vs/releases/tag/0.1.6 ## Test plan - [x] `npm test` (111 passing) - [x] `npm run compile` - [x] Packaged `llama-aio-vs-0.1.6.vsix` and attached to release `0.1.6` - [ ] On NixOS without nix-ld: install backend → warning with fix options - [ ] On NixOS with `steam-run` on PATH: Start server wraps successfully - [ ] On NixOS with nixpkgs `llama-cpp` on PATH: falls back when downloaded binary can’t run - [ ] On Ubuntu/Debian: unchanged direct launch

author: thodson-usgs
body:
Phase 0 cleanup from #1. Bug fix, no API change.

## The bug

`openURL` combines its `verify` argument with the `Authentication` object's using
a boolean `and`:

```python
verify = verify and auth.verify        # owslib/util.py:175
```

`verify` is tri-state — `True`, `False`, or **a path to a CA bundle** — and `and`
returns its second operand when the first is truthy:

```python
>>> "/etc/ssl/certs/custom-ca.pem" and True
True
```

So a caller-supplied bundle path is replaced by `True` whenever `auth.verify` is
`True`, which is its default. The path is silently dropped and verification falls
back to the system trust store. No error, no warning — the request simply
succeeds against a different set of certificate authorities than the caller asked
for.

## Reproduce on `master`

```python
from unittest import mock
from owslib.util import Authentication, openURL

with mock.patch('owslib.util.requests.request') as request:
    request.return_value = mock.Mock(status_code=200, headers={})
    openURL('http://example.com/wms',
            verify='/etc/ssl/certs/custom-ca.pem',
            auth=Authentication())
    print(request.call_args[1]['verify'])

# master: True          <- the CA bundle path is gone
# fixed : /etc/ssl/certs/custom-ca.pem
```

## Fix

Combine the two explicitly. Either side turning verification **off** still wins,
and an `Authentication` carrying its own bundle still takes precedence, so the
only behaviour that changes is the case that was losing the path.

| `verify` | `auth.verify` | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `True` | `True` | `True` | `True` |
| `True` | `False` | `False` | `False` |
| `False` | `True` | `False` | `False` |
| `False` | `False` | `False` | `False` |
| **`/ca.pem`** | **`True`** | **`True`** | **`/ca.pem`** |
| `/ca.pem` | `False` | `False` | `False` |
| `True` | `/auth.pem` | `/auth.pem` | `/auth.pem` |
| `/ca.pem` | `/auth.pem` | `/auth.pem` | `/auth.pem` |

One row changes. Every test in `tests/test_util_verify.py` covers a row, and the
suite fails on `master` with exactly that one:

```
FAILED test_ca_bundle_survives_a_default_authentication
E   AssertionError: assert True == '/.../custom-ca.pem'
1 failed, 8 passed
```

## Relationship to #609

Related, but **not** the problem that issue describes. The reporter's complaint
was that `auth.verify` gets mutated; the current code assigns to a local, so that
part appears already resolved. This is a different defect on the same line.

## Verification

```
tests/test_util_verify.py    9 passed  (1 fails on master)
full offline suite         246 passed
flake8 owslib/             clean
```

body:
## Purpose

Finish the runtime acceptance for `demeet2k/Athena#160` by proving that one-call agent bootstrap/refresh survives **real cold MCP process succession** and by repairing the source-parity race discovered while designing that witness.

## BOOT-003 — pre-snapshot shared Git freshness

The promoted R4 bootstrap composed prompt/world state first and could allow continuation hydration to shared-sync Git only afterward. A clean-behind cold process could therefore return a packet whose `git_head` was observed before the same call fast-forwarded to the shared continuation tip.

This PR adds an outer `agent_bootstrap_shared_fresh` membrane:

```text
SYNC_SHARED_GIT
→ COMPOSE prompt/frontier/issue/sibling world snapshot
→ COMPOSE continuation/handoff snapshot
```

Modes:
- `REQUIRED`: failed/unverified shared sync -> `BOOTSTRAP_HOLD` + `BOOTSTRAP_SHARED_FRONTIER_HOLD`;
- `BEST_EFFORT`: explicit unverified boot state;
- `DISABLED`: local/offline mode with no shared-current claim.

Unless explicitly overridden, continuation freshness inherits the same boot-level mode.

`BOOT_SYNC_SHARED_GIT_BEFORE_COMPOSITE_SNAPSHOT`.

## Direct BOOT-003 regressions

- clean-behind checkout fast-forwards **before** packet `address.git_head` is computed;
- dirty REQUIRED checkout holds instead of falsely claiming shared freshness.

## Hermetic SCHED V3 contract identity

The cold-process fixture vendors the exact three SCHED V3 contract bytes already pinned by FrontierRuntime and verifies them using `git hash-object` before the witness starts:

- `reducer.py` -> `122802a3cec6f50b692d819b18024b50be39bab8`
- `ready.py` -> `975d61ab5ddf42e6e06c7304fc0fc330ca4b24d5`
- `claim.py` -> `4757f4eaf8180cf356dc0e940b9019177f1c0a8a`

These fixtures are identity inputs only; the child MCP does not dynamically execute repository scheduler code.

## Real stdio MCP cold-process acceptance

`tests/test_agent_bootstrap_cold_process_continuation.py` launches actual independent processes via:

```text
python -m athena_mcp --db <isolated.sqlite> --git-root <isolated clone>
```

and communicates only through JSON-RPC stdio.

Acceptance chronology:

1. Prep MCP creates one valid rehydration loop transition and publishes it to a shared bare Git remote, then exits.
2. Two new clones + two new MCP processes start only after that transition is shared.
3. Both discover/call `athena_agent_bootstrap` and reconstruct the same factorized shared address + same continuation/handoff digest.
4. Cold process A creates and advances the second verified transition and publishes it through the public Git remote-publish membrane.
5. Process B receives **no packet from A**; it calls only its own `athena_agent_refresh` and must observe a changed `rehydration_continuation_digest` with `rehydration_handoff` in the affected cone.
6. A third brand-new clone/process C cold-boots after transition two and must independently reconstruct the exact address B obtained through refresh.

The issue-pressure sensor is exercised through a local HTTP fixture using the real GET-only provider code path via `ATHENA_GITHUB_API_URL`; there is no external GitHub network/token dependency in the child processes.

## No chat-memory transport

The child MCP processes share only:
- the Git remote;
- the read-only local issue-provider fixture.

No runtime object, prompt text, handoff packet, or session state is copied from A to B/C.

## Authority boundary

- `BOOT_PACKET != HIGHER_AUTHORITY`
- `CONTINUATION_STATE != EXECUTION_AUTHORIZATION`
- `WHAT_NEXT != WHAT_TO_REHYDRATE`
- `ONE_CALL_BOOT != SKIP_FRESHNESS`
- `LOCAL_BOOT_VIEW != SHARED_CURRENT_BOOT_VIEW`

## Promotion/closure boundary

This PR remains draft until its **exact head** passes the full five-gate MCP CI:
- syntax
- full unit suite (including the real stdio cold-process acceptance)
- complete critical-invariants
- MCP smoke
- host-verified PROMOTION.2

After exact-head PASS, master must be re-read and compare must remain `behind_by=0` before merge.

body: This updates the rapier dependency to 0.35.0, bring massive performance improvements. This actually uses a special version of rapier: `0.35.0-glamx0.2` which is essentially the same as `0.35.0` but with its glamx dependency pinned to `0.2` instead of the latest `0.3`. That way, `bevy_rapier` can be compatible with bevy 0.19 which still depends on an outdated version of `glam`. We will switch to the "normal" rapier version `0.35.0` when bevy 0.20 gets released with the latest `glam`. You can see more there: https://github.com/dimforge/rapier/pull/973 I’m attaching the summary on performance improvements below (copied from the Rapier PR) for visibility. ----- The graphs show performance comparisons of various 2D and 3D physics engines in single-thread and multi-thread mode. The benchmarks are run on a Macbook Pro M4 Max. The general trends are that the new rapier is: - about 50% (single-thread) or 300% (multi-thread) faster than the previous version. - about on-par-to-slightly-faster than Box3D (especially on single-threaded simulations). - about on-par-to-slightly-slower than Box2D (especially on multi-threaded simulations). - about 150% (single-thread) or 280% (multi-thread) faster than Avian. - about 50% (single-thread) or 100% (multi-thread) faster than Jolt. It is also significantly more stable on stacks than Jolt.

## Summary

Adds a temporary maintenance mode to the Telegram bot that pauses all functionality when there are no active power disconnections. This allows the bot to gracefully handle periods of inactivity without processing user commands.

## Key Changes

- **Added `BOT_MAINTENANCE_MODE` configuration**: New environment variable (defaults to `true`) that can be toggled via `serverless.yml` to enable/disable maintenance mode
- **Implemented `setupMaintenanceMode()` method**: When enabled, the bot replies to all incoming messages with a maintenance notice instead of processing commands
- **Added maintenance notice message**: Ukrainian-language message informing users that the bot is paused and will resume when disconnections resume
- **Updated bot initialization**: Constructor now checks maintenance mode flag and skips normal menu/keyboard setup when active

## Implementation Details

- Configuration is centralized in `src/config.ts` following project conventions
- Maintenance mode is checked early in `BotService` constructor to avoid unnecessary initialization
- The maintenance handler is simple and lightweight - just replies with a notice message
- All changes are marked with TODO comments indicating this is temporary functionality
- Message includes a link to the project's Telegram chat for user support

## Deployment Notes

To re-enable the bot when disconnections resume:
1. Set `BOT_MAINTENANCE_MODE: 'false'` in `serverless.yml`
2. Deploy the changes
3. Remove the temporary code blocks (marked with TODO comments)

author: josebert2001
body:
Adds lecture notes for **PHY 128 — General Practical Physics II**, transcribed from Section 1 of the departmental practical manual (*First Year University Physics Practical Manual (Light, Sound, Electricity and Magnetism), Volume 2*) — the four theoretical-background chapters a student is expected to have read before walking into the lab.

Section 2 (the experiments themselves, pp. 31–98) is **not** transcribed yet; that is the natural next pass.

## What's here

- `src/data/lectureNotes/phy128.js` — four topics, one per manual chapter: general introduction & lab-notebook rules, geometrical optics, sound waves, electricity & magnetism. 165 sections, 50 display equations, 249 inline expressions. The manual's own equation numbers are preserved as captions so a student can cross-reference the printed copy.
- `public/lecture-notes/phy-128/` — 21 figures, WebP, 1.5 MB total (down from 16 MB of PNG), via `scripts/optimize-lecture-images.mjs`.
- Wired into **both** catalogues that take the course, each with its own `noteCoverage` — the two PHY 128 outlines diverge sharply, and the shared note file carries no indices of its own (as `departments.test.js` requires).

## Judgement calls worth a reviewer's eye

**Fig 2.2 (concave mirror) is omitted.** It is clipped in the source document itself — the scan begins below the top of the ray diagram, leaving only the mirror arc and one ray — so there is no crop that recovers it. A `note` section stands in its place, explaining the concave case against the convex figure rather than showing a broken diagram. Worth a re-scan of that page if the original is available.

**The scans are page regions.** Each carried a band of surrounding body prose and reverse-page bleed-through, so all 21 were cropped to the diagram plus its printed caption. Because the caption is inside the image, the `caption` prop says what the figure *shows* rather than repeating its number.

**Five genuine errors in the manual are corrected**, each with a `note` beside it so a student reading the printed copy is not confused:

| Where | Printed | Correct |
|---|---|---|
| p.11 example (ii) | squares the tension → `m = 0.09 kg/m` | `8.65 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m` |
| p.12 example (iii) | `936.4 N` — does not follow from its own substitutions (they give 9216 N), and uses `ℓ = 0.32` for its own `0.34` | `900 N` |
| p.19 eqn 4.10 | internal resistance of *n* cells in parallel = `n/r` | `r/n` — as the manual's own "To Note" says four paragraphs later |
| p.8 §2.4 | `r = 890°` | `90°` |
| p.8 §2.3 | "equation 5.8" | equation 2.8 (there is no Chapter 5) |

Cross-reference slips that change no physics (figure 7.3 for 4.3, 7.10 for 4.10, Figure 4.4 for 4.5, Figure 4.3 for 4.11) and scanning damage to a few words are silently right, and listed in the file header.

**Coverage gaps are recorded rather than papered over.** The Cybersecurity outline has no optics or sound items, so chapters 2–3 claim nothing there. Data Science gets no coverage for capacitors, and — despite its title — Chapter 4 contains no magnetism content, so that outline's tangent-galvanometer topic stays unclaimed.

## Verification

- `node scripts/validate-modules.mjs` — passes (49 modules / 4 tracks, 112 courses / 2 catalogues)
- `npm test` — 305 tests, 29 files, all pass
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (4 pre-existing warnings elsewhere in the tree)
- `npm run build` — passes
- Every figure reference resolves to a file on disk, with none unused
- Every LaTeX expression (50 display + 249 inline) renders through KaTeX without error

The `phy128-*.js` chunk in the build output is the pre-existing shared lecture-notes chunk (cos121 + ent221 + ent221Quiz + mth121) that rolldown renamed when this file joined it; it builds at 837 kB with these notes in it. It stays outside the 300 kB precache limit by the deliberate design documented in `vite.config.js`.

`sharp` was installed with `--no-save` for the image pass and removed afterwards; `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are untouched.

author: kirillinda
body:
## What this fixes

Reported: bolts and rivets came out as unrecognisable blobs, circles became long
smears, and parts that were drawn isometric ended up looking flat. Baked-in
lettering suffered too.

The cause is not that the model is weak — it is that it was doing exactly what it
was trained to do. `4x-UltraSharpV2` is trained with a degradation pipeline (JPEG,
noise, blur), so it has learned that small high-frequency structure is **noise to
remove** before resynthesising a clean surface. Hand-placed 2–4 px game art sits
squarely in that band, so the model erased real detail and invented a smooth
surface over it.

Measured across the whole archive with the new `tools/gsr/scan_detail.py`
(gradient-energy retention: 1.0 = fine structure survived): **143 assets had lost
more than 30% of their fine structure, 23 more than half.** Concrete failures:

| asset | what happened | retention before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DATA/gui/sideex.bmp` | a **square** icon ring came out **circular** | 0.72 | 0.94 |
| `special.bonus/hp100.bmp` | round speckles became diagonal gashes | 0.50 | 0.98 |
| `enemy_gold/roger.bmp` (strut/bolts) | melted strut, soft bolts | 0.89 | 1.00 |
| `enemy_gold/roger.bmp` (lettering) | mushy baked-in "ROGER" | 0.85 | 0.99 |

![Detail preservation before/after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kirillinda/jng-gold-hd/95be989dbf3f95996bde7ac0ad64b86924b103d2/docs/images/detail-preservation.png)

*Both columns are real pipeline output; "before" is the same code configured the old way.*

## On the classifier idea

The suggestion was to detect object classes (bolt, pipe, window, wing) and run a
separate upscale per class. I didn't take that route, for reasons that the
measurements make concrete rather than theoretical:

- It doesn't address the actual failure. The problem isn't that a bolt needs a
  *different style* — it's that a 3 px bolt is below the scale the model treats as
  signal. Handing the same 3 px bolt to a differently-tuned GAN gets the same
  erasure, because no new information exists at that size.
- Compositing per-class results reintroduces seams at every class boundary, on
  sprites often smaller than 32×32.
- There are no labels for 90s pixel art, and zero-shot detectors are unreliable at
  these sizes — a mislabel silently corrupts art with no way to notice.

But the *instinct* — that the pipeline should adapt per image instead of applying
one global setting — is right, and it's what this PR implements. It just keys off
**measurable image properties** instead of semantic classes, which needs no labels
and produces no seams.

## How it actually works

Two independent corrections, because they fix different halves of the problem:

- **Scale matching** — NEAREST-upscale 2× before the model, BOX-downscale 2× after.
  Invents nothing (each source pixel becomes an exact 2×2 block) but presents a
  3 px rivet as a 6 px structure, above the band the model learned to destroy.
  *This is what fixes geometry* — it's what turns the circle back into a square.
- **Detail re-injection** — add the source's own fine structure back on top of the
  model output, at a strength **solved per image** so the result's gradient energy
  matches the source's. *This is what fixes texture*; scale matching alone can't.

Both candidates (plain and scale-matched) are generated and the better one kept per
image, because scale matching is a large win on detailed art but a small loss on
smooth glow/flare sprites and dithered flats, where no fine structure was at risk
(Atarix's green LCD drifted olive under it). All decisions are made **once per
image**, never per frame — a sheet's cells are consecutive animation frames, and
switching approach mid-animation would make the texture pop.

`tools/gsr/lab.py` renders any set of settings side by side with scores; it is how
every choice here was made.

## Also in this PR

- **`frames = N, -1, -1` sheets.** The defs declare animation layout two ways and
  only one was parsed, so **141 sheets** — every walking and dying character among
  them — were upscaled as a single image, smearing detail across frame borders. The
  orientation was determined from the pixels (adjacent-frame similarity), not
  guessed. A `MIN_CELL` guard also catches 9 pre-existing misparses that were
  slicing images into 1-px strips.
- **`4x-UltraSharpV2` was silently doing nothing.** Its attention blocks overflow
  FP16 and return all-NaN; the plausibility guard then substituted LANCZOS for
  *every* image, so the "max quality" model produced no AI upscaling at all. Now
  detected at load and run in FP32.
- **Sprites ship as real 32-bit BMPs** (`BITMAPV4HEADER`, explicit alpha mask)
  instead of TGA bytes written to `.bmp` paths, so the art opens in GIMP/Krita/any
  viewer. Safe for the engine: `CRXTexture::Load`'s colour-key pass masks alpha out
  of its comparison (`and $0xffffff`) and only overwrites exact key matches, and BMP
  is decoded by SDL2 core so it carries none of PNG's Windows risk.

## Throughput

Chasing the runtime turned up a separate 30x problem. Every sprite is a different
size, so the model saw a new tensor shape on nearly every call (1555 distinct
shapes) and MIOpen re-selected kernels each time. Measured on 24 forwards of
identical total pixels, fresh process:

| | per image |
|---|---|
| all the same shape | **0.042 s** |
| all different shapes | **1.263 s** |

Inputs are now padded up to one of ~250 ladder shapes and cropped back — ~5%
wasted pixels, output-neutral to within 2/255 (FP16 noise). Steady-state
throughput went from ~0.5 to ~5.9 images/sec.

Worth recording the negative result too: raising `GSR_TILE` to use more VRAM makes
it **slower**, not faster (300 s / 68 s / 35 s for tile 2048 / 512 / 256 on the
same large art). The numbers are in `run.sh` so the trap isn't re-sprung.

## Verification

Full clean rebuild of all 1854 assets, **0 retries and 4 LANCZOS fallbacks**.

- `verify_hd.py` — 1854 entries, 1643 MB, every image exactly 4×, manual correctly
  excluded. **OK**
- `scan_quality.py` — 1783 paired images, median error 2.45/255, max 23.80, **zero**
  above the corruption threshold. **CLEAN**
- `scan_detail.py` — structure retention across the archive:

  | | before | after |
  |---|---|---|
  | median retention | 0.908 | **0.972** |
  | assets losing >30% of fine structure | 143 | **35** |
  | assets losing >50% | 23 | **9** |

- `verify_sdl_bmp.py` drives the **real libSDL2** through `ctypes` and confirms the
  alpha round-trips byte-for-byte; ImageMagick and GdkPixbuf also open the files
  with alpha.

One caveat on `scan_detail`: it compares the AA output against a magenta-keyed
source, so small sprites with a lot of perimeter score artificially low (the hard
key edge becomes a soft alpha edge). It is reliable as a before/after comparison —
both sides share the bias — but the absolute numbers understate small sprites.

## Caveat

The build is verified by measurement and inspected by eye, but **not yet
playtested** end to end.

body:
💡 **What**:
- Modified `init_db()` in `app/routes.py` to create composite indexes `idx_roasts_user_created` and `idx_roasts_ip_user_created` to turn full table scans into covering index searches.
- Restructured `index()` route rate-limit queries from un-indexable function evaluations like `date(created_at) = date('now')` to index-friendly range-based scans like `created_at >= date('now')`.
- Added comprehensive unit tests in `tests/test_routes.py` to assert correct index creation, index utilization via SQLite's `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, and rate-limiting functionality.
- Documented key learnings in Bolt's performance journal `.jules/bolt.md`.

🎯 **Why**:
Using `date(created_at)` prevents SQLite from using indexes on `created_at` (causing O(N) full table scans). Combining this with a lack of composite indexes meant rate-limiting checks and history loading on every request degraded linearly as database records grew.

📊 **Impact**:
- Turns $O(N)$ full table scans into extremely fast $O(\log N)$ covering index scans for rate limiting.
- Avoids temporary memory B-Tree sorting for history loading.
- High efficiency and scalability.

🔬 **Measurement**:
Verified using SQLite's `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` showing zero full-table scans or temporary B-Trees, and all 5 unit tests pass.

author: brayflex
body:
### Controls & Keyboard Shortcuts
- **Arrow Key Panning:** Added the ability to pan the canvas workspace using the standard `Arrow` keys (panning 5 cells / 100px per press).
- **Ctrl+Drag Panning:** You can now hold `Ctrl` to pan around the canvas. The cursor changes to a "grab" hand (mirroring the Spacebar panning behavior).
- **Clear Selection (Backspace/Delete):** Hitting `Backspace` or `Delete` now explicitly erases the cells within your active selection. It is safeguarded to do nothing if no selection is active, preventing accidental full canvas wipes.
- **Invert Shortcuts:**
  - `i`: Inverts the bits (pixels) within your current selection (or the entire canvas if no selection is active).
  - `Shift+i`: Inverts the selection area itself, selecting all previously unselected cells and deselecting all selected cells.

### Tools & Layout
- **Toolbar Layout:** Moved the Size slider out of the main toolstrip and into the secondary canvas controls bar (left of the Invert/Clear buttons).
- **Canvas Tabs:** Moved the Main Canvas / Test Canvas tabs to the far right of the secondary toolbar for better visual hierarchy.
- **Size Display Syncing:** Fixed an issue where the displayed size number on the size button didn't update when switching between tools (e.g., from a size 3 Pencil to a size 1 Circle). The button now strictly respects and displays the active tool's remembered size.

### Selection, Paste & Cut Bug Fixes
- **Select Tool Improvements:**
  - Shift-clicking a single pixel with a drawing tool (like the Pencil) active no longer accidentally draws or erases that pixel before creating the selection.
  - The cursor now reliably turns into a crosshair `cell` pointer when holding Shift.
  - Holding Shift seamlessly highlights the Select tool button, unifying the visual feedback without duplicating logic.
- **Paste Centering:** When you paste, the preview overlay and the final pasted pixels are now perfectly centered on your mouse cursor, rather than awkwardly affixing from the top-left corner.
- **Paste Bounds:** Pasting now rigorously respects your active selection boundaries. Pixels outside the selected area will not be pasted.
- **Cut Fix:** Fixed a bug where using the Cut tool wasn't actually removing the pixels from the original selected area. The pixels are now correctly erased after copying to the clipboard.

author: seantalts
body:
Roadmap item 4, partially: `Model.optimize()` runs stan's own L-BFGS — the one behind CmdStan's `optimize` — over the same gradient the sampler uses.

```python
r = model.optimize(seed=1)
r["mu"], r.lp        # every CSV column at the mode, and the lp there
r.unconstrained      # the point on the sampler's scale

fit = model.sample(inits=r.unconstrained)   # which is the reason to have it
```

## It returns the posterior mode, and refuses CmdStan's default

CmdStan's `optimize` defaults to `jacobian=0` — the penalized maximum likelihood. stanli cannot offer that: the change-of-variables Jacobian is folded into the graph at lowering time, and the model adapter ignores the template flag entirely. So `jacobian=False` would have silently returned the posterior **mode** under the other name, and the two differ for any constrained parameter — which is most models.

Both the C ABI and Python refuse it and say why. Excluding the Jacobian is possible in principle (`lower.cpp` already collects `jac_slots` separately) and that is what a real fix would be.

## What it took

`ExecutorModel` grew the rest of the stan model concept the services reach through: `log_prob` in its `std::vector` form as well as its Eigen one, `constrained_param_names`, `write_array` in both forms, `get_dims`, and a `transform_inits` that throws — unconstraining a user's starting values needs the **inverse** parameter transforms, and only the forward ones exist.

One of those was a real bug the test caught: `constrained_param_names` must **append**. The services push their own leading columns and then call it to add the model's, so assigning wipes them and leaves every row wider than its header.

## Verification

The oracle is a conjugate normal whose posterior mode is a precision-weighted mean, computed as arithmetic rather than by a second implementation — "the optimizer returned something" and "the optimizer returned the mode" look identical otherwise. It also pins the reported `lp` to the model's own lp at that point, since `BFGSLineSearch::logp()` already un-negates the objective and negating it again is a silent sign slip.

32/32 ctest, 17/17 `tests/test_python.py`, 119/119 corpus unchanged.

## Pathfinder is deliberately not here

The adapter is now complete enough that stan's single-path service compiles and runs against it and returns `rc=0` — but the draws come back empty, because the parameter writer is never called. An entry point that silently returns nothing is worse than none, so it is cut rather than shipped. That looks like one debugging session, not a design problem.

Multi-path is a harder blocker: it runs its paths through `tbb::parallel_for` and this build stubs TBB out (`tests/tbb_stub.cpp` provides the one symbol stan-math's rev core needs), so it does not link at all.

author: sriram-52
body:
Prerequisite for the TypeScript 7 bump, which is blocked on the layout this fixes. ## The problem `worker` imported `core` by reaching into its source tree: ```ts import { connectJetstream, buildConsumer } from '../../core/src/nats' ``` and `worker/tsconfig.json` included `../core/src`. That inclusion is what pushed tsc's inferred `rootDir` up a level and produced the doubled `dist/worker/src` + `dist/core/src` layout — which `docker-compose.yml`, the deployment manifests and `mikro-orm.config.ts` all hardcoded. Any tsconfig change that moved the inference relocated the output silently: build green, container dead. `core` was never a consumable package at all. Its manifest claimed `"main": "index.ts"` and **that file did not exist**; there was no `exports`, and `worker` never declared it as a dependency. The workspace added in #6 was decorative for this relationship. TypeScript 7 makes it unavoidable: it rejects the inferred rootDir outright (`TS6059` on every `../core/src` file). Pinning `rootDir: ".."` silences it while keeping the flaw, so this fixes the cause instead. ## What changed `core` builds itself — index barrel, `main`/`types`/`exports`, its own emit to `core/dist`. `worker` declares `"@bemi-db/core": "workspace:*"`, imports it by name, and its tsconfig no longer reaches outside its own directory. `mikro-orm.config.ts` loses both globs over the emitted tree. Entities are imported classes, so a layout change is now a compile error instead of an ORM that silently starts with **zero entities**; the migrations directory is exported by `core`, the only package that should know its own layout. A shared `tsconfig.base.json` replaces the drifting copies. It sets `module`/`moduleResolution` to `node16` — TS7 removes `node10` outright, not just deprecates it. Emit was diffed against the old output: still CommonJS, still **15** `design:type` metadata calls on `Change`, which MikroORM depends on. `turbo.json` expresses build order as a graph. `worker`'s build script used to start by building `core`, which is a workspace fact, not a worker fact. **This also fixes a latent CI failure**: `pnpm --recursive run typecheck` never built core, so worker's typecheck could not resolve `@bemi-db/core`'s types on a clean checkout. Verified by deleting `core/dist` and re-running — it failed before, passes now. Tooling is shared: a pnpm `catalog:` for everything both packages use (`typescript` had already drifted, `^5.4.5` vs `^5.5.4`), prettier moved to the root, `lint`/`format:check` routed through turbo like the other tasks, and hooks moved from a hand-rolled `core.hooksPath` to husky + lint-staged. Two traps worth knowing, both hit during this work: - **prettier's config resolves upward, its ignore file does not.** It comes from the working directory. The package scripts pass `--ignore-path ../.prettierignore`; dropping that as redundant makes every ignore entry silently stop applying. Noted in the file itself. - **`prepare: husky` breaks the image build.** husky is a devDependency, so the `--prod` stage cannot run it, and the build context has no `.git`. Guarded with `|| true`. ## Coordination The entrypoints move: ``` dist/worker/src/index.js -> dist/src/index.js dist/worker/src/reset.js -> dist/src/reset.js ``` `docker-compose.yml` and the Dockerfile are updated here. The deployment manifests that name these paths live outside this repo and are updated separately. Merge order does not matter and merging affects nothing running, since those manifests are only read at deploy time and nothing deploys automatically. The one thing to hold to is that **both sides are in before the next deploy** — otherwise the containers point at paths that do not exist and fail at start with a module resolution error. ## The gate now runs in CI It was being run by hand and pasted into descriptions. That is the wrong place for it: one local run was **silently flaky** — `grep -q` under `pipefail` reports SIGPIPE as failure once the log outgrows a pipe buffer, so identical code passed or failed depending on how much Debezium had logged. Evidence copied by hand is evidence nobody can check. `scripts/compose-gate.sh` now runs on every PR and replaces the old job that only built the image. Runners: 2vcpu for the fast checks, 4vcpu for the gate. Debezium's image pulls `debezium-server-dist` from Maven with no layer cache, so the gate is the slow job — the 30 minute timeout is sized for that, not the tests. ## Not in this PR The TypeScript 7 bump itself. 7.0.2 is verified to typecheck clean and emit identical decorator metadata against this layout, so it should be close to a version change — but it is a separate variable and belongs in its own PR.

Greptile Summary

This PR turns `core` into a buildable workspace package and updates `worker` to consume its public package interface rather than its source tree. - Adds shared TypeScript, dependency-catalog, formatting, linting, and Turbo task configuration. - Separates core and worker build outputs and updates Docker, Compose, MikroORM, and runtime entrypoints accordingly. - Replaces the image-only CI job with a full Compose regression gate. - Moves pre-commit handling to Husky and lint-staged.

Confidence Score: 5/5

The PR appears safe to merge based on the reviewed package, build, container, ORM, and CI paths. The workspace dependency graph builds core before worker, the runtime image includes both compiled outputs and production dependencies, and the updated entrypoint and migration paths align with the new emitted layout.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | core/src/index.ts | Adds the package’s public barrel exports and a runtime-relative path to compiled migrations. | | core/package.json | Defines consumable JavaScript and declaration entrypoints and adds a standalone core build task. | | worker/mikro-orm.config.ts | Replaces emitted-tree globs with imported entity classes and the migration path owned by core. | | worker/Dockerfile | Builds workspace dependencies through Turbo and assembles the worker and core package outputs into the runtime image. | | turbo.json | Encodes core-before-worker build ordering and ensures typecheck and test tasks build package dependencies. | | scripts/compose-gate.sh | Adds an end-to-end gate covering baseline replication, downtime, reset behavior, back-pressure recovery, deduplication, and service restarts. | | .github/workflows/build.yml | Moves CI to the shared root tasks and replaces the image-only build with the Compose regression gate. | | tsconfig.base.json | Centralizes Node16 module resolution, ES2022 output, declarations, source maps, and decorator metadata settings. |

Flowchart

```mermaid %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%% flowchart LR Turbo[Turbo task graph] -->|build dependency first| CoreBuild[Build @bemi-db/core] CoreBuild --> CoreDist[core/dist package] CoreDist --> WorkerBuild[Build @bemi-db/worker] WorkerBuild --> WorkerDist[worker/dist] CoreDist --> Image[Worker container image] WorkerDist --> Image Image --> Reset[stream-setup reset.js] Image --> Worker[worker index.js] Reset --> Migrations[Core migration directory] Worker --> ORM[MikroORM entities] Worker --> NATS[NATS JetStream] ``` Reviews (1): Last reviewed commit: ["ci: run the compose regression gate on e..."](https://github.com/ateliahealth/bemi-io/commit/9bd9cce05e261aa5420a3db191d9288740f3f16d) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=51502357)

author: zmanian
body:
Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-trace-withdrawal-design.md`.

## Why

The contributor CLI's consent prompt already tells people they can revoke
submitted traces. There was no endpoint, so the promise was false. It is also
the only honest exit for the traces sitting quarantined for operator privacy
review that nobody has reviewed: today a contributor in that position has no
recourse and no explanation.

## What

`POST /v1/account/traces/{submission_id}/withdraw`, authenticated by the
**account session** rather than the device key -- withdrawal is an
account-level act and should survive losing a device. Tenant-scoped through
the existing RLS predicate; another tenant's id 404s rather than 403s, so
existence is not disclosed. Idempotent.

Three tiers, reported in the response so the client can tell the contributor
the truth rather than a generic success:

| State | What withdrawal does |
|---|---|
| not in the commons | content deleted, nothing was distributed |
| accepted, not used downstream | content deleted, excluded from future exports |
| accepted and already in a published export | deleted and excluded going forward; copies already distributed cannot be recalled, and the API says so |

Credit already awarded is **not** clawed back. Withdrawal is not a punishment,
and treating it as one would deter honest use.

Withdrawal also evicts the trace from the vector index and dedup cluster --
otherwise the content survives in derived form.

## Three things that did not survive contact with the code

1. There is no `submitted` status; the storage enum is
   `Received | Accepted | Quarantined | AwaitingPiiBackstop | ...`, so tier 1
   is "anything not `Accepted`".
2. `trace_commons_record_from_storage_submission` maps `Received` to `None`,
   so the existing account handlers 404 those traces. The withdraw handler
   deliberately works from the storage record instead, or `received` traces
   would be permanently un-withdrawable. A test pins this.
3. The migration took **V43, not V42** -- V42 is held by the unmerged
   `db-authoritative-invites` branch. Wired explicitly into the hand-rolled
   `run_migrations`, into `TRACE_COMMONS_RLS_TABLES`, and into both lists in
   the RLS coverage guard.

## Verification

The DB-backed ingest suite requires `--test-threads=1`; parallel runs are
self-corrupting. Measured serially with `DATABASE_URL` set:

- baseline on untouched `b7dbcd8`: **1366 passed / 104 failed**

author: mrveiss
body:
Closes #13758

## Thinking Path

The issue's hypothesis was that the by-path load causes two module identities of `DeclarativeBase`.
It is simpler and more specific than that: **the test's own stubs are the cause**, and they became the
cause without anyone touching the test.

`_load_slm_role_module` installed a `MagicMock` over `sqlalchemy` (plus a dummy
`user_management.models.base`) before executing the SLM `role.py`. That was correct when `role.py`
*declared ORM classes* — the stubs let the column decorators run without an engine. **#12647 turned
that file into a pure re-export shim**: it now does nothing but

```python
from autobot_shared.user_management.models.role import (SYSTEM_PERMISSIONS, SYSTEM_ROLES, ...)
```

which pulls in `autobot_shared/user_management/models/__init__.py` → `base.py` →
`class Base(AsyncAttrs, DeclarativeBase)` — evaluated against the **mocked** `sqlalchemy`. Two
MagicMock attributes as bases is exactly what `TypeError: metaclass conflict` means. From #12647
onward the stubs were not protecting the load; they were the only thing breaking it.

So the answer to the issue's third acceptance criterion: the by-path load is **not** inherently
unsafe here, and the two `user_management` packages do coexist — because the SLM shim no longer
imports `user_management.*` at all. Verified directly:

```
$ python -c "<load role.py by path, no stubs>; ..."
loaded by path, no stubs: ['Permission', 'Role', 'RolePermission', 'SYSTEM_PERMISSIONS', 'SYSTEM_ROLES', 'UserRole']
SYSTEM_PERMISSIONS is shared object: True
SYSTEM_ROLES is shared object: True
Role is shared Role: True
```

The by-path load is kept rather than replaced with a plain import — it is what proves the SLM shim
itself resolves and that the SLM backend's `user_management` package does not shadow the shared one.

## What Changed

- `autobot_shared/auth/test_slm_permission_parity.py`
  - `_load_slm_role_module` loads the shim with a **real** sqlalchemy; the stub install/restore
    machinery and the now-unused `sys` / `types` / `MagicMock` imports are gone.
  - Two new guards. `test_slm_role_module_re_exports_the_shared_objects` asserts **identity**, not
    equality — nothing else checked that the shim stayed a shim, and if it ever regrew its own copy of
    these constants, the parity tests would keep passing while comparing the copy against itself.
    `test_the_shim_loads_against_a_real_sqlalchemy` asserts `Role` is a real `DeclarativeBase`
    subclass, making the condition that used to fail explicit rather than implied by "it collected".

No production code changed.

## Verification

Collection, the acceptance criterion (before: `1486 tests collected, 1 error` + `Interrupted`):

```
$ venv/bin/python -m pytest autobot_shared/ -q -p no:randomly --collect-only
1496 tests collected in 2.16s
```

Full package:

```
$ venv/bin/python -m pytest autobot_shared/ -q -p no:randomly
1496 passed, 26 warnings in 24.08s
```

**Deliberate-failure check** — the drift detector must still detect drift. Adding a `DIVERGENCE_PROBE`
member to the shared `Permission` enum without seeding it anywhere:

```
FAILED test_every_permission_assigned_to_at_least_one_role
FAILED test_admin_role_contains_all_permissions
FAILED test_slm_admin_role_covers_all_shared_permissions
3 failed, 7 passed
```

Including the SLM-side assertion, so the parity comparison is genuinely live and not passing by
construction. Reverted after the check.

## Model Used

author: zkochan
body:
## Summary

The action verified the release archive against the `digest` GitHub publishes for it. GitHub serves both the asset and the digest, so whoever can replace one can replace the other — that catches a corrupted download, not a tampered one.

The npm registry carries the same executable, **byte for byte**, and npm signs `<name>@<version>:<integrity>` with a key `get-pnpm` pins. That signature can't be produced without npm's private key, and behind it sits the maintainer's approval of the staged publish. **Every version this action installs now comes from the registry**, and is refused unless the signature *and* the checksum both check out.

I verified the executables are identical across both sources before relying on it:

| v12.0.0-rc.1 | GitHub release | npm platform package |
|---|---|---|
| linux-x64 | `f58dff16…` | `f58dff16…` |
| darwin-arm64 | `180f2c62…` | `180f2c62…` |
| win32-x64 (`pnpm.exe`) | `290aac61…` | `290aac61…` |

v11 was going to stay on the release asset, because the registry copy declares `@reflink/reflink` as a dependency where the tarball bundles it, and this action has no step that would install it. That reasoning did not survive testing — an A/B with the dependency present and absent clones either way, and the tarball's bundled copy carries no native binding at all — so v11 comes from the registry too.

That is the more important half: `latest` resolves to v11, so until now the *common* case was the one verified only by GitHub's digest.

## Two things fall out of not touching the GitHub API at all

- **`token` is unused.** It existed to lift the anonymous 60 requests/hour limit on the release lookup, which no longer happens. Kept as a deprecated input so workflows passing it keep working.
- **Versions published to npm without a GitHub release now install**, instead of hitting the "Some prerelease versions are published to npm but not released as downloadable binaries" error this action used to raise.

With no source left that needs it, the release lookup, the asset naming, the sha256 check and the archive extraction are all gone — `download.ts` loses about 200 lines.

## Testing

Every spec form, end to end against the real registry, each one placed and executed:

| input | resolves to | placed |
|---|---|---|
| `next-12` | 12.0.0-rc.1 | `dist, pn, pnpm, pnpx, pnx` |
| `latest` | 11.20.0 | `dist, pn, pnpm, pnpx, pnx` |
| `^11.0.0` | 11.20.0 | `dist, pn, pnpm, pnpx, pnx` |
| `11.20.0` | 11.20.0 | `dist, pn, pnpm, pnpx, pnx` |

The existing smoke matrix covers Ubuntu (x64 + arm), macOS and Windows.

## It uses `get-pnpm` rather than its own copy

The verification first landed here as its own implementation, because the package that does the same thing wasn't published. It is now (`get-pnpm@0.0.1`, from [pnpm/get.pnpm.io](https://github.com/pnpm/get.pnpm.io/tree/main/get-pnpm)), so the second commit deletes ~140 lines and depends on it.

`downloadPnpm` verifies and places the executable and nothing else — it exists precisely so a caller that manages its own directory can use it without the global install and shell-rc editing that `pnpm setup` does. The action keeps what is genuinely its own: version resolution with semver ranges, the alias hardlinks, and PATH.

That also puts the pinned keys in one place. `get.pnpm.io` refreshes them for all three of its installers on a schedule, so a rotation reaches this action as a dependency bump rather than by someone noticing.

`get-pnpm` is excluded from `minimumReleaseAge` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` — pnpm added that itself when I installed a package published minutes earlier. Worth a look if you'd rather wait for it to age instead.

---
Written by an agent (Claude Code, claude-opus-5).

author: tylerbutler-release-bot[bot]
body:
## v0.11.0 - 2026-08-08


### tag

#### Breaking

- **`publish.package_tags` replaces `tag_mode`: list the tags each package gets.** An entry names how much of the version its tag keeps — `exact` (`lat_cli-v1.2.3`, immutable), `major` (`lat_cli-v1`) and `minor` (`lat_cli-v1.2`), both moving. `exact` substitutes into `exact_tag_format`, every series level into `series_tag_format`. During 0.x, `major` is the only way to get a plain `lat_cli-v0`.

  A 1.x package that moved `{name}-v1` under `tag_mode = "series"` now moves `{name}-v1.2`; list `major` to keep the one-part tag. The default is unchanged — `["exact"]`, immutable per-version tags only — so a workspace that configured no tag keys tags exactly as before.

  Each removed key fails the load naming its replacement, rather than being ignored and silently writing different tags:

  ```toml
  tag_format                  → exact_tag_format
  tag_mode = "exact"          → package_tags = ["exact"]
  tag_mode = "series"         → package_tags = ["minor"]
  tag_mode = "both"           → package_tags = ["exact", "minor"]
  tag_mode_overrides          → package_tags_overrides, keyed by member-path glob
  [publish.repository_series] → repository_tag_package, repository_tag_format,
                                repository_tags — all three required together
  ```

#### Fixed

- **A package's series tag no longer follows commits that did not release it.** `tag create` moved a series tag whenever it did not point at `HEAD`, so in a monorepo one package's release force-pushed every other package's series tags onto a commit that never touched them, and a docs-only commit moved all of them. A series tag now moves when its own package's manifest version changes, and a commit that releases nothing reports `every releasable package version is already tagged`.

#### Changed

- **A `series_tag_format` without `{name}` is deprecated, and removed at 1.0.** Dropping `{name}` gave the whole repository one shared series tag, but the template then matches every member, so `trellis ci tag-package` cannot resolve such a tag to a package. `doctor` now warns on the shape whether or not a second package has made it ambiguous, as `workspace_config` rather than `tag_collision`. The tag still moves and releases still work.

  To migrate, restore `{name}` and declare the repository tag instead: `repository_tag_package`, `repository_tag_format`, `repository_tags`. It is repository metadata, so unlike the shared package tag it never resolves through `ci tag-package` or `publish --tag` — keep a `{name}`-ful series tag for anything that routes CI on a tag.

author: chriswong6031-creator
body:
## Incident

The 2026-08-08 weekly deep-dive commit 901282ec209 wrote `site/hk_regime_timeline.json` with **9 trailing inflation nulls (2026-07-28..08-07)** while `data/hk_regime/regime_history.parquet` in the **same tree** carries values on every one of those dates. The nulls crashed the landing hub (consumer null-guard healed in the #5032/#5033 context). `build_hk.py` maps NaN→null honestly — the question was what fed it NaNs, and how one commit came to contradict itself.

## Root cause — three stacked layers

**1. Macro ffill budget undershoots the publication lag** ([hk_inputs.py](engine/hk_inputs.py)). China CPI/PPI prints are stamped on their reference month (June → 2026-06-01) and the next print publishes ~5 weeks after month end (~Aug 9). At `ffill_limit=40` bdays the June stamp ran dry on **exactly 2026-07-28** — the null window's first day. `china_inputs.py` took the 90-bday fix for this exact failure already ("the axes collapsed onto the market-proxy legs"); the HK mirror kept 40 — loud sibling fixed, silent sibling dark.

**2. Weekly ran on a stale workspace cache** ([weekly.yml](.github/workflows/weekly.yml)). `weekly.yml` restored the S&P trio + Russell caches but **never the hk/china constituent-close caches** — on the persistent self-hosted workspace, `build_hk` consumed a weeks-stale leftover `data/hk_breadth/_closes_cache.parquet`, so `infl_basket` (5-bday ffill) was dark over the window too. With all three inflation components NaN, the axis went NaN (wsum=0 → honest NaN). Fingerprint receipts: shipped JSON `i`=0.2 on 07-24/27 matches a dark-basket recompute exactly (committed parquet: 0.0, 3-component); 2019/2022 timeline values match the committed parquet while 2024/2025 drift — a stale ~3y-window cache, not an absent one.

**3. The structural divergence** ([weekly.yml](.github/workflows/weekly.yml) W0b). `hk_run.run()` recomputes the full history and overwrites the parquet in-tree; `build_hk` builds the timeline **from that regeneration**; then the commit step's W0b guard (`git reset -- data/hk_*`) deliberately unstages the parquet while `git add site/` ships the JSON. A degraded recompute therefore ships its artifact and discards its store — the committed tree contradicts itself by construction.

## Fix

- **[engine/store_guard.py](engine/store_guard.py) (new):** `check_coverage_regression` compares the recompute against the store it is about to overwrite and **refuses** (line-start `::warning` + raise) when previously-computed cells go null or the history end moves backwards. `build_hk`/`build_china` already treat an engine raise as skip-pages — last good committed state keeps serving, heals on the next healthy run. `REGIME_ALLOW_COVERAGE_REGRESSION=1` unblocks a legitimate permanent revision (warning still prints). `pending_quad` excluded: its null encodes *no flip pending* (state), not availability — live-fire showed honest recomputes relocate its episodes. Wired into [hk_run.py](engine/hk_run.py) and [china_run.py](engine/china_run.py) (same W0b discard class).
- **[engine/hk_inputs.py](engine/hk_inputs.py):** monthly-macro ffill 40 → 90 bdays (`MACRO_FFILL_LIMIT_BDAYS`), china_inputs parity.
- **[weekly.yml](.github/workflows/weekly.yml):** restore the hk/china breadth caches (asia-close key prefixes; `weekly-`-prefixed save keys so this job's post-run saves can never shadow asia-close's under its own restore prefix), and add both `regime_history.parquet`s to the W0b carve-out — a good weekly recompute now commits parquet + timeline as **one coherent pair** (same THIS-run freshness rationale as the ladder records; the guard bounds the degraded case).

## Receipts

- Cold-cache repro from the committed tree reproduces the exact incident: cpi/ppi die 07-28, `inflation_score` NaN ×9 (2026-07-28..08-07).
- Incident replay (40-bday budget patched back) against the committed parquet: guard **refuses** with `inflation_score: 9 cells (2026-07-28..2026-08-07)` (+ `raw_quad: 9`), store untouched, annotation at line start.
- Post-fix `hk_run.run()`: passes, **0 nulls** in the window even with a cold cache; `china_run.run()` passes and regenerates its parquet byte-identical.
- Tests: [tests/test_store_guard.py](tests/test_store_guard.py) (10 cases incl. line-start annotation law, state-null relocation, end-shrink, escape env), [tests/test_hk_macro_ffill_budget.py](tests/test_hk_macro_ffill_budget.py) (pins the incident calendar: 90 bridges the gap, 40 died on 07-28, budget still expires on a real outage). Downstream sweep: 316 passed, 2 skipped (hk/china suites + every weekly.yml-parsing guard + `test_gh_annotation_line_start`).

## Self-heal

Yes, independently twice over: the next asia-close `build_hk` (Sun ~06-11Z) commits `data/` + `site/` together from a warm cache, and the July CPI print (~Aug 9, stamped 07-01) re-covers the window for any cold build. Current origin/main still serves the 9-null JSON until then; the consumer null-guard holds the hub meanwhile.

author: nickboy
body:
Four commits, split so any one can be reverted alone. Handed off from the scratchpad session's brief; two additions came out of review.

## 1. Untrack `~/.claude/settings.json`, install the shared half instead

It had **two writers** — this repo and Claude Code itself, which rewrites it on `/model`, `/theme` and `/plugin` (hence the nested `enabledPlugins` and `extraKnownMarketplaces` nobody hand-writes). Tracking also published a personal model, effort level and plugin set from a public repo.

Untracking alone would have been a **regression** — bootstrap never touched `.claude`, so a fresh machine would lose the statusline, theme and hooks. `claude-settings-sync` installs only what this repo actually ships (`statusLine`, `theme`, and the two hooks whose scripts are tracked) and never writes `model`, `effortLevel`, `enabledPlugins`, `extraKnownMarketplaces` or `tui`.

**The merge is a union, not an overwrite.** jq's `*` deep-merges objects but *replaces arrays* — a plain `. * $shared` would silently delete any existing Notification/SessionStart hook, which is the exact failure this change exists to prevent. Hook arrays union per event with an order-preserving dedup keyed on `(matcher, sorted commands)`: a stranger's hooks survive, keep their position, and re-runs are idempotent. Malformed JSON fails loudly and leaves the file untouched; the write is temp-then-`mv`.

The herdr SessionStart hook is deliberately **not** injected — herdr generates that script and owns its command and timeout, so a hardcoded copy would restore the two-writers problem and go stale, and a machine without herdr would get `exit 127` every session.

## 2. Statusline: per-machine switches, not a template

Templating would duplicate ~345 lines that are byte-identical on both machines. `SHOW_COST`/`SHOW_BURN`/`SHOW_RATE_LIMITS`/`SHOW_HERDR` default on, overridden from the untracked `~/.config/claude-statusline/config.sh`.

Cost needed restructuring rather than a guard — the 💰 was baked into the final `printf` format string. **No-regression proof:** baseline captured from a real payload, then old and new run in the *same second* (the reset countdown drifts across minutes and false-flags a diff) → byte-identical, 654 bytes.

## 3. Untrack the vendored `obsidian-cli`

A **9.1 MB Mach-O universal binary** of Yakitrak's project was committed here. Not ours to redistribute, and Homebrew already provides it (Brewfile installs the renamed `notesmd-cli` 0.3.6; brew's `obsidian-cli` 0.2.3 is also present — both verified working).

It was **not inert**: `which -a obsidian-cli` resolved the tracked copy *first*, so a frozen February build was shadowing the package-managed one.

## 4. Correct the PATH order in `CLAUDE.md`

The list was inverted. Live order is `~/.cargo/bin` (11) → `~/.local/bin` (12) → `/opt/homebrew/bin` (13), with mise/bob shims ahead of all. This is the file every agent reads first, and the wrong order implies a tracked `~/.local/bin` binary is harmless — which is precisely how #3 went unnoticed.

## Known hazard, documented

Untracking is a **deletion** to git. On every other machine the next pull either stashes the file (if locally modified) or **deletes it** (if clean) — both reproduced in a scratch repo, and `.gitignore` does not protect it. The checklist now carries mandatory pre/post-pull steps: back the file up, then run `claude-settings-sync`.

Suite 132/132, markdownlint clean, shellcheck clean.

author: vitramir
body:
Installing was two charts with a person between them: sign in, authorize the overlay by hand, register the runner through the Console, copy a token shown once into a Secret, then install the second chart. The docs described that sequence in four phases and warned that order mattered.

The release provisions its own resources now, so the sequence is gone. One chart, no operator step inside it, and no ordering to observe — every precondition becomes true at a moment the chart cannot predict, so nothing is sequenced and anything not yet possible is retried.

What replaces the manual phase is a **verification** one: the declarations carry conditions, so a platform that installed without provisioning is visible as objects that are not ready rather than as a job whose logs have to be read. Including the one that surprises people — a declared cluster administrator stays pending until that person first signs in.

Also records the two things an operator now has to know:
- **Naming cluster administrators is the one part of the values they must fill in.** A release that declares none installs a platform nobody can administer.
- **Every bundled dependency is off until they switch it on**, so an upgrade will not deploy a second Postgres behind their back.

Touches `install.md`, `upgrades.md`, `uninstall.md` and the section README. Part of [one-step-install](https://github.com/agynio/architecture/blob/main/changes/2026-08-08-one-step-install.md).

Encerra a subida do #44.

## O workflow sai

Cumpriu as três etapas: apagar o cache na escala antiga (#45), destravar o job de regeneração (#46) e verificar o deploy pela tabela regenerada (#47).

**Verificação, com o resultado real de produção:**

```
regenerate-opportunities | 2026-08-08 23:10:49+00 | sucesso

 category | count |  min  |  max  | media
----------+-------+-------+-------+-------
 acoes    |    63 | 65.00 | 89.00 |  76.0
 fiis     |    36 | 66.00 | 84.00 |  76.7

 bdrs = 0                          <- piso de evidência ativo
 FII: 18 notas distintas em 36      <- eram 3 em 45
```

Topo: BNBR3 89, PETR4 86, PETR3/TAEE4/TAEE3 85, ISAE3/MCRE11/ISAE4 84, DVFF11/TRXF11/MRSA3B 83 — **idêntico ao que a medição local previu**, o que confirma que é o build novo rodando (o #44 não adiciona rota nova, então o teste de 404-vs-401 do `replit.md` não serviria aqui).

## Correções no replit.md

Dois pontos passaram a ser **falsos** com o #44 e foram corrigidos:

- o corte das oportunidades (`score >= 60` → `>= 65`, o piso da faixa Estavel recalibrada);
- o `riskLevel`, que passou a comparar o beta direto — com as curvas interpoladas, `volatility.score >= 85` deixaria de significar o beta 0,7 documentado.

## Registro do que foi aprendido

Três blocos novos: por que a escala antiga não separava nada, por que FII precisa de régua própria, e por que existe um piso de evidência. Cada um com os números medidos, para que a próxima pessoa (ou sessão) não precise redescobrir.

Fica registrado também o **método**: antes de mexer em qualquer limiar, congelar os fundamentos do universo em disco e rodar os dois motores sobre a mesma entrada — foi o que expôs os defeitos de FII e BDR, que já existiam e estavam apenas escondidos pela compressão da escala antiga.

author: damianqnz
body:
PR 3/3 de la auditoría de proxy + arquitectura. Cierra las red lines de i18n del `CLAUDE.md`.

**Balance:** 45 ficheros, +430 / −706.

## Hallazgo que definió el PR

El namespace `booking` **ya existía** en los tres `messages/*.json` — 73 claves, paridad perfecta, espejo exacto de `_i18n/types.ts` — con **cero consumidores**. Alguien migró los datos y nunca recableó los componentes. El trabajo era recableado, no traducción.

## Bugs vivos corregidos

- **`bookT()` caía a castellano siendo `DEFAULT_LOCALE = 'pt'`.** Un tenant portugués veía el funnel de reserva en español.
- **`domains/billing/service.ts:51`** tenía `locale = 'es'` como parámetro por defecto: servía nombres de servicio en castellano a tenants PT **vía Stripe Checkout**.

## Cambios

- Elimina `(tenant)/[tenant]/book/_i18n/` — 5 ficheros, 481 L. Los 9 consumidores pasan a `useTranslations('booking')` / `getTranslations('booking')`.
- Sustituye el hack `format()` basado en `.replace()` por ICU MessageFormat nativo.
- Añade `calendar.months.*` y `calendar.days.*` como **claves con nombre** (19), nunca arrays indexados. `Step2Calendar` reconstruye el orden posicional con `MONTH_KEYS`/`DAY_KEYS` locales.
- Monta `NextIntlClientProvider` en `ConsumerShell`, que pasa a `async` y resuelve `getMessages()` internamente — así ningún root layout puede olvidarlo. Envuelve `children` **y** el `<Toaster>`.
- Erradica fallbacks literales de locale en 24 sitios. Donde el valor viene de cabecera usa `localeFromHeader()`: además de defaultear, **valida** — una cabecera manipulada ya no fluye como locale espurio.
- Cubre una **segunda forma sintáctica** de la misma red line, invisible al regex `?? 'pt'`: parámetros por defecto (`locale = 'es'`). 5 sitios.
- Extrae `toIntlTag()` a `src/i18n/intl-tag.ts` y deduplica la copia inline de `success/page.tsx`.
- `PublicHeader`: `BOOK_LABEL` y `SECTIONS.label` (mapas i18n inline) migrados a `tenant.header.*`. El hack `(locale as ...) in { pt: 1 }` sustituido por `isSupportedLocale`.

## Validation Gate

- `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0
- `npm run build` → exit 0, 30 rutas intactas
- Paridad de claves **836 = 836 = 836**, missing 0 / extra 0
- `rg "_i18n"` → sin resultados de módulo (solo colisiones de substring con las columnas Drizzle `nameI18n` / `descriptionI18n`)

## Deuda NO abordada aquí (ticketada)

El review automático marca 7 violaciones. **Las 7 son preexistentes** — el propio review lo admite en cada una ("The PR's only change is X"). Se dejan fuera deliberadamente para no mezclar deuda histórica con este cambio:

- **A11Y-01** — `(dashboard)/layout.tsx:116` tiene `<html lang="es">` hardcodeado siendo `DEFAULT_LOCALE = 'pt'` (WCAG 3.1.1). No es un one-liner: `locale` se resuelve en la línea 41 dentro de `DashboardShell`, que vive en `<Suspense>` porque `cacheComponents` de Next 16 rechaza datos de request en el layout externo cacheable. Convertirlo a `async` es cambio arquitectónico de caching.
- **I18N-04** — copy hardcodeado en `book/success/page.tsx`, `me/citas/page.tsx`, `export-customers.ts` (`STATUS_LABELS`), `NewAppointmentForm.tsx` (cobertura i18n cero) y `AppointmentDetailModal.tsx` (mapa `SC`).
- **PR 4** — deduplicar las 14 copias de `INTL_LOCALE_MAP` contra `@/i18n/intl-tag`; migrar `NAV_LABELS`, `SIDEBAR_LABELS`, `UserMenu.COPY`, `week-utils`, `MonthView`, `MobileWeekDaySelector`.

## Nota de tooling

El hook `pre-commit` pasa de `gga run` a `gga run --pr-mode --diff-only`. `run` a secas revisa el **contenido íntegro** de cada fichero staged, así que tocar una línea en un fichero con deuda vieja devolvía esa deuda entera como bloqueante (28 hallazgos / 12 ficheros, todos preexistentes). PR mode revisa el diff de rama contra base.

author: mattgodbolt
body:
Found while looking for a 40 track ADFS disc to test #775's work against.

`knownDiscExtensions` in `src/utils.js` lists `uef`, `ssd`, `dsd` and `adl`, but not `adf` or `adm`. `guessDiscTypeFromName` handles all of them and `loadAdf` reads them fine, so the only thing standing between an archived ADFS disc and the emulator was the list the zip reader checks:

> Couldn't find any compatible files in the archive

That is every one of the 23 ADFS discs in the Stairway to Hell Electron collection, the Welcome disc included. Fixed, and all 23 unzip now. A zip test alongside the existing SSD and ROM ones covers it.

Also here, since it is what sent me looking:

```js
const AdfsSmallByteSize = 80 * 16 * 256;   // 327680, which is 320K
```

That is ADFS **M**. S is 40 tracks on one side and half the size; M is 80 on one side; L is 80 on both. The constant is used as the size of a blank `.adf` or `.adm`, where the M size is the right answer, so only the name was wrong. Renamed, with the three sizes written down next to it.

## Note on `sth:`

This is not the whole story for the archive. `StairwayToHell.fetch` throws away the name of the file it unzipped (#795), so an ADFS disc from `sth:` will now unzip and then be loaded as an SSD. Both need fixing for `?disc1=sth:...ADFS...` to work; this one is the half that stops the file being found at all, and it fixes local zips and `http://` zips on its own.

## And a negative result worth recording

The reason I was in here was to detect 40 track ADFS (ADFS S) the way #791 detects 40 track DFS. Of the 23 real ADFS images: 22 are M and one is L. **None is S.** Two are worth knowing about: `Plus3GamesDisc` is 160K on disc, exactly the S size, but its free space map claims 1280 sectors, so it is a truncated M; `LazerChess` is 21K and claims the same. Size would have called both of those 40 track. The map does not.

So ADFS S detection is speculative: the rule would be sound (S is 640 sectors at offset 0xFC of sector 0, three bytes little endian, and nothing else is), but no disc I can find needs it. I have left it undone rather than ship a rule with no example behind it. #799 covers ADFS held in a flux image, since the surface sniff there reads sector headers and asks nothing about the filesystem.

author: breezenash24-droid
body:
Stacks on fix/popup-polish — merge that first.

── A welcome email when someone signs up ───────────────────────────────

A code on screen is gone the moment the tab closes. With the toggle on (Marketing → Email Popup → The discount → Welcome email) the code is emailed too, which also puts you in their inbox on day one.

Two surfaces, one owner each, so neither can drift from the other: whether it sends is the popup's business and lives in the popup config; the wording is the Emails section's business and lives in email_settings.popup_welcome, editable at Appearance → Emails → "Email popup welcome" alongside every other email. It goes through the same theme, shell and log as the rest, so it inherits your fonts, colours and logo instead of being a one-off that drifts from them.

{code} and {discount} are the placeholders. Both are empty when the popup is collecting emails without an offer — the default wording reads correctly either way, and with no code the code block is not drawn.

It sends in the background via waitUntil: the shopper already has the code on screen, so making them wait on a mail provider would be the tail wagging the dog, and an outage cannot fail a good signup. Every send is logged, success or failure — a welcome email that silently never sends is exactly the sort of thing nobody notices for months.

── Unpublished landing pages are no longer public ──────────────────────

'landing_pages' is the DRAFT half of the landing pair and it was in the anon read allow-list, so anyone could fetch unpublished pages straight from the REST API. No guessing was needed: the key name ships in the JavaScript.

Nothing actually needed that. landing.js now always asks for the published key; the builder's own preview pane never depended on the read anyway — it gets its config pushed over postMessage, which is the live in-editor state and fresher than the saved draft; and the admin preview link supplies drafts through /api/preview-config, which verifies a signed token and reads with the service key.

That closes the route through the site. The direct-API route needs the policy changed, which is supabase-hide-drafts.sql — and unlike the other SQL here, the application cannot work around this one. As long as the policy lists 'landing_pages', the REST endpoint hands unpublished content to anyone who asks. It is worth running.

All four existing allow-list files were updated to the same new canonical list, so whichever gets run produces the same policy — caught by the CI guard added earlier, which failed the moment the lists diverged and is exactly why it exists.

── Verification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

239 tests. New: the welcome email (off by default, non-boolean does not enable it, placeholders filled, code in the body, no code block in email-only mode, every send logged, sending never blocks the response) and the draft-privacy change (the key appears nowhere in landing.js's code, the builder pane still works, the SQL drops the right key and keeps the published one).

Closes #328.

The workflow described local advisory review prompts but had no accepted contract for independent evidence, two-phase timing, unavailable reviewer behavior, or deterministic scope checks.

author: trexkalp
body:
Adds the live broadcast layer and moves the book to shared Postgres so we both see the same markets.

## The channel

`/live`, and a Live tab in the nav. A rolling markets channel: an anchor with native lip-synced audio, voice-over over live charts, segment stings, and breaking interrupts driven by real price swings.

It reads the engine only through `GET /api/markets`, `/api/markets/:id/history` and the `/events` SSE feed — the seam the README asks for. **It never writes to the book.** Everything lives under `src/broadcast/`, and it is gated behind `BROADCAST=1`, so `npm run dev` behaves exactly as before unless you opt in. That matters because it generates video and costs money.

Segments: the tape, karma check, lightning round, where it came from, crossfire, long shot, resolution watch, final trades, and teases. Only the opening beat of most segments renders as video (~20s); the rest are voice-over (~3-6s), so spend stays proportional.

## SQLite → Neon

`DATABASE_URL` is now required and `DATABASE_PATH` is gone. `PostgresStore` mirrors `SqliteStore` method for method — same validation, same errors, same ordering — but async, since no synchronous Postgres driver exists.

Money movement runs in a transaction on **one pooled client**, and reads inside a transaction use that client. Otherwise the balance checks see pre-transaction state. That race did not exist against a local file and does against a shared database.

SQLite stays for the in-memory unit tests only. Running those against the shared book would be slow and would let a test mutate live data.

## A bug class worth knowing about

Converting the call sites surfaced something TypeScript cannot catch: routes that pass store results straight into `response.json()` type-check fine while serialising a **Promise** to `{}`. There were nine. The history route did exactly that, and the broadcast then crashed the whole server on `.map` of a non-array. All nine now await, and the renderer guards the shape rather than trusting it.

The same trap is waiting in any new route — `response.json()` takes `any`.

## Sign in with X

A button in the nav, showing the linked handle once signed in.

It points at `/auth/x/connect/start`, **not** `/auth/x/start`. The latter is `startBot()`; as a public login it would let any visitor authorise themselves as the market bot and overwrite its stored credentials.

## Also

- `/markets` renders the index. It 404'd while `/markets/:id` resolved, which reads as broken.
- Charts use the real series from `/api/markets/:id/history`.

## Verified

`/` `/markets` `/live` all 200, `/auth/x/connect/start` 302, all 5 tests pass, zero runtime errors. Against Neon: buys move price 93.0% → 26.7%, balances debit exactly, positions and history persist, and the overspend guard still returns `INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE`.

## Before merging

This replaces the database layer, so **you will need `DATABASE_URL` set** — your local SQLite data will not carry over. Worth coordinating, since `sqlite-store.ts` is a file you have been actively editing.

| Insight   | Capture sessions created (wizard)        | https://eu.posthog.com/project/244134/insights/7JRiBWNp               |
| Insight   | Workspace exports (wizard)               | https://eu.posthog.com/project/244134/insights/PSG5mESj               |

The wizard also published a full setup report as a PostHog notebook: [PostHog setup (wizard) – voice-workspaces](https://eu.posthog.com/project/244134/notebooks/CormDTMs).

## How to verify

1. Deploy this branch (after setting the environment variables below), or run it locally with `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` set in `apps/web/.env`.
2. Sign in, start and stop a recording, export a workspace topic, and sign out.
3. In PostHog, check [Activity](https://eu.posthog.com/project/244134/activity/explore) — you should see `recording_started`, `recording_stopped`, `workspace_exported`, `capture_session_created`, and `capture_session_closed` events arriving, attributed to your identified user.
4. Open the [Analytics basics (wizard) dashboard](https://eu.posthog.com/project/244134/dashboard/884287) — the five insights should start populating once traffic arrives.

## Environment variables

Production is deployed via **Coolify**, which builds and runs `docker-compose.prod.yml`. Every other secret in this app (`DATABASE_URL`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, etc.) follows the same pattern: the compose file only declares `${VAR}` references, and the actual values live in Coolify's own environment variable settings for this resource — nothing with real values is committed to this repo.

The PostHog variables need one extra wrinkle: `NEXT_PUBLIC_...` variables are baked into the browser bundle at *build* time, not read at container start. So a plain runtime env var wouldn't reach the client bundle. This PR's second commit wires that up automatically:

- `apps/web/Dockerfile` now declares `ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN` / `ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` and sets them as `ENV` before the `next build` step.
- `docker-compose.prod.yml` passes them through to the build as `args:` on the `web` service, sourced from `${NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN}` / `${NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST}`.

**Action still needed:** the actual values need to be added to this app's environment variables in the Coolify dashboard (the same place `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` and friends already live) — I can't set those from this repo. Environment variables are just named settings your hosting provider passes in when it builds/runs the app, so it can use real values (like the token below) without them being hardcoded in the code.

| Name                                | Value                          |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN`  | `phc_wawrMVDGDv4WLxA9YPxLwBiuK6E9MQyUsy6QTzwAutYB` |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST`           | `https://eu.i.posthog.com`     |

To set them in Coolify:

1. Open the Coolify dashboard and go to this app's resource.
2. Go to the **Environment Variables** tab.
3. Add both rows above (mark them as build-time/available-at-buildtime if Coolify distinguishes that).
4. Redeploy — the next build will pick them up and PostHog will start receiving events.

## CI

This repository has no `.github/workflows` (no CI configured), so there are no automated checks to wait on for this PR. Locally, `pnpm build` and `pnpm typecheck` both pass with these changes. `pnpm lint` fails, but that's pre-existing and unrelated — `apps/web`'s `lint` script calls `next lint`, which Next.js 16 removed (verified by running it against `main` before this branch's changes).

author: edrees
body:
## Summary
Fixes an N+1 client-side fetch pattern where every FavoriteButton instance on a page independently fetched the entire favorites list, causing dozens of duplicate /api/favorites requests per page load for logged-in users.

## Root cause
FavoriteButton.tsx called fetch('/api/favorites') inside its own useEffect on mount to determine whether its specific tool was favorited. Since tool listing pages render one FavoriteButton per tool card (up to ~100 on some pages), this meant one full favorites-list fetch per card, all firing near-simultaneously. Vercel logs confirmed this: a single real logged-in user browsing a listing page produced ~90+ /api/favorites requests within a 27-second window, all from the same session/browser.

## Changes
- src/context/FavoritesContext.tsx (new) — fetches the favorites list once per session/page load, exposes a shared favoritesMap (toolId -> favoriteId) and a refetch() function via React context
- src/theme/ThemeRegistry.tsx — wraps the app in FavoritesProvider, nested inside SessionProvider (context depends on useSession)
- src/components/tool/FavoriteButton.tsx — removed its own fetch/useEffect entirely; now reads favorited state from useFavorites() context, computed directly during render instead of via effect-derived state. Click handler still performs its own POST/DELETE for the actual favorite/unfavorite action, then calls refetch() to resync the shared map

## Scope
- Client-side favorites-check fetching only. The favorite/unfavorite POST and DELETE actions themselves are unchanged.

## Not in scope
- src/components/dashboard/FavoritesList.tsx — has its own separate /api/favorites fetch for the dashboard's full list view; not yet migrated to use the shared context. Candidate for a follow-up.

## Testing
- [ ] Log in and visit /ai-tools with many tools visible — confirm only one /api/favorites request fires (check Network tab), not one per card
- [ ] Confirm favorite/unfavorite toggle still works correctly and updates the icon immediately
- [ ] Confirm favorited state persists correctly across different pages/cards showing the same tool (e.g. featured tools + main listing)
- [ ] Confirm logged-out users see no /api/favorites calls and buttons default to unfavorited, redirecting to /login on click
- [ ] Confirm no ESLint/build warnings remain (react-hooks/set-state-in-effect)
